<meta>This page follows the dedication to Achilles de Harlay. ### *Extract from the King’s Privilege.*

**B**y the grace and privilege of the King, permission is granted to Abel l’Angelier, Sworn Bookseller of the University of Paris <note>A "Sworn Bookseller" (Libraire Juré) was a prestigious rank of publisher officially recognized and regulated by the University and the Crown.</note>, to print or have printed the present book entitled *The Continuation of Philostratus’s Descriptions, translated from Greek into French by Blaise de Vigenère* <note>Philostratus was a 3rd-century Greek sophist; his "Descriptions" (Imagines) described a series of paintings. Blaise de Vigenère was a renowned French diplomat and scholar whose translations were highly influential in the development of French prose.</note>: And very express prohibitions are made to all other booksellers and printers against printing or selling the said book without the consent of the said l’Angelier, for a period and term of ten years, under penalty of a fine of one thousand *écus* <term>écus</term> <note>The écu was a gold or silver coin; a fine of 1,000 was an enormous sum, intended to be a powerful deterrent against piracy.</note>, namely: five hundred *écus* to the King, two hundred and fifty *écus* to the poor, and the remainder to the petitioner <note>The "petitioner" (suppliant) refers to the publisher, Abel l'Angelier.</note>, as well as the confiscation of all books that may be found. Furthermore, we wish that this present Extract of the Privilege, being recounted in this book, shall be duly notified to all booksellers and printers of this Kingdom, as is more fully declared in the King’s letters patent. Given at Paris, February 22, 1597.

BY THE KING

->Signed Ruze.<- <note>Martin Ruzé, Seigneur de Beaulieu, was a Secretary of State under Kings Henry III and Henry IV; his signature validated royal documents.</note>

### *The Images or Tableaux of <term>flat painting</term> by Philostratus the Younger.* <note>The term "flat painting" (original: "platte peinture") refers to two-dimensional painting on panels or canvas, as opposed to sculpture or architectural relief. ### PREFACE.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter "N" decorated with a human figure, possibly a classical or mythological character, entwined with elaborate foliage and scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>

Let us not take away from the arts and sciences their perpetual duration by considering <term>antiquity</term> <note>In this context, "antiquity" refers to the classical Greek and Roman era, which Renaissance thinkers both admired and sought to compete with.</note> so terrifying at first glance that it cannot be overcome: in such a way that if something has already been achieved by the ancients who preceded us, we must abstain from it in all respects, without it being permissible to imitate it; masking our fearful cowardice under a noble pretext. On the contrary, we should rather insist on surpassing them ourselves; for by reaching the goal of our intention, we shall do something commendable. And if it happens that we commit some fault therein, at least that <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the thought continues on the following page.</note>

->### PREFACE.<-

it will appear praiseworthy that we have set for ourselves a goal of glorious imitation. But why is it necessary to say this at the outset? Because those of my lineage, and even my maternal grandfather <note>The author, Philostratus the Younger, is referring to his grandfather, Philostratus the Elder, who authored the first famous book of "Images" (descriptions of paintings) in the 3rd century CE.</note>, made it a special point to describe works of <term>flat painting</term> <note>original: "platte-peinture"; this refers to two-dimensional painting on panels or canvas, as distinct from sculpture.</note>; a pursuit most suitable and fitting for the <term>Attic tongue</term> <note>original: "langue attique"; the Attic dialect of Greek was prized by Renaissance scholars for its elegance, clarity, and philosophical precision.</note>, arising from an occasion that was highly esteemed at the time, having been undertaken spontaneously and elegantly pursued through <term>scholarly discourse</term> <note>original: "conference"; a formal discussion or lecture.</note> and debate. 

If we wish to follow in those footsteps, it will be necessary, before we venture to undertake anything, to touch upon the general principles of painting in passing. This will ensure that our discourse has its own proper foundation, one that is appropriate to the specific subjects when we come to treat them individually. This is the best instruction one could propose, and it is of no small importance. For it is essential that anyone wishing to prove themselves worthy of this art must know—as a master knows his principles—the exact <term>anatomy</term>, which constitutes the nature and <term>workmanship of man</term> <note>original: "fabrique de l'homme"; a term used in the Renaissance to describe the complex biological and mechanical design of the human body.</note>. 

Furthermore, he must be quick and discerning in identifying how outward appearances reflect the internal state <note>original: "conditions interieures"</note> of every person, even when they are silent; and he must recognize what is revealed in the disposition of

He, therefore, who knows how to properly conceive all this in his mind, will have a hand fit and capable of representing all sorts of characters <term>personages</term> <note>original: "personages"; here referring to the figures or types of people depicted in a painting.</note>, such as a madman and a fury; an angry man; one who is calm and in his right mind; one who is gay and joyful; one moved by emotion; one possessed by the spirit of love; and finally, he will be able to well portray <term>portraire</term> <note>original: "portraire"; an archaic term for "to depict," "to draw," or "to represent."</note> whatever is appropriate for each of them. For to attach oneself to things that do not exist, just as if they were real, and to let oneself be transported by them, believing them to exist—since no harm can come to you from it—how is it that you would not rightly receive some satisfaction from it without being rebuked?

### A N N O T A T I O N .

*The **YOUNGER** Philostratus <note>Philostratus of Lemnos, known as "the Younger" to distinguish him from his grandfather, the author of the first two books of "Images."</note>, author of the seventeen subsequent paintings, was the son of the daughter of the one who wrote those of the two books above, as he himself testifies in this preface; I have been unable to find anything else of him anywhere, except what we have brought from **Suidas** <note>original: "Suidas"; now commonly known as the **Suda**, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> at the beginning of the first book. He follows, moreover, in the footsteps <note>original: "brisées"; a hunting term referring to broken branches used to mark a trail. Here, it means following a stylistic or intellectual path.</note> of his grandfather, who was the second of this name; and he strives to imitate him step by step, as much in his inventions as in the elegance of his **Atticism** <term>Atticism</term> <note>A style of Greek rhetoric and writing that mimicked the pure, classical language of 5th-century BCE Athens, avoiding the perceived "corruption" of later eras.</note>, to which they are entirely devoted—even with affectation, in the manner of the **Sophists** <term>Sophists</term> <note>In this context, professional rhetoricians and teachers in the Roman Empire who prized stylistic brilliance and performative oratory.</note>; but this one much more than the other. Furthermore, he is far more constrained, purposely trying to obscure his meaning so as not to be understood at first glance, in order to make himself be read more than once: for he seeks out ambiguous words, equivocations, and those which have diverse meanings, some even contrary to one another. And he goes so far as to dig up certain passages from ancient poems—those least common and well-worn—from which he weaves a context difficult to unravel. In short, he is very rough in several places; added to this is the depravity of the copies, which are constantly corrupted in the Greek: a fact which may have discouraged many from setting their hand to it. Therefore, let us be forgiven if we have been constrained most of the time to proceed as if blind and by touch; and since he is ordinarily very concise and cuts himself short with half-words in his sentences, we have added something at times to give a clearer understanding to the readers.*

The Greeks likewise on their side had three other conditions to fulfill to succeed in their enterprise: for they specifically had to capture the enchanted horses of Rhesus, King of Thrace, before they had drunk from the river Scamander, otherwise known as the Xanthus—which Diomedes and Ulysses executed, as is written in the 10th book of the *Iliad* and the 13th of Ovid's *Metamorphoses*. Afterwards, they had to obtain the arrows of Hercules, which Philoctetes had in his keeping; to which the same Ulysses was deputed, as will be more fully explained hereafter in the painting of the said Philoctetes. Thirdly, that they should have with them one of...

*Scyros is named thus for the stone fragments and shards with which it is scattered, much like the chips that come off marble and other such hard stones when they are carved; for the word <term>Σκύρος: Skyros (Greek), meaning "stone" or "rubble"</term> signifies this. It was formerly called Syphnus, Meropee, and Acis; anciently inhabited by the <term>Pelasgians: an ancestral group of people who preceded the Hellenes in Greece</term> and the <term>Carians</term>, according to Stephanus in his book on cities. The same Pliny (Book 36, Chapter 17) recounts a strange marvel about it: that the stones of this island float in water when they are whole, but sink to the bottom when ground into powder. This is the characteristic of pumice stone, which does the same thing without needing to seek out a miracle further afield: for the natural reason is quite apparent, since the pumice stone that the Latins call <term>Pumex</term> and the Greeks <term>κίσηρις: kisēris</term>—a word also similar to <term>Σκύρος</term>—he also notes in Chapter 21 that the excellent pumice stones used, according to Catullus <note>Gaius Valerius Catullus, a Roman poet who mentions using pumice to smooth parchment or skin.</note>, to polish the skin and make it softer to the touch, were found on the islands of Scyros, Melos, and the Aeolians. <header>A C H I L L E S</header>

Lycomedes and Deidameia. <note>Lycomedes was the King of Scyros; Deidameia was his daughter and the mother of Achilles' son, Neoptolemus.</note> This is what the artistry of this painting, rendered in such a small scale, wishes to teach us; it is represented here just as it provided the poets with a subject for their writing.

# ANNOTATION.

*Scyros* is so named because of the stone chips and rocky plateaus with which it is strewn, much like the scales that come off marble and other such hard stones when they are carved, for the word <term>Scyros</term> <note>original Greek: "Σκύρος," likely related to "skyros" meaning stone chippings or debris.</note> implies this. Furthermore, it is an island in the archipelago or Aegean Sea, situated almost directly opposite the mainland of Ionia, halfway between Negropont <note>The medieval name for the Greek island of Euboea.</note> and Mytilene, <note>The main city of the island of Lesbos.</note> having a city of the same name. It is numbered among the fifty-three islands called the <term>Cyclades</term>, as Pliny records in Book 4, Chapter 12, where he states it measures some seven or eight leagues in circumference. In ancient times, it was called Syphnus, Meropee, and Acis, and was formerly inhabited by the Pelasgians and the Carians, according to Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary of names.</note> in his *Book of Cities*. But because it is very flat, allowing the winds to blow freely from all sides, this may have moved Sophocles to give it the epithet <term>windy</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀνεμώδης" (anemōdēs).</note>. The same Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 17, recounts a strange marvel concerning it: that the stones of this island float on the water when whole, but when reduced to powder, they sink to the bottom. This is the specific property of the pumice stone, which performs this same miracle without having to look further afield for an explanation. The natural reason for it is quite apparent, especially since the pumice stone—which the Latins call <term>Pumex</term> and the Greeks <term>kiseris</term> <note>original Greek: "κίσηρις."</note>, a word similar to *Scyros*—is mentioned by Pliny in Chapter 21. He notes that the excellent pumice stones used (according to the poet Catullus) to polish the skin and make it softer to the touch, were found on the islands of Scyros, Melos, and the Aeolians. The pumice, then, in its whole state being very rare and spongy, with many holes and cavities where there is trapped much—*

# ACHILLES

...creations of earth <note>original Greek: πλάσματα (*plasmata*), meaning things formed or molded</note>, or works of clay; and perhaps this is what the Apostle meant in Romans 9, saying: *Does the potter not have power over the clay, to make from the same mass one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?* What is said afterward—that **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods.</note> wished to meddle with **Thetis** but was diverted by the warning of **Prometheus**, for fear that he would father a child by her who would be greater and more famous than himself (as the Fates had decreed) and who would drive him from his kingdom just as he had done to his father **Saturn**—this denotes that **Jupiter**, who is taken to represent fire (for **Zeus** <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς</note>, which signifies Jupiter, comes from a word meaning "to boil" or "to heat" <note>original Greek: ζέω (*zeo*)</note>), would be extinguished if he mixed with water. Furthermore, at the wedding of **Peleus** and **Thetis**, **Discord** alone was not invited; this is because in the generation of a human being, there must be no discord among the elements, such as might exist between fire and water, which cannot immediately endure one another. Thus, **Peleus**, or the earth, represents the flesh and the bones; **Thetis** represents the water or the humors; and **Jupiter**, who is the fire or natural heat, joins and binds them together in the generation of the creature, and by warming them, he animates and gives them life. For the soul, according to the greater part of the philosophers, is of the nature of fire.

**Discord**, therefore, not having been invited to these nuptials, arrives unbidden to serve a dish of her own making: this is the **golden apple**, which is taken to represent covetousness, because in a golden apple there is nothing but the sight of it, and nothing to taste. This closely resembles what **Moses** touches upon in *Genesis*: that the apple by which the serpent or the devil (who is **Discord**) seduced our first parents into eating, had been prohibited to them by the Creator; yet they tasted it against his command.

All the other gods had been invited there; for the Pagans attributed each limb and principal part of man to one of them: such as the head to **Jupiter**, the eyes to **Mercury**, and the arms to **Juno**, for which reason **Homer** usually gives her the epithet "white-armed" <note>original Greek: λευκώλενος (*leukolenos*)</note>, because of the transparent clarity of the air she represents. He notes **Minerva** <note>Goddess of wisdom and war, known as Athena to the Greeks.</note> principally by her eyes, calling her "bright-eyed" <note>original Greek: γλαυκῶπις (*glaukopis*), often translated as owl-eyed or gleaming-eyed</note>; the chest to **Neptune**, and the heat of the body to **Mars**—all of which **Homer** likewise touched upon in these verses:

# MARSYAS.

## ARGUMENT.

<image-desc>A large rectangular woodcut decorative initial letter M featuring leafy vines and floral patterns.</image-desc>MINERVA, they say, was the first who invented flutes and oboes <note>The original French 'haultbois' refers to the shawm or early oboe, a loud wind instrument.</note> from a deer bone which she fashioned into this instrument; having taken it upon herself to want to play it at a feast held by the gods, *Juno* and *Venus*, seeing her thus with her cat-like eyes—green and grayish—puffing out her cheeks when she blew to sound them, began to laugh. Wherefore, out of spite, she went to a fountain on Mount *Ida*, where, having gazed at herself in the water playing in the same way, she found that they had rightly mocked her, and she threw her flutes away in great anger; cursing with cruel execrations <note>Solemn curses or denunciations.</note> whoever might pick them up, and devoting them to a most severe punishment. By chance thereafter, a certain shepherd named *Marsyas*, son of *Oeagrus* and one of the *Satyres*, found them, and by practicing incessantly, he improved to such a degree that he dared to challenge *Apollo* regarding the superiority of his oboe over his lyre. Thereupon the Muses were, by common accord, chosen as judges and arbiters of the dispute; they were already hesitating whether to award the prize to *Marsyas*, when *Apollo* began to sing, accompanying the instrument with his voice, whereby he added such grace that *Marsyas*, unable to do the same, remained defeated. And *Apollo*, having tied him to a *Plane tree*, had him flayed and dismembered into small pieces by a *Scythian* <note>In classical art, a Scythian slave is often depicted sharpening the knife for Marsyas's punishment.</note> who was passing by; then he gave him to be buried by one of his disciples named *Olympus*. From his blood, a small river was formed, which since then was called the *Marsyas* after his name. This is how *Hyginus* <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Latin author of the 1st century AD known for his 'Fabulae' or mythological stories.</note> recounts it in the 165th of his mythological narratives; and some others recount it differently, but it all comes to the same conclusion.

...Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note> relates in his *Description of Greece* (within the book on Phocis <note>original: "Phocaiques," referring to Book 10 of Pausanias's work</note>) that after Silenus <note>In many accounts, Marsyas is identified as a Silenus, a forest spirit or companion of Dionysus.</note> had been defeated by Apollo in the competition of their instruments, his flutes were thrown by the god, in a fit of spite, into the river Marsyas. This river carried them downstream into the Meander, where its waters flow. There, upon the bank, a shepherd found them and dedicated them within a temple of Apollo located nearby. By the passage of time, a musician named Saccadas <note>A famous musician from Argos known for his performances at the Pythian Games.</note> became the first of all to play them during the Pythian Games <note>One of the four Panhellenic Games of Ancient Greece, held in honor of Apollo at Delphi.</note> celebrated in honor of Apollo. This act was the reason for the god to finally appease the wrath he had conceived toward all those who made a profession of playing <term>cornets</term> <note>A curved woodwind instrument, common in the Renaissance, not to be confused with the modern brass cornet.</note>, flutes, <term>hautboys</term> <note>original: "haulbois," an early form of the oboe.</note>, and <term>shawms</term> <note>original: "chalumeaux," a single-reed woodwind instrument.</note>, and similar wind instruments, because of the presumption Marsyas had shown in challenging him. Furthermore, in the book on Attica <note>original: "és attiques," referring to Book 1 of Pausanias.</note>, mention is made of a statue of Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena.</note> striking Marsyas for having retrieved the flutes that she herself had cast away, despite her aforementioned <term>commination</term> <note>A formal threat of punishment or divine vengeance.</note>. This serves only to demonstrate the punishment that this unfortunate creature incurred, following the curse of the goddess. Fulgentius and Palaephatus <note>Ancient authors known for their allegorical interpretations of myths.</note> offer some allegory or other regarding this fable concerning the laws and rules of music, but that subject has already been touched upon in the descriptions <note>original: "Tableaux," literally 'pictures' or 'paintings,' referring to previous chapters in this work.</note> cited above. Diodorus and Eusebius, in his *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: "preparation euangelique," a work of Christian apologetics by Eusebius of Caesarea.</note>, seem to attribute this contest between Apollo and Marsyas to a certain jealousy they felt for the goddess Cybele, with whom they were both in love; but leaving them both behind, she gave herself to Attis <note>original: "Atys."</note>.

## ANNOTATION.

Achelous is a river having its sources in Mount *Pindus* in *Perrhaebia* <note>An ancient district in northern Thessaly, Greece.</note>; and from there it comes to cross *Acarnania* which it separates from *Aetolia* according to *Pliny, Book 4, Chapter 1.* Then finally it empties through two branches into the *Corinthian* Gulf, and *Strabo, Book 9* [mentions it] joining the Island of *Artemita* <note>Modern-day Echinades islands that were eventually connected to the mainland by sediment.</note> to the mainland by the constant silt that it carries. He says the same of the *Echinades; Book 2, Chapter 87.* And *Statius* in the 2nd book of the *Thebaid*: *Turbid Achelous leaves behind the opposing Echinades.* <note>original: "Turbidus obiectas Achelous Echinadas exit."</note> It was previously called *Thoas*, as *Stephanus* claims in his book of cities; also *Thestius*, and *Axenus*; and *Acarnanas*, named by the inhabitants of those parts. Then at last it took this name from one *Achelous* who came from *Thessaly* to settle in those quarters with *Alcmaeon*, son of *Amphiaraus*, who killed his mother *Eriphyle* <note>A famous tragic story; Alcmaeon killed his mother because she had betrayed his father for a necklace.</note>. Today, in the common tongue, it is called *Aspropotamo* <note>meaning "White River"; original: "Aspri"</note>, and according to others *Catochi*, and *Gerombea*. Between it and the *Nestus*, a river of *Thrace*, *Lions* are produced, and in no other place in *Europe*—fiercer, more cruel and powerful than those of *Africa* or *Asia*, according to the same *Pliny, Book 8, Chapter 16.* And in Book *37, Chapter 10*, he notes that within it is produced the stone called *galactites* <term>milk-stone: a stone traditionally believed to have the color of milk and various medicinal properties</term>, the color of milk, which when hung around the neck of...

# AND ACHELOUS.

...nursing mothers, it increases the milk in their breasts. In small children, it provokes saliva if their mouths are too dry; for the water melts there if it is held for a short time, though it is said to dull the memory. He was the son, according to the *Poets*, of Ocean and Earth—or of *Thetis*, as *Servius* <note>A 4th-century Grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> maintains, who makes him the father of the *Sirens*, with the Muse *Calliope* being their mother. They were three in number: *Parthenope*, *Leucosia*, and *Ligeia*. They were half young maidens and half birds; one of them used her voice and sang most divinely, another played the flutes, and the third played the lyre. Together, they formed such a sweet and melodious concert of music that it caused the sailors passing by to perish if they paused to listen to them, as *Homer* relates in the 12th book of the *Odyssey*. 

This *Achelous*, then, engaged in the combat with *Hercules* depicted in this painting. This was on account of *Deianira*, daughter of *Oeneus*, King of *Calydon*, whom he wished to take in marriage by force. Despite the fact that he transformed himself into many shapes—most notably into a Bull—*Hercules* nevertheless overcame him and tore off one of his horns. This was later called the <term>horn of plenty</term> <note>Also known as the Cornucopia, a symbol of abundance and nourishment.</note> or cornucopia, after it was filled with all kinds of flowers and fruits by the <term>Naiads</term> <note>Water nymphs who inhabited rivers, fountains, and springs.</note>. 

*Strabo*, in Book 10, explains this allegorically: because of the kinship *Hercules* formed with *Oeneus*, he used dikes and levees to stop the floods of this river, which frequently ruined most of the territory of *Calydon*. He dried up one of its branches that was most prone to overflowing. Furthermore, according to *Plutarch* at the beginning of the treatise:

> *That a Philosopher should converse with great men,* <note>original: "Qu’il faut qu’vn Philoſophe conuerſe avec les grands."</note>

...he is said to have had a reputation for being highly expert in the management of water. We have already touched upon the rest in the description of the painting of *Meles*, and have included in this place the verses of *Sophocles* from the tragedy *The Women of Trachis* <note>original: "Trachynienes."</note>, which *Strabo* cites on this subject; it is from this work that *Philostratus* borrowed the entire opening of this painting's description. *Ovid*, in the 9th book of the *Metamorphoses*, treats this fable very elegantly and in great detail.

He came to Aetolia with Sthenelus, son of Capaneus, and made war against Opopas, son of Agrius, whom he put to death. He drove Agrius from the Kingdom he had usurped, restoring it to his grandfather, whereupon Agrius killed himself out of regret.

*Hercules* comes by as a matter of casual detour. In the Greek, it says "a side-task of the journey" <note>original: ὁδοῦ πάρεργον</note>. This has passed into a proverb used when one does something incidentally that was not directly part of one's main purpose and intention; "foreign to the matter at hand" <note>original: *aliena à re propoſita*</note>, as *Cicero* would say; or as *Caesar* writes in several places, "to attack while on the march" <note>original: *Ex itinere aggredi*</note>.

Of this *god* <note>Refers to the river god Achelous, who fought Hercules for the hand of Deianira.</note> along with the invincible Hero. It was the custom of the ancients in paganism to call rivers gods and to sacrifice to them as such; the *Phrygians* even did so to the *Meander* and to *Marsyas*. You may have seen this previously in the painting of *Antilochus* <note>Likely referring to a description of a painting in the *Imagines* by Philostratus, or a specific commentary on Homeric scenes.</note> from the 23rd book of the *Iliad*, where *Achilles* had vowed to offer his first lock of hair to *Spercheios* <note>A river god in Thessaly.</note>.

->AT THE REVERSE.<-

Amphitryon, Prince of Thebes, son of Alcaeus—from whom Hercules, as if from his grandfather, took the name "Alcides," according to Pindar in the 6th of the *Olympians* and Proclus in his commentary on Plato’s *Cratylus*. This name was also given to Minerva by the Macedonians, as Livy writes in his 42nd book: *Perseus, having completed a royal sacrifice of a hundred victims to Minerva, whom they call Alcides* <note>original Latin: "Perses centum hostiis sacrificio regaliter minervae quam vocant Alciden, confecto." Note that "Perses" refers here to King Perseus of Macedon.</note>. However, in this instance, this word comes from *strength* <note>original Greek: ἀλκὴ (alkē)</note>, as it very well might also do in the case of Hercules. He received the name *Heracles* <note>original Greek: ἡρακλῆς</note> from *Hera* <note>original Greek: ἥρα</note>, or Juno; thus the oracle willed it, because of the glory he acquired by means of her persecutions. 

Amphitryon, then—son of Alcaeus and Laonome, daughter of Guneus, according to Pausanias in his *Arcadics*—married Alcmene, daughter of Electryon and Lysidice (who was the daughter of Pelops and Hippodamia). He married her under the condition that he avenge the death of her brother, whom the Teleboans, a people of Aetolia, had wickedly massacred. While he was occupied with this task, Jupiter, having taken on Amphitryon's appearance, came to find Alcmene as if he were returning from his enterprise. Under this pretext, he lay with her, recounting from start to finish everything he had done on this journey. He found such favor with the lady that he prolonged this night by the length of a day and the following night; this moved Lycophron to call Hercules the *three-night lion* <note>original Greek: τρισέπερος λέων (trisperos leōn)</note>, as Lucian also does. 

Having thus fathered Hercules within her—though she was already pregnant with Iphicles by her husband Amphitryon—Amphitryon himself arrived amidst these events. Seeing how little account she made of him, like one who thought she had just recently been intimate with him, he complained; she replied: "How is it that you have only just left, having been with me this whole long night, and having told me such and such a thing about your journey?" From this, Amphitryon perceived that it was some deity who had come to visit her in his absence, so that from then on he abstained from touching her further. When her term arrived, she gave birth to Iphicles by Amphitryon and Hercules by Jupiter, according to Pliny, Book 7, Chapter 11. But Hercules was born with great difficulty and labor; for Juno stationed the goddess of childbirth, Lucina, who, instead of helping Alcmene to deliver, hindered her...

Proserpina <note>The queen of the Underworld, also known as Persephone.</note> granted to this man, even after he had passed away, the gift of continued intellect, and to be uniquely prudent and wise, while others are but light shadows easily tossed about. Fulgentius, in the 3rd book of his *Mythologies*, allegorizing on the fable of this **Tiresias** and his transformations, suggests that this name comes from *summer* <note>original Greek: θέρος (theros)</note> and *age* or *eternity* <note>original Greek: αἰῶν (aion)</note>. He argues that Spring represents the man, because all seeds are knotted and budding there, and Summer represents the woman, insofar as they expand and open into flowers, leaves, and fruits—just as a woman does when giving birth to the creature that was conceived and formed in her womb. Thus, both animals and plants, when touched by heat, take on a sort of feminine nature. 

And because Autumn is equal to Spring, both in the equality of days and nights—for the male is more equal and tempered than the female, just as these two seasons are more so than the other two, of which one (namely Winter) exceeds moderation in coldness and the other (Summer) in heat—and because conceptions occur in Autumn, **Tiresias** resumes his original masculine form, which is drier and less humid than the feminine. This is why leaves, lacking the moisture that leaves them, fall from the trees at that time and dry up. 

Afterward, **Jupiter** is taken to represent fire, as has been said elsewhere; and **Juno** represents the air. And since the air is more suited to generation and production, more pleasure is also attributed to her than to **Jupiter**. For having offered this fair judgment <note>Tiresias was famously asked to settle a dispute between Jupiter and Juno over who experiences more pleasure in love; he sided with Jupiter, stating women feel more, which angered Juno.</note>, **Tiresias** is rendered blind by **Juno**, which signifies the fogs and cloudy weather that reign in Winter, following immediately after Autumn. But **Jupiter**, while the cold compresses and restrains the saps in appearance...

->### AT THE CRADLE.<-

...from the outside, resuscitates in them anew a silent and secret movement to bloom in the coming springtime; which is like a production of the future. This is the same reason why **Janus** is depicted with two faces, representing the month of **January**; one looking backward, to denote the year that is past and revolved through its four completed seasons—or rather three, according to the doctrine of the **Egyptians**—and the face in front looking toward the future which one is entering. This is how **Fulgentius** <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a Latin writer of the late 5th or early 6th century known for his allegorical interpretations of mythology.</note> moralizes upon it, though for the most part, his interpretations are forced and far-fetched.

He is painted as if he were rapt in ecstasy. The rapture that the Greeks call <term>ecstasy <note>original: ἔκστασις (ekstasis)</note></term> is an abstraction, alienation, and illumination through which the soul, having descended from on high to this world below, is once again elevated. This occurs through a very strong and profound contemplation which, withdrawing the soul like a prisoner from the bonds of the bodily senses where it is held in captivity, seems to leave the body where it resides as if extinguished and deprived of life. So powerful is the agitation of this **Ecstasy** that one may sometimes see those who are seized by it struggle no differently than if they were in the final throes of death. This is even as **St. Augustine** recounts of a certain **Calaminian priest**, who in these raptures and acts found himself so alienated from all feeling that he remained for a long time without breathing or moving, regardless of any fire applied to him or any iron instrument; thus he truly seemed to have passed away. This also happens to those who faint from some vehement swoon; so powerful is the strength of the soul when it predominates over the body and can somewhat deliver itself from it. For then it deploys its faculties, just like a lit candle enclosed in an opaque lantern where it remains as if buried; but if one opens the shutter, it suddenly spreads its light here and there. This is why even those who suffer from the <term>falling sickness <note>An archaic term for epilepsy, from the French "mal caducq."</note></term>, while they are in the midst of a fit, are sometimes accustomed to predict many future things. Such is read of **Hercules**, who was very subject to this condition, which led to it being called the **Herculean disease**. ->## HERCULES ##<-

...terror, and almost driven senseless, when the prophetic spirit came to be introduced into them, as this passage here by **Cicero** in his books on divination shows well enough: the spirit of man never divines except when it is so untied from the body that it no longer has communication with it, or very little. **Plato** calls this the flowings or descents of superior intelligences into the human spirit (the **Cabalists** would say the <term>Sephirot <note>original: Zephirots; the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite is revealed.</note></term>) which enlighten it just as a torch would our sight in darkness; where by means of its light our eye apprehends the things it could not otherwise discern in the obscurity that defrauds it of its visual faculty and action. And **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: Mercure Trismegiste; a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with a cycle of philosophical and religious texts.</note> posits that the demonic spirits, which paganism named the <term>Eurydes <note>likely referring to the *Eurythei* or divine spirits of inspiration</note></term> or **Pythons**, thrusting themselves into human bodies, used their organs to announce future things. This is something that **Plutarch** also touches upon in his work on the cessation of oracles. But much more Christianly, **Cicero**, following the opinion of the **Stoics**, does not wish to attribute the knowledge of the future to anyone but the gods; this does not stray far from this passage of **Isaiah 41**:

> *Tell us what is to come hereafter, and we shall say that you are gods.*

To which **Ptolemy** also shows he wishes to conform, though he was a pagan: "There are only those who are inspired by the divinity who know how to predict particular things." But true prophecy came from divine inspiration alone, as **St. Peter** testifies in his second Catholic <note>The "Catholic" or General Epistles are those addressed to the church at large rather than specific cities or people.</note> epistle, chapter 1:

> *Prophecy was never brought by human will, but holy men, being inspired by the Holy Spirit, have spoken.*

**Plutarch**, in his treatise on the *Daemon of Socrates*, identifies several species of divinations, some of which are performed by means of certain physical signs, such as by the movement and course of the **stars**; <term>geomancy <note>divination by means of lines or signs on the earth</note></term>, <term>hydromancy <note>divination by water</note></term>, <term>chiromancy <note>palm reading</note></term>, and similar methods: by the entrails of victims; by the flight and song of birds, and infinite others that consist of art and rules. And finally, he describes interior inspiration, which in this case has no need of external things; such as were the **Prophets**, the **Sibyls**, and the oracles, of which that of **Tiresias** ended with an earthquake in the city of Or[chomenus]...

->### IN THE CRADLE ###<-

[Or]chomenus <note>original: "chomene"; an ancient Greek city in Boeotia, home to a famous oracle of Trophonius.</note>, and was rendered entirely silent according to **Plutarch** in the aforementioned treatise *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*; assigning the cause of these predictions and responses to the exhalations and vapors which, proceeding from the earth more in one place than another and at certain periods of time—for they are not everlasting—can be extinguished by floods, by enclosed winds, and similar accidents. Thus, these vapors, introducing themselves into the vital spirits of persons, alienate their common course and function of understanding; they render them as if frantic, whereby the demon—who is clear-sighted—imprints himself more easily when he encounters a material subject fit to receive his impression. It is no more nor less than fire in naphtha, or gunpowder, and similar flammable substances, as was discussed previously regarding the depiction of **Phorbas** or the **Phlegyans** <note>In Greek mythology, Phorbas was a king of the Phlegyans who was punished for his hubris against the gods, particularly for desecrating the temple at Delphi.</note>. In this manner, the demon can do very little without this exhalation and vapor, and even less can the vapor do without the demon, who accommodates himself to it and makes use of it. It is just as musical instruments would not sound by themselves if someone did not handle them; yet the musician, on the other hand, could do nothing without the instruments. 

But the **Sibyls** <note>Ancient prophetesses in the Greek and Roman world who were later interpreted by Christian scholars as having foretold the coming of Christ.</note> proceeded from a much higher degree, namely from the divinity that descended into them and enlightened their souls like a ray of sun in the knowledge of things past and future, as well as present—for to the divinity, everything is present. Thus, they approached much closer than the oracles to the spirit of prophecy and were like intermediaries between the **Prophets**, illuminated by the Spirit of God, and the oracles, which all proceeded from the evil, deceptive demon. For although those women were pagans and idolaters, they often spoke through the spirit of truth, and of things belonging to the glory and honor of God—indeed, of the principal points of our religion and belief, such as the advent of the **Messiah**, his passion, his resurrection, and his everlasting reign. Now, when I say "the spirit of truth," it must not be inferred from this that the demons and oracles have not often predicted things that were found to be true by the events and effects that followed; but these were commonly worldly and frivolous things, and almost...

Of dreams, there are first of all two kinds: the false and the true. Of the false, again, there are two: those that are entirely vain and idle, which mean nothing and signify nothing, according to the 29th chapter of **Isaiah**: *As when a hungry man dreams he is eating, or a thirsty man dreams he is drinking; but when he awakes, his soul is empty.* Among other vain dreams, we include those that come to us in autumn, when the leaves fall from the trees; for which **Aristotle** attributes the cause to new fruits <note>Referring to the consumption of the recent harvest affecting digestion and sleep.</note>; and other reasons are deduced in the 8th book of **Plutarch’s** *Table Talk* <note>Original title: *Symposiaques* (Symposiacs).</note>, question 10. ### H E R C U L E S
<note>original: "H E R C V L E." In this context, Hercules likely serves as a title for a specific section or emblem within the work, often used in Renaissance literature to symbolize heroic virtue or the pursuit of divine wisdom.</note>

...weaknesses; for from Tiphereth <term>Tiphereth: The sixth Sephirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing Beauty, Harmony, and the "Sun of Justice" that balances the divine flow.</term>, or the Sun of Justice which is on high within the Ein Sof <term>Ein Sof: From the Hebrew 'infinite'; in Kabbalah, it refers to the Godhead prior to any self-manifestation.</term> or the infinity of eternity, proceed the intelligences that are separated and abstracted from matter. The Kabbalists <note>Scholars of Jewish mysticism.</note> call this species of vision *Belpecalariot* <note>original: "Belpecalariot," likely a corruption of the Hebrew *Be-aspaklaria*, meaning "in the mirrors."</note>, or the mirrors; and Saint Augustine calls it the "morning knowledge" <note>original: "matutinale." Augustine distinguished between "morning knowledge" (knowing things through God) and "evening knowledge" (knowing things through their own nature).</note>. *Bath Kol* <note>original: "Batchol," from the Hebrew *Bath Kol*, literally "Daughter of a Voice"—a divine echo or heavenly proclamation.</note> as well, or the "daughter of the voice," is sometimes taken for a revelation of a formed voice coming from heaven, as in Saint Matthew, chapters 3 and 17:
> Behold a voice from heaven, saying: "This is my beloved son, in whom I have taken my good pleasure."

And in the 14th chapter of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, "Then I heard a voice from heaven, saying to me:"
> Write: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord."

For just as there is a great agreement between a vision and a dream, so too is there between a vision and revelations, of which there are two principal kinds. One is a full and articulate voice, like those mentioned above, but without seeing God; just as in the 19th chapter of Exodus:
> Behold, I will come in the darkness of a cloud, to the end that the people may hear me speaking to you.

For they did not see Him, as it is said in the 4th chapter of Deuteronomy:
> You heard the voice of His words; but you saw no form at all.

And in the 15th chapter of Genesis, the word of the Lord came to Abraham by vision, saying:
> Abraham, fear not.

But more expressly still in chapter 22, when God said to him: "Abraham, Abraham." For this redoubling denotes a great emphasis, just as in the 3rd chapter of Exodus, where the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire in the midst of a burning bush, and said to him: "Moses, Moses." Likewise in the first book of Kings, chapter 3 <note>Commonly known today as 1 Samuel.</note>, when God wishes to notably manifest Himself to Samuel—for previously these were only preparations and summons, wherefore He did not redouble his name—but finally, when He wishes to come to the effect, He says: "Samuel, Samuel." And he responds:
> Speak, Lord, for your servant listens.

The other species of revelation is in vision, face to face, which is the highest and final degree of prophecy; of which it is written in the 12th chapter of Numbers:
> I speak with Moses my servant mouth to mouth, and he sees the Lord manifestly; not in obscurity, nor by riddles.

Which will be [granted] to us, if God please...

->### AT THE CRADLE.<-

Night is also depicted there, illuminating herself with a lamp. It is a very clever invention to attribute the figure of a person to an insensible thing like Night, which is, after all, merely the absence of light; by which means, because of the darkness she usually carries with her, she requires some accidental light to show what is happening within her. This is also to denote the terror that the serpents sent by Juno <note>Juno, the queen of the gods, was famously jealous of Hercules (the son of her husband Jupiter and the mortal Alcmene) and sent two snakes to kill him in his cradle.</note> were meant to bring, in order to kill the infant Hercules—occurring by night when everyone is at rest, rather than by day, which is always less terrifying than the shadows, which are usually accompanied by horror, following what was previously brought forth from

From the *Astronomica* of Manilius.</note> sown with stars, with a crescent moon: haggard and withered in her flesh, with a drip hanging from her nose, all damp and drenched with humidities and evening dews; smoky, brown, and tarnished: enveloped in an unseemly cloak of black trellis-work, and her skin entirely dark, as inferred by this description of the Chest of Cypselus <note>A famous cedar-wood chest dedicated at Olympia, described by the ancient traveler Pausanias. It featured intricate carvings of mythological scenes.</note> in the *Description of Greece* by Pausanias: On the other side there was a woman carved in half-relief, carrying in her right hand, raised high, a sleeping child of white flesh; and in her left she held another, black like an Ethiopian, who seemed to be slumbering; both had crooked legs: the inscriptions declared them to be—and even if there had been no writing, one would not have failed to imagine it—that they were **Sleep** and **Death**, of whom Night is the nursing mother. # H E R C U L E S

And Virgil, following him in the 10th book of the *Aeneid*: *Eyes are closed in eternal night.* <note>original: "In æternam clauduntur lumina noctem." Virgil uses this phrase to describe death in battle.</note> The same Pausanias, in his *Description of Attica*, notes that Night had a temple called the Temple of Divination, because revelations are better received at night when the spirits are more composed, especially in darkness and while sleeping. According to the philosopher Strato, the spirits are more penetrating and alert in seeking knowledge [at night] than by day in the light of the sun, which dissipates and scatters them. For this reason, Night was called <term>Euphronē</term> <note>original: "εὐφρόνη." A Greek name for night, literally meaning "the kindly one" or "the well-disposed."</note>—meaning wise and prudent—according to Phurnutus <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher who wrote on Greek mythology.</note> and the poet Epicharmus, who said that the thoughts of the night were more studious and perceptive than those of the day.

Plutarch, in the eighth book of his *Symposiacs* <note>A collection of dinner-table discussions on various philosophical and scientific questions.</note>, Question 3, argues very learnedly that the night air is more settled, tranquil, and less noisy or turbulent than that of the day. This is partly because all things are then in a quiet rest and silence, allowing the voice to be sent forth more fully—and much less interrupted or weakened before reaching our senses—and partly because of the noise that the sun usually carries with it, which, upon its appearance, stirs, excites, and awakens even the smallest things anew. This is because the air in which the voice is formed is then more agitated and moved by the sun’s rays than in their absence, according to Anaxagoras and other reasons he deduces there. For as Democritus says: The sun, by mixing its light with the actions of men who are called by it to new labor, consequently weakens their meditations; for this, obscurity is more suitable than darkness. Nostradamus was not ignorant of this in his *Centuries* of quatrains:

> Sitting by night in secret study,
> Alone, resting upon the brass stool,
> A meager flame coming out of solitude,
> Makes him utter what is not believed in vain. <note>This is the famous opening quatrain of Nostradamus's *Prophecies*, describing his method of divination using a tripod (the "brass stool") and water.</note>

And for this reason, churches are commonly dim and dark, so that by this means the thought may be more focused on a devout and profound contemplation. But night is actually nothing other than the shadow of the earth that deprives us of the light of the Sun, as Pliny writes in Book 2, Chapter 10, following Empedocles and Speusippus; and Cicero in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*: *The shadow of the earth itself, obstructing the sun, creates the night.* <note>original: "Ipsa vmbra terrę soli officiens noctem efficit"</note> Here, by using the word *officiens* (obstructing or hindering), he alludes to the etymology of <term>nox</term> (night), which is derived from <term>noceo</term> (to harm). <note>The author is following a traditional but linguistically debated etymology linking the word for "night" to the word for "injury" or "harm."</note> This is why Heraclitus used to say that if there were no sun, there would consequently be no night; because light, whose source is the Sun, creates shadow when an opaque body like the earth is placed in its way, and thus darkness follows. For this reason, the Poets feigned that Night was the daughter of the Earth and the mother of the Fates or Destinies, because of their shared obscurity. Thus Night, by means of her shadows, deprives us not only of the benefit and contentment of the beautiful light of day—of which nothing can be more pleasing to man—but of almost half of all our joys and pleasures, if we are to believe the same Pliny in Book 36, Chapter 1.

> As if indeed the darkness of the nights did not take away these joys from half of every person's life.
> <note>original: "Ceu vero non tenebris noctium dimidię parti vitæ cuiusque gaudia hęc auferentibus."</note>

But what moved him to say that is the assumption that we are sleeping then; for as Ariston says, sleep is like a tax-collector and extortioner who demands from us and cuts away half of our life. And one of the gnomic poets <note>Poets who wrote short, pithy maxims or aphorisms.</note> says on this same subject:

-># H E R C U L E S<-

Otherwise the proposition would be false, since most good times happen at night—not only the most solemn feasts, but also masquerades, ballets, comedies, jesters, <term>matachins</term> <note>A fast-paced sword dance performed in fantastic costumes.</note>, and other such amusements. These possess a much greater grace and please more by the light of torches than they do by day, as was shown in the painting of Comus <note>The Greek god of festivity, revelry, and nocturnal dalliances.</note>. Furthermore, the most pleasant activities arranged for the practice of Lady Venus <note>The goddess of love and beauty.</note> find far more freedom there than in broad daylight, which is the mortal enemy of lovers and their desired enjoyments. Thus, Ovid in the second book of his *Amores* <note>A collection of love poems; specifically Elegy 12.</note> called the night lewd and voluptuous, and fit for taking one's pleasure: *the wanton joys of the night*. <note>original: "lasciue gaudia noctis"</note>

This is partly why Homer, Pindar, Mopsus, and other Greek poets gave Venus the epithet <term>helikopis</term> <note>original: ελιϰωπις</note>, "with dark eyes," because the night—where this goddess reigns supreme—is black and dark. It is also more humid than the day, so that it puts nature to sleep and occupies it, according to Plutarch in the third book of the *Symposiacs* <note>A series of books recording dinner-table discussions on various philosophical and scientific topics.</note>, Question 6. Because of this, a person becomes more inclined to debauchery following dissolute desires, since darkness chases away fear and shame. Curio very elegantly deduces this in the second book of the *Pompeian War* <note>Referring to the civil wars of Julius Caesar.</note> in Caesar: *For matters of this kind are restrained by either shame or fear, to which things the night is most hostile.* <note>original: "Namque huiufmodi res aut pudore aut metu tenentur, quibus rebus nox maxime aduerſaria eſt"</note> Here, Caesar, according to his custom, uses the word "hostile" as an <term>antiphrase</term> <note>A figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its literal meaning; in this case, "hostile" means "favorable."</note> for its complete opposite—meaning something convenient and proper—as he intends it.

From this, Venus supposedly took one of her other nicknames, <term>Melanis</term> <note>original: μελανις</note> or "the Black One," according to Pausanias in his *Description of Greece* <note>Specifically in the book regarding Arcadia.</note>, because men attend to her more by night than by day. This is also touched upon by Plutarch in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*; and Pindar says that the night is the favorite of Venus. Homer, moreover, maintains that she [Night] existed before the day, and darkness before light. This differs little from the Mosaic traditions at the beginning of Genesis. Likewise, Hesiod in his *Theogony* <note>The Greek poem describing the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note> calls her the oldest of the gods: daughter of Chaos, and mother of Aether and Day; and Aratus in his *Phaenomena* <note>A didactic poem on astronomy and meteorology.</note> calls her <term>archaie</term> <note>original: αρχαιη</note>, meaning "first" or "ancient." <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a child-like figure standing amidst foliage within a square border.</image-desc>Orpheus, son of Oeagrus <note>A king of Thrace in Greek mythology</note>, or according to others, of Apollo and the Muse Calliope; whatever the case, a native of Thrace according to Pliny himself (Book IV, Chapter 11). Along the shores of the Euxine Sea <note>The ancient name for the Black Sea</note> are the Morisini and Sithonians, ancestors of the Poet Orpheus. He was a most excellent—indeed, the first—of all Poets, Musicians, and Lyre players, given that until his time there was no one who made a profession of it, nor of other stringed instruments either; instead, they recited their verses only to flutes. And he became so accomplished in it, that it was believed that through his melodious Music, he made the woods and rocks move from their places; halted the flow of rivers; and rendered the fiercest and most cruel wild beasts so gentle, tamed, and tractable, that they stood still to listen to him, remaining peaceful without harming one another, nor even the tame and domestic animals. As he attempted to force himself upon her and she fled before him, a serpent hidden in the grass bit her foot, from which she died. Orpheus fell into such great sadness that, unable to forget her, he went to seek her in the underworld, where by means of his songs he moved Pluto and Proserpina to return her to him: but on the condition that he would not cast his gaze upon her until he had returned to the world above.

Because he could not restrain himself, overcome by an amorous impatience, she returned once more to the underworld. This brought him such regret that he henceforth abstained from the company of all women; indeed, he persuaded others to do the same, and to turn away from them toward the foul and filthy love of young boys, of which he is said to have been the first author, at least among the Thracians. Consequently, for this reason, he was dismembered by the Maenads <note>Female followers of Bacchus known for their ecstatic and violent rituals</note> celebrating their rites on Mount Pangaeum. They were moved to this by Bacchus, who had become indignant against him because, while in the underworld, Orpheus had sung the genealogy of all the gods but had forgotten him; and therefore Bacchus incited his female ministers to this massacre.

# H E R C U L E S <note>While the header reads "Hercules," the text continues the biography of Orpheus from the previous page, likely due to a printer's error or a transition between mythological figures.</note>

...the women of Thrace, having fallen in love with Orpheus, while each wanted him for her own and to take him away with her, in this dispute he came to be dismembered. However it may be, the Muses gathered up the pieces and gave them burial, except for the head, which with its lyre was carried downstream by the current of the Hebrus river as far as the island of Lesbos. There, the head was buried by the inhabitants of the place, and the lyre was translated to the heavens among the stars, being composed of nine stars. Ovid treats this fable very elegantly in the 10th and 11th books of the *Metamorphoses*. 

And Plato, in his *Symposium* <note>original: "banquet"</note>, posits that Orpheus was sent back from the underworld without being able to obtain anything of what he had gone there to seek. He was shown only the shadow and phantom of his wife, and not her actual self returned in truth, because he had behaved too faint-heartedly in the matter—behaving like the musician <note>original: "ioueur d'instruments," literally "player of instruments"</note> that he was. He did not have the courage, in imitation of Alcestis <note>A heroine who volunteered to die in place of her husband, Admetus</note>, to die for the sake of love, but instead sought I know not what little tricks and expedients to be able to descend to the underworld while alive. Thus, the gods did not let this cowardice go unpunished, for they destined for him the penalty of being put to death by women. 

This was the reason, as it is said in the 10th book of the *Republic*, that after his death he chose to return here below in the body of a swan, no longer wishing to be born of women because of the hatred he bore them. To this agrees the passage by Horace in the last Ode of the 2nd book of his poems to Maecenas <note>referring to Horace, *Odes* 2.20</note>, verse 3, where he says that after his death he will take the form of a swan, which will fill the whole circle of the earth with its songs:

> Henceforth to my legs there clings
> Rough, withered skin;
> And I am transformed into a white swan
> From above: all along my fingers,
> And from my weak shoulders,
> Feathers grow in abundance.

And there, a column is visible on the right hand, upon which is placed an urn, where the inhabitants of the country maintain the bones of **Orpheus** are kept. The river **Helicon** is also nearby, which, after flowing for about three leagues, loses itself underground; and a league from there, it is reborn again, changing the name Helicon to that of **Baphyra**, being navigable from that point onward. The people of **Dium** <note>original: "Diotois"</note> allege that in the beginning, its course continued without intermission above ground, but because those murderous women went to wash their bloody hands in it, the water—refusing the ritual cleansing <term>expiation</term> <note>the act of making amends or purifying oneself of the guilt of a crime</note> of their misdeed—chose to hide itself at that spot. ...near which was the burial place of Orpheus. It is said that the inhabitants of the place had received an oracle from **Bacchus** in **Thrace**, stating that their city would be ruined from top to bottom by a sow, should the sun ever see the bones of Orpheus uncovered. They did not trouble themselves much over this, thinking that no animal, however robust or powerful, had the strength to do such a thing. 

But it happened that a shepherd, around midday in the heat of the day, having fallen asleep against this column where the casket of Orpheus lay, began to sing his verses so melodiously that the others who were guarding their flocks nearby—as well as those laboring in the fields and hoeing the vines—leaving all their work, ran there in such a crowd that they overturned the column. Thus, the urn broke into pieces, and the bones of Orpheus were left uncovered. Thereupon, during the following night, there occurred such a great flash flood from the extreme rain that fell, that the torrent called **Sus**—which also signifies a sow or pig—having overflowed its banks, overturned the walls of **Libethra**, along with all the houses. The inhabitants were drowned, and the city was entirely lost. 

As for his hymns, those who wish to look closely cannot doubt that they are his, even if they are not entirely well-measured throughout; but the **Lycomides** <note>An ancient Athenian family who held the hereditary priesthood of certain mysteries</note> make use of them and sing them in their sacrifices and solemnities. Consequently, after those of **Homer**, they enjoy the greatest popularity and authority; and even the immortal gods grant them more than men do. 

*This is what **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer</note> alleges regarding these hymns; as for the rest of Orpheus's works that we have in our hands, many doubt that they are by the ancient Orpheus in question here, but rather by some more modern figure of the same name, or someone who wished to borrow that name to give them more authority. Nevertheless, this passage from **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note> (Book XXV, Chapter 2), along with the above from Pausanias, gives some reason to think that if Orpheus, the first of all of whom we have memory, did set down...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Orpheus’s works, transitioning from his burial and the legends of his tomb to the specific botanical and theological content found in his hymns and their influence on later philosophers like Pythagoras and Plato.</meta>

# O R P H E U S .

...brought to light something curious regarding these herbs. And after him, **Musaeus** and **Hesiod** admired the **Polium** <note>original: "Poliot"; a medicinal Mediterranean herb, *Teucrium polium*, believed by ancients to have protective properties</note>. **Orpheus** and **Hesiod** greatly admired incense and perfumes; **Homer** also celebrated several herbs specifically by their names. For in the hymns of Orpheus, one can clearly see how he assigns to each God or divine power their own specific **offerings of smoke** <term>suffumigations: the ritual practice of burning incense or herbs so that the smoke rises as an offering</term>, according to their nature and properties. Now, whoever authored them, they are of such quality—as **Plato** testifies in the 8th book of the *Laws*, speaking of these hymns and those of **Thamyris** <note>A legendary Thracian singer who competed with the Muses</note>—that they are the sweetest and most pleasant poems of all others. They are, moreover, full of sacred mysteries, so much so that in the 2nd book of his *Republic*, **Musaeus** and **Orpheus** are said to have been born of the Moon and the Muses, and from there brought forth a great abundance of religious secrets.

**Iamblichus** also wrote that **Pythagoras** skimmed all the philosophy—or rather, the theology—of **Orpheus** to form and build his own, and that the Pythagorean moral sayings and maxims were called "sacred" because they flowed from the traditions of this same Orpheus. This applies as much to the doctrine of numbers as to all the other beautiful and sublime considerations his doctrine achieves, as if from their primal source; although everything there is enveloped and hidden beneath the "rinds" of poetic fictions. So much so that if one took them literally and crudely, they would seem at first glance to be nothing but frivolous fables and vain nonsense; yet nonetheless, very high mysteries are contained beneath them. In several places he speaks of God so "Christianly"—if one may be permitted to say so—that it would not be possible to do so more. This, among other things besides his hymns, is alleged by **Clement of Alexandria** in his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromates"; a major work of early Christian theology</note>: "I shall speak to those for whom it is lawful, but close the doors to the profane." <note>original: "φθέγξομαι οἷς θέμις ἐστί, θύρας δ' ἐπίθεσθε βεβήλοις."</note> This passage exists in various versions, of which I have chosen the most plausible:

> I wish to speak to those to whom
> It is lawful that I speak,
> But to the profane, whoever they may be,
> The door must be closed against them;
> And you, **Musaeus**, listen to me,

-># IN COLCHIS.<-

Marks or signs of some lineage of the sun. This is said because Aeetes was believed to be the son of the Sun and of Perse, daughter of Ocean, as Dionysius of Miletus <note>A historian from the 5th century BCE who wrote about the Argonauts.</note> records in the first book of his *Argonauts*: That the sun fathered two male children in Scythia, Aeetes and Perses; the latter reigned in the Tauric Chersonese <note>The modern-day Crimean Peninsula.</note>, where he took a wife and had a daughter named Hecate. She was very devoted to and expert in hunting, as well as in the knowledge of herbs and simples <term>simples: medicinal plants used on their own rather than in a mixture</term>; especially poisonous and harmful ones, of which she was said to have demonstrated the first use and practice, along with other similar poisons. Indeed, she even caused the death of her own father with them. After this was done, she retired to Colchis where she married her uncle Aeetes, according to Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note> and the interpreters of Apollonius of Rhodes, and had by him Circe and Medea, to whom she gave such a great share of her knowledge that they eventually surpassed her in that field. The abundance of poisonous herbs and similar pestilential drugs found in Colchis has partly given cause to think of it in this way, according to Horace in the second book of his *Odes* <note>original: "Ille & venena Colchica"; translated: "He [is steeped in] Colchian poisons."</note>; but more particularly Virgil in the 8th Eclogue:

> Often summon spirits from the depths of the graves,
> And move standing crops from one field to another.

# THE PLAYERS.

### ARGUMENT.

## ANNOTATION.

To provide a clearer understanding of the present painting, it will do no harm to bring here this entire passage from the 22nd chapter of Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus (64 BC – AD 17) was a Latin author whose *Fabulae* provided summaries of Greek and Roman myths. Chapter 22 specifically covers the story of Aeetes.</note>. Aeetes, son of the Sun, was told by an oracle that he would enjoy his kingdom for as long as the ram's skin—which Phrixus <note>In myth, Phrixus fled to Colchis on the back of a winged golden ram; he later sacrificed the ram and gave its fleece to King Aeetes.</note> had dedicated in the Temple of Mars—was preserved there. Consequently, when Jason arrived at Colchis to obtain it, Aeetes proposed this condition to him: that he must first yoke the bulls that breathed fire from their nostrils to a diamond yoke <note>original: "ioug diamantin." This likely refers to adamant, a mythical, indestructible metal or stone frequently mentioned in ancient texts.</note>.

And he was to plow a field to then sow the dragon's teeth from within a helmet <note>original: "sallade ou casquet." A "sallet" was a type of light, rounded combat helmet common in the 15th and 16th centuries.</note>; from which great troops of armed men would suddenly be born, who would then kill one another. Whereupon Juno—who had undertaken to safeguard Jason in all his enterprises because of the goodwill she bore him, ever since the hour when, wishing to test the hearts of people here below, she disguised herself as an old woman who begged passersby to carry her across a river—found her opportunity. While all the others paid her no mind, Jason alone did her this courtesy. 

Wishing to reward him for this, and as she foresaw that he could not succeed in his undertaking in Colchis without the help and means of Medea, she requested Venus to make Medea fall in love with him. This is what saved him from all the dangers that had been prepared for him. For having plowed the field with the bulls and sown it with the serpent's teeth, from which many armed men were produced, by the Princess’s <note>Referring to Medea, the daughter of King Aeetes.</note> advice, he threw a large stone into their midst, whereupon they began to fight among themselves and kill each other. Then, having taken the Golden Fleece from the temple where it was hanging, he fled with Medea.

Furthermore, this painting is titled **THE PLAYERS**, specifically those playing with **Knucklebones** <term>original: "Astragales." These are the small bones from the heel of a sheep's hind legs used in an ancient game similar to jacks or dice.</term> or trinkets; or those made in their likeness from ivory or ebony, having only four sides; for dice, which are cube-shaped, have six. This was previously discussed in the commentary on the painting of the Elephantine Venus. *Pliny, Book 34, Chapter 8*, speaking of bronze sculptors and their works, mentions this regarding *Polycletus* <note>Polycletus was a famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BC, renowned for his mastery of the human form.</note>, which seems to relate somewhat to these players: "He also made two naked young boys playing with knucklebones, hence called the *Astragalizontes* <note>Greek for "knucklebone players."</note>, which are in the palace of the Emperor *Titus*; a masterpiece which many consider to be the most perfect of all."

### THE PLAYERS

...once a King on the island of **Cos** named **Merops**, who had as his wife a beautiful Nymph named **Ethemee**; she, having shown herself negligent in revering and serving **Diana**, was pursued by the goddess with arrows. However, **Proserpina** transported her while still alive to the underworld, for which **Merops** felt such regret that he wished to kill himself. **Juno**, taking pity on him, converted him into an eagle and placed him in the heavens; this was done for fear that if she had left him in the form of a man, always remembering the misfortune of his dear spouse, he would incessantly and immoderately bathe the earth with his tears. 

But **Aglaosthenes** <note>An ancient Greek author who wrote about the history of Naxos.</note> has written that **Jupiter**, having been taken from **Candie** <note>The historical name for the island of Crete.</note> where he was born, was then transported to **Naxos**. Having reached manhood there, just as he was on the point of setting out for the war against the **Titans**, an eagle appeared to him carrying a lightning bolt. Taking this as a good omen, he thereafter took the eagle under his recommendation and protection.

Others say that **Mercury**, having fallen in love with **Venus** because of her excellent beauty without being able to have his way with her, was consuming himself with spite and vexation. **Jupiter** took pity on him; once, while the goddess was bathing in the river **Achelous**, he had an eagle snatch one of her sandals <term>original: "pattins." A type of elevated overshoe or clog, here referring to a classical sandal.</term> and carry it to **Egypt** to **Mercury**. When **Venus** pursued the bird to recover it, she finally gave herself to him. For this favor, he translated the eagle to the heavens, where it has four stars: one very bright one in the head; one in each of the two wing-joints <term>original: "mahuttes ou moignons des esles." Archaic terms for the pinions or shoulders of the wings.</term>; and one in the tail. 

As for the arrow that it holds in its feet, they say it is the one with which **Apollo** put the **Cyclopes** to death, because they had forged the lightning bolt with which **Jupiter** killed his son **Aesculapius**. ## JUNO

JUNO represents the active life, mostly occupied with amassing wealth, of which she is the Queen. Under this quality, the Romans revered her, having moved her cult from Veii to Rome; for this reason, she is attributed a sceptre to show the majesty of her power. She has, moreover, her head veiled to show that riches are hidden in the depths of the earth, especially metals and gemstones, which are extracted with extreme labor. This also denotes that those who aspire too ardently to amass goods are blinded; and for such a reason Pluto, the god of wealth on the other hand, is depicted. 

But insofar as Juno is taken for the air, as her name suggests—in Greek, *Hera* <note>original: "ηρα"</note>, which when transposed makes *Aer* <note>original: "αηρ"; the author is noting that the letters of the goddess's name can be rearranged to spell "Air."</note>—and for this reason the vulture was attributed to her, which is said to conceive from the air or the wind; the veiling of the head signifies the impressions of the air, which is darkened and troubled. And this was also represented by the upper eyelid that covers the eye, which was anciently dedicated to her. This also relates to the fable told of Ixion <note>A king in Greek myth who was punished for trying to seduce Hera/Juno.</note>, who, when pressing this goddess for intimacy, she presented him with a cloud having her likeness, from which he fathered the centaurs who de-

*NOW, so as not to leave anything out of what might serve for the clarification of these images, which are so brief and summarized with half-words; and to bring some satisfaction to readers; Fulgentius <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a Latin writer of the late 5th or early 6th century whose "Mythologies" interpreted classical myths as moral allegories.</note> in book 2 of his Mythologies, interprets word for word the portraits of these three goddesses: which he relates to the three kinds of life found in men: and their triple inclinations, according to the three parts that concern them; namely the spirit, the goods of fortune, and the body, which relate to the contemplative, the active, and the voluptuous life:*

*the first of which is designated by Minerva, who for this reason is imagined to have been born and produced from the Brain of Jupiter, since understanding consists in the brain. She is painted armed, because the spirit and industry make the true guard of the body, and defense of man, who without this would be the weakest and most feeble animal of all others. The Gorgon is added inside her buckler <term>targue</term> <note>original: "targue," a small shield</note> and Breastplate; which denotes the fright and terror that war and arms bring, where Minerva presides; and also that effort and courage consist in the heart, which lies and is lodged in the chest. This goddess has plumes, and a high-raised crest upon the crown <term>tymbre</term> <note>original: "tymbre," the top part of a helmet</note> of her helmet, to show how much the human spirit can raise itself high in contemplations which are its proper pursuit <note>original: "gibier," literally "game" or "quarry," implying the natural object of a hunt</note> and vocation; and in an instant it can flutter everywhere, there being nothing it does not penetrate, and very quickly, for the promptness of the will is designated by the plumage. She holds in her fist a javelin, to denote that the prudence and wisdom of man reach far; and that there is no offensive weapon whose blow is as dangerous as a well-spoken tongue and eloquent pen. Finally, one attributes to her the owl, which is a nocturnal bird, to show the vigilance of the contemplative and studious man, and of the warrior likewise, as Homer knew very well to remark in the 2nd book of the Iliade, where Jupiter sends the dream under the resemblance of the wise Nestor.*

...signify the various changes of the air. Moreover, she is made to be the goddess of childbirth <note>Juno Lucina was the Roman goddess invoked by women in labor</note>, because riches are accustomed to carry with them a new and disordered appetite, much like the cravings of pregnant women, to always heap up more and more; so that most of the time this is the cause of "miscarrying"—that is to say, they plunge those insatiable people who covet wealth too greedily into great misfortunes, even to a final ruin. The **Peacock** is attributed to her, because riches draw to themselves the desire and the eyes of everyone, just as the feathers of this beautiful bird do. And as it gazes at itself and takes pride in the beauty of its plumage, riches likewise are accustomed to make people more proud and insolent; besides which, they are the principal instrument and means of adorning oneself. And just as the peacock, when it fans its tail <note>original: "fait la roue," literally "makes the wheel," describing a peacock's display</note>, truly adorns the front well, yet at the same time unworthily uncovers its rear, this relates to our perverted actions and our wicked behaviors, which wealth during our life can somewhat brighten and cover; but after death everything is made manifest, following the saying of the wise man in the eleventh chapter of *Ecclesiasticus* <note>A book of the Apocrypha, also known as Sirach. The reference is to Sirach 11:27: "the end of a man is the revealing of his works."</note>; the end of man is the manifestation of his works. Finally, the **rainbow** is added to her, in which she is completely enveloped, to show the variety of riches and their beautiful luster and brilliant radiance, but accompanied by uncertainty, because the eye cannot properly discern the colors of this bow, because they wave over one another and mingle in such a way that they escape our sight just when one would think to grasp them separately. And so it is with riches, whose instability cannot be better represented than by this atmospheric phenomenon <note>original: "impreſſion de l'air"</note>, which, embracing the entire hemisphere from one end to the other—as do the outrageous and immoderate cravings of the greedy—is of such short duration that it vanishes almost as soon as it appears.
