And just as the rose is very delightful for a time, but does not last long: so it is with <term>voluptuousness</term> <note>original: volupté; refers to intense sensual or physical pleasure</note>: regarding which the great <term>Basil</term> <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), an influential Greek bishop and theologian who often used nature as a moral allegory.</note> would have said, and very aptly, that in the beginning the rose had no thorns, but that afterwards they were added to it, so that through the pain which accompanies the pleasure one receives from such delights, one might be reminded of their transgression and correct themselves. The doves likewise were assigned to her, because the pigeon is a very warm and lascivious bird. Furthermore, the Three Graces are included, of whom two have their faces turned toward us, and the third shows her shoulders; this is because pleasure is double at its arrival, and very simple when it departs: or else to show that a grace or benefit ought to be repaid twofold: and that when one confers a favor, they must hide themselves, so as not to be seen doing so out of vainglory or the expectation of some reward. Finally, Venus is depicted sailing upon a shell in the sea, to denote that usually those who give themselves over to her are in danger of shipwreck, and of drowning in a water of bitterness. There would be many other things to allegorize upon this, most of which have been touched upon in her description in the second book, along with her hymn: therefore, nothing remains here but the hymn of the Graces.

Concerning the ship, moreover, and all its specific details, they have been discussed sufficiently before in the description of the painting of Glaucus <note>Glaucus was a mortal fisherman who became a prophetic sea-god after eating a magical herb.</note>.

Now you can see clearly that there is artistry in the painting, the goddess being dressed in a robe of gold cloth, etc. In this, the artist makes an allusion to the fact that poets, both Greek and Latin, nickname Venus "the Golden," even Virgil in the 10th book of the *Aeneid*: *But the golden Venus, on the other hand, says a few things in response.* <note>original Latin: "At non Venus aurea contra Pauca refert."</note> But Hesiod, long before him, wrote in the *Shield of Hercules*: *Delighting in the gifts of golden Aphrodite.* <note>original Greek: τερπόμενος δώροισι πολυχρύσου Ἀφροδίτης (terpomenos dōroisi polychrysou Aphroditēs)</note> And Homer also in the 3rd book of the *Iliad*: *Do not cast in my teeth the lovely gifts of golden Aphrodite.* <note>original Greek: μή μοι δῶρ’ ἐρατὰ πρόφερε χρυσῆς Ἀφροδίτης (mē moi dōr' erata prophere chrysēs Aphroditēs)</note> Do not reproach me for the gifts of Venus, the golden goddess. This signifies nothing other than "beautiful," "excellent," or "agreeable," just as gold is superior to all other inanimate things. For the same reason, Virgil said elsewhere, *golden wife* <note>original Latin: "Coniux aurea"</note>; and Horace, *golden morals* <note>original Latin: "mores aurei"</note>; Cicero also, *golden name* <note>original Latin: "nomen aureum"</note>; and Ezekiel 28: *The gold of your beauty.* <note>original Latin: "Aurum decoris tui." In the biblical context, this refers to the splendor of the King of Tyre.</note> Furthermore, Ovid in the first book of the *Metamorphoses* says: *The golden age was the first to be sown.* <note>original Latin: "Aurea primo sata est ætas." This refers to the mythical first age of man, characterized by peace and prosperity.</note> And there are infinite other similar examples.

Venus might likewise have been called "golden" because, just as gold delights in the fire that refines and gladdens it, the <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Strong desire or lust, specifically associated here with the heat of passion.</note> of the Venus-like act depends upon heat; so that gold symbolizes fire here below, and the sun there above, as Pindar infers at the very beginning of his songs <note>A reference to Pindar's First Olympian Ode, which compares the excellence of gold to a "flaming fire in the night."</note>. To this point, Euripides in *Medea* introduces her exclaiming thus about the disloyalty of Jason:

> *O Zeus, why have you given to men clear signs* <note>original Greek: Ὦ Ζεῦ, τί δὴ χρυσοῦ μὲν ὃς κίβδηλος ᾖ / Τεκμήρι’ ἀνθρώποισιν ὤπασας σαφῆ</note>
> *To know if gold is counterfeit,*
> *But on the body of man,* <note>original Greek: Ἀνδρῶν δ’ ὅτῳ χρὴ τὸν κακὸν διειδέναι / Οὐδεὶς χαρακτὴρ ἐμπέφυκε σώματι</note>
> *There is no mark by which to recognize the wicked?*

He intended to kill her on the spot, until she called out for the help of Hercules; by this means, Telephus learned the whole truth of the matter.

Afterward, having been made King of Mysia—a province of Asia Minor <note>original: "la petite Asie"</note> along the Hellespont near the Troad—he took it upon himself to block the passage of the Greeks as they traveled to besiege Troy. He was wounded by Achilles in a skirmish; and being unable to find any relief for his wound, he was warned by the oracle that the remedy lay in the very iron <note>original: "ferrement"</note> by which he had been struck <note>A classic mythological theme: "the wounder must heal."</note>. Therefore, having reconciled with Achilles, he obtained from him the scrapings from the iron of his spear (which was made of bronze), from which a plaster was composed that healed him entirely.

Eurypylus, therefore, born of such a lineage, brought a great reinforcement of Mysians to the aid of Troy. He did this partly because he was their close neighbor and ally, and even the nephew of Priam, but also because he intended to marry his first cousin Cassandra, with whom he was enamored. Upon their arrival, he and his men performed many fine enterprises and exploits of arms; there he killed with his own hand Nireus, son of Charops and Aglaia, who was King of the Island of Naxos <note>The text specifies Naxos, though Homer traditionally associates Nireus with the island of Syme.</note>, of whom Homer speaks in this manner in the second book of the *Iliad*:

Following this, there was depicted with most excellent skill the valiant and courageous **Hippolyta** <note>Queen of the Amazons.</note>, whom [Hercules], having seized by her long hanging tresses, throws from her horse to the ground; there he strips her of her rich bandolier and belt, while her **Amazons**, having withdrawn to the side, look on, greatly terrified, without daring to rescue their Queen, whom he presents as a gift to **Theseus**.

ALL the rest of the description of these arms placed here, especially the shield, has been taken word for word from the 18th book of the ***Iliad***, where things are in many places detailed more clearly and intelligibly than does ***Philostratus*** <note>Philostratus the Elder, a Greek sophist to whom the descriptions in the "Imagines" are attributed.</note>, who takes pleasure in entangling and obscuring his writing. For this reason, it will be necessary to compare them together, for they will explain each other. And it must be known in the first place that ***Homer’s*** goal here is to represent the universe, which consists of the heaven and the earth, entirely in conformity with ***Moses*** at the beginning of his ***Pentateuch*** <note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament; the author is drawing a parallel between classical mythology and Biblical creation.</note>. The heaven is assigned to the stars, of which it seems to be the dwelling, just as the earth is that of men, for whom everything was made: the course and path of their life consisting of peace and war; in walled cities and in the countryside. Peace consists of Justice and policy, by which cities must be regulated to govern and rule that which is under them. Tillage and the feeding of livestock concern the lands outside the cities, and trade concerns both. War is divided into offensive and defensive; attacking strongholds and defending them: in combats, skirmishes, and encounters in the open field of pitched battle; in ambushes and other such <term>stratagems</term> <note>Deceptive maneuvers used to outwit an enemy.</note>; and in the booty and sacking which are the prize of victory. 

All this is represented by ***Homer*** with a most sovereign artifice, and in imitation of him by this ***Sophist*** in free prose. In this description, ***Vulcan*** forges these most notable armors from four metals: namely bronze, which those of those distant ages used in place of iron and steel, as was declared previously regarding the painting of ***Rhodogune***. And that metal denotes the earth; for he wishes by these four metals to designate the four elements of which all things are composed, both above in heaven and down here: **Tin** represents water; **silver**, the air; and **gold**, fire. This is according even to the poet ***Pindar*** at the very beginning of his songs: <note>original: "ὁ δὲ χρυσὸς αἰδομένον πῦρ" (ho de chrysos aidomenon pyr)</note> "and gold is a blazing fire." Here then is how ***Homer*** speaks of it. From these four metals, ***Vulcan*** forges in...

**HERE ARE** the Pleiades, which provide the warnings and signs of the sowing season and of the harvest, according to their setting and their rising. The same is said by *Plutarch* <note>A famous Greek historian and essayist.</note> in the treatise on *Natural Affection* and in that of *Osiris*, that the month which the *Athenians* call *Pyanepsion*, and the *Boeotians* *Damatrien*—which is to say *Cereal* <note>Associated with Ceres, the goddess of agriculture.</note>—corresponds to our *October*; it is the month in which the Pleiades set and one begins to sow. Then, one harvests when they rise. They are so named from <term>πλεῖν</term> <note>plein: to sail</note> to sail, because at their rising they announce the season for navigation; otherwise they are called the *Vergiliae* <note>The Roman name for the constellation, derived from "Ver" or Spring.</note>. They are seven stars noticed in the tail of the *Bull* <note>The constellation Taurus.</note> according to *Pliny*, Book 2, chapter 41. But *Hyginus* <note>An author of astronomical myths.</note> situates them between the Bull's muzzle and the tail of the Ram, and *Aratus* in his *Phenomena* places them near the Bull's knee: though, as he says, the space is not large enough to hold them all. They are faint for the most part, being of the fifth and lowest magnitude of brightness. Others say that, having resolved to keep their virginity, they had on this occasion devoted themselves to the service of Diana <note>The goddess of the hunt and protector of virgins.</note> and to the exercise of hunting, to which they applied themselves incessantly in the deep forests. Orion <note>A giant hunter in Greek mythology.</note>, who had fallen in love with them, pursued them so closely that they had no means of escape; in this extremity they called upon Jupiter <note>The king of the gods.</note>, who transformed them into stars. But to come to what Philostratus <note>A Greek author whose descriptions of art this text comments upon.</note> touches upon here—that they are signs of the sowing season at their setting and of the harvests at their rising—Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman author and natural philosopher.</note> says on this subject in Book 18, Chapter 26: "Thus it is generally on the 6th day before the Ides of May, which is the rising of the Vergiliae" <note>original Latin: "Sic fere in vi. The **Vergiliae** <note>The Roman name for the Pleiades.</note> particularly belong to the fruits, as those at whose rising Summer begins, and at whose setting, on the other hand, Winter begins, for the space of a semester; they encompass within them the harvests, the vintages, and the ripening of all fruits. Even the vines and the olives conceive, as he says in Book 16, Chapter 26, at the rising of these stars. And if it rains then (Book 17, Chapter 2), it is greatly harmful to them: "Indeed, for it to rain around the time of the Vergiliae is most harsh for the vine and the olive, since that is the time of their union" <note>original Latin: "Circa Vergilias quidem pluere immitiſſimum viti & oleæ, quoniam tunc coitus eſt earũ." The term "coitus" here refers to the botanical fertilization or "conception" of the fruit.</note>. Ptolemy's almanac notes that they begin to rise on the 7th of May in the morning. The 8th is the beginning of Summer, or rather of the heat; on the eleventh they appear; and on the 12th they have risen. In November, on the eleventh, they set. This is also confirmed by Pliny in Book 18, Chapter 31: "Then on the 3rd day before the Ides of November, the Vergiliae set in the evening" <note>original Latin: "Deinde III. Idus Nouembris Vergiliæ Veſperi occidunt"</note>. They took the name **Vergiliae** from the fact that they rise in the morning toward the Spring Equinox, called *Ver* in Latin. But all the above must be related to the more Eastern and warm regions; as even in Palestine, where sowing is delayed, and conversely the harvest is advanced, more so than here among us Westerners.

[They] produce great rains, for which reason the Latins call them *Succulae* <note>Latin for "little pigs."</note>. Pliny <note>A Roman natural philosopher.</note> says in Book 2, Chapter 39: *Just as we perceive to happen with the "little pigs," which the Greeks for this reason call the Hyades, a name signifying rain* <note>original Latin: "Qualiter in Succulis sentimus accidere, quas græci ob id pluuio nomine Hyadas appellant"</note>. This is what some ignorant people, he says in Book 18, Chapter 26, have estimated to proceed from the word *Sus*, which in Latin signifies a sow or a pig—an animal that delights in filth (*and the sow, friend to the mud*, says Horace <note>A Roman lyric poet.</note>)—which is made of earth soaked with water, as occurs during the rains: *While the Greeks call these stars Hyades, our people [the Romans], thinking by a mistake of names that they were so named because of sows, out of ignorance called them "little pigs"* <note>original Latin: "Hyadas appellantibus græcis has stellas, quod Nostri à similitudine cognominis græci propter sues impositum arbitrantes, imperitia appellauere suculas"</note>. To such an extent that the Latin interpreter of Aratus <note>A Greek poet who wrote on astronomy.</note> wishes instead to derive the name from *Succus* <note>Latin for "juice," "sap," or "moisture."</note>, which presupposes humidity.

Hyginus <note>A Latin author of mythological handbooks.</note>, in his treatise on the celestial signs, lists seven of them in number, like the *Pleiades*, following the Athenian Pherenydes <note>An early Greek mythographer.</note>, who says they were the nurses of Bacchus <note>The god of wine and fertility, also known as Dionysus.</note>. Previously they were called the *Dodonid Nymphs*, from Dodona, a city in Epirus; their names were *Ambrosia, Eudora, Pedile, Coronis, Polyxo, Phyto, and Thyone*. These nymphs, seeing themselves persecuted by Lycurgus <note>A king of Thrace who banned the cult of Dionysus.</note> at the persuasion of Juno—who was jealous of Jupiter regarding this Bacchus, whom he had fathered by Semele, otherwise called *Hyen* according to the same Pherenydes—fled to Thebes and carried him with them to protect him, where they entrusted him into the hands of Ino. Jupiter, wishing to recognize their service, translated them into the number of the *stars*.

In this regard, Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and philosopher.</note> in his treatise *On Osiris* writes that Dionysus or Bacchus was called *Hyes* <note>A Greek epithet meaning "the Rainer."</note> because he presides over moist nature. This is also confirmed by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia.</note> under the entry *ὕης* <note>Hyes</note> following Clidemus, where he says it is an epithet of Bacchus because it was customary to sacrifice to him when it rained. Musaeus <note>A legendary Greek poet.</note>, moreover, who lists only five *Hyades*, recounts that from Atlas and Pleione were born fifteen daughters and one son named Hyas, whom his sisters loved singularly. When he was killed by a lion while hunting, the first five sisters named wept for him so much that they died of grief; for this reason, they were generally called *Hyades* after the name of their brother *Hyas*. According to Theseus in his commentary on Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet.</note>, Hyas practiced the hunting of serpents, by which he was bitten. The Poets, and among others Ovid in the 5th book of the *Fasti*, recount that Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury, having joined company to make their circuits and visits down here upon the earth, arrived late one evening at the hut of a poor laborer named Hyreus. He received them very courteously, even though he did not recognize them as gods, and killed the only ox he owned to treat them. At this, Jupiter, admiring such honesty, granted him the favor of requesting whatever he might wish for; which was to have a child, without, however, remarrying, because he had promised and solemnly sworn this to his wife when she died. And thereupon, these gods, having the hide of the ox sacrificed for their arrival brought to them, all three urinated into it, and ordered him to bury it in the earth without moving or uncovering it for ten months. At the end of this time, from this mingled urine was born a child, who from that—by the change of a single letter—was named Orion <note>A folk etymology linking the name Orion to "ourion," the Greek word for urine.</note>. In this regard, her ministers and priests in Comana, a city of Cappadocia, would draw blood from their own arms and shoulders to offer to her, being as if possessed by a fury. # PYRRHUS AND

...having been obscured there quite intentionally, following their custom of affectation, believing they would gain more grace thereby, if it were not clarified by Homer himself, who made it more apparent in this manner:

> <note>original Greek: Ἱ'έμενοι νεοῖο βαθεί ης τέ λσον ἵκεσθαι. Η' δ' ἐμελαί νετ' ὄπισθεν, ἀρηρομἐ η δὲ ἐῴκει, Χρυσείη περ ἐοῦσα. τὸ δή περὶ θαῦμ' ἐτέ τυκτο.</note>
> Striving to reach the end of the deep field; and the soil turned black behind them, and looked as if it had been plowed, though it was made of gold; this was the great wonder of the work.

Desiring to reach the end of the field, which turned black behind them and appeared to be plowed even though it was of gold—therein lay the cause for admiration. For it is common that the surface of the earth, being dried by the rays of the Sun and the wind, appears whiter than when it is freshly turned, because of the moisture trapped within which makes it darker, as one can see by experience. Therefore, making the gold "turn black" does not mean that the gold from which the shield of Achilles and Pyrrhus was made actually blackened, but rather that the laborers were diligently performing their work and finishing the plowing of the field; as the earth was overturned by the plow, it appeared to blacken, despite it being only gold, which underwent no actual change. Thus, the artistry represents the thing to us through its visual effect.

Regarding the domestic vines, it should suffice for you to imagine some kind of enclosure made of tin; however, silver is required for the vineyard in the open country. This has likewise been obscured by Philostratus, <note>Philostratus the Elder (c. 190 – c. 230 AD), a Greek sophist who wrote descriptions of paintings (*Imagines*).</note> who wished in this place to add something of his own to Homer—though in truth he did so quite delicately—whereas Homer had only said:

Philostratus, therefore—though the passage is somewhat corrupted—intended to expand upon this a little: *For it is enough for you to imagine the fence around the domestic vines to be of tin. But the silver belongs in the vineyard.* <note>original Greek: ἀρκεῖ γὰρ σοι τὸ περὶ ταῖς ἡμερίσιν ἕρκος ἐν τῷ κασιτερῷ νοεῖν. ὁ δ' ἄργυρος ὁ ἐν τῷ ἀμπελῶνι.</note> It is sufficient for you to perceive around the domestic vines a fence of tin, but the vineyard deserves one of silver. As if he meant to say that because the verjuice <note>term: verjuice (French: verjuz). The tart, acidic juice of unripe grapes, often grown on domestic trellises rather than for fine wine.</note> usually produced by the trellises (which he understands as domestic vines) is not as precious as wine, it is likewise not reasonable that their fence be of such rich material as that of the vineyards where wine grows: which he indicates by tin and silver.

TO THE CADENCE of an Evian and Bacchic note <note>Evian refers to "Evoe," the ritual cry of the followers of Bacchus (Dionysus), the god of wine.</note>.
Homer puts it differently; *And he sang the beautiful Linus* <note>original Greek: Λίνον δ' ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄειδε</note>; that is, he sang the beautiful Linus, namely the hymn composed about Linus. Lexicons or dictionaries state that *linos* is a type of folk song <note>original French: vaudeville, used here in its archaic sense of a popular street song or satirical poem.</note>; but Pausanias, more to the point in his *Description of Boeotia*, writes that Linus, son of the Muse Urania and Amphimarus (son of Neptune), was the most excellent musician of his time. He was equal in playing the lyre and in singing to Apollo, who, moved by envy for this reason, put him to death. The regret for this death reached even the most foreign and distant lands, so that the Egyptians composed a lay or song about him and his disaster called "Linus"—though otherwise they called common songs in their language *Euaneres*. But among the Greek poets, Homer, knowing well that the calamity of Linus was one of the Greek songs, in describing the shield of Achilles, also expressed there a youth who, playing the lyre, sang at the same time this beautiful song made of the misfortune of Linus. However, Pamphus, who composed the oldest hymns of the Athenians, not wishing to recall this name of Linus because of the sorrow felt for it, called him Aetolin. Sappho of Lesbos borrowed this word "Aetolin" from the verses of Pamphus to apply it to Adonis, whom she also calls Aetolin. This is what Pausanias records, which will serve to clarify this passage.

Here, Philostratus <note>Philostratus the Elder, a Greek author known for describing a gallery of paintings in his work "Imagines."</note> first places the Galley fleeing by force of oars, with Medea aboard; then the Dragon coiled around the Beech tree <term>Fousteau: an archaic French term for the beech tree.</term>; and after that should follow (so he says) the combat with the bulls—that is to say, the labor Jason had in binding them, given the resistance they must have shown. Truly, he should have spoken of the bulls before the dragon and the fleeing lady. But it is arranged in this manner following the rules of painting, which always places the most recently completed actions closest to our sight, and from there moves backward to the most distant events by way of perspective.

Hymns comprise both of these—both Psalms and Canticles—as can be seen in those of <term>Orpheus</term> <note>The legendary Greek musician whose "Orphic Hymns" were a collection of poetic invocations to various deities.</note>.

Furthermore, the brevity of time does not allow us to describe exactly the beauty of this Princess; especially as the uncertain doubt she has for her life, and the anguish with which her spirit is buffeted by the things she sees with her own eyes, withers the natural bloom of her complexion. Nevertheless, she gives enough cause to conjecture from what is visible what her perfection must be when she is in her accustomed state.

### ANNOTATION.

*Since this painting is so particularly expressed and depicted, there remains little to say about it; only it seemed to us fitting to bring in word-for-word what Palaephatus <note>original: "Palephate"; an ancient Greek author who wrote "On Incredible Tales," seeking to explain myths as misunderstood historical events.</note> attempts to allegorize, especially regarding the monster in question here. As for this Whale, Sperm Whale, or other such sea monster <note>original: "Cetus Balenie, Physetere"; Cetus is the Latin term for a large sea creature, while "Physetere" refers to a blowing whale.</note>, which it is sometimes told was accustomed to emerge from the sea to throw itself upon the Trojans—to whom, if they exposed their daughters to be devoured, it would return without doing harm, otherwise it would waste the whole country—who is he who does not see quite openly what great simplicity <note>In this context, "simplicity" refers to naivety or foolishness.</note> it would be to believe those people were so idiotic and ill-advised as to present their own daughters to a cruel monster? It is much more likely that this "Cetus" was some King or other Prince so named, who, being very powerful at sea, ruined a marsh that the Trojans possessed along the coast, and imposed a tribute upon them, which is called in Greek tribute <note>original: "δασμός" (*dasmos*); meaning a portion, tax, or tribute.</note>, for in those times they used no gold or silver, but only goods and utensils. Thus, then, this King named Cetus imposed on the cities of those quarters: on some a certain number of horses, and on others virgin daughters. If they refused to pay him this imposition, he would sack their territory. And it happened by chance that he arrived to collect it before Troy at the same time that Hercules had arrived there with an army of Greeks; Laomedon took them into his pay <note>original: "print à sa soulde"; hired them as mercenaries.</note> against Cetus, who was defeated and put to death, which would have given rise to the fable.*

*It is incredible how such grandeur could have been represented in so small a volume. This relates to what Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and natural philosopher.</note> in Book 35, chapter 10, says of Timanthes, an ancient painter among the most inventive and ingenious. Timanthes was of a marvelous spirit: and by him is this Iphigenia so celebrated by the—*

### ANNOTATION.

This painting being so precisely described and depicted, not much remains to be said about it; it only seemed right to us to include, word-for-word, what Palaephatus <note>An ancient Greek author known for "rationalizing" myths—explaining supernatural stories as misunderstandings of historical events.</note> attempts to interpret allegorically, specifically regarding the monster in question here. As for this Whale, Sperm Whale <note>original: "Cetus Balenie, Physetere"; references to large sea monsters or whales.</note>, or other such sea beast, which is sometimes said to have been in the habit of emerging from the sea to fall upon the Trojans—to whom, if they offered up their daughters to be devoured, it would return without doing harm, but otherwise it would lay waste to the whole country—who cannot see quite clearly what great naivety it would be to believe those people were so idiotic and ill-advised as to offer their own daughters to a cruel monster? 

It is much more likely that this "Cetus" was some King or other Prince of that name, who, being very powerful by sea, ruined a marshland that the Trojans possessed along the coast and imposed a tribute <note>original: "δασμὸς" (dasmos); a Greek term for a tax or tribute.</note> upon them. For in those days, gold and silver were not used, only goods and utensils. Thus, this King named Cetus imposed on the cities of those regions a requirement: for some, a certain number of horses, and for others, virgin daughters. If they refused to pay this tax, he would pillage their territory. And having arrived by chance to collect it before Troy at the same time that Hercules had landed there with an army of Greeks, Laomedon hired them <note>original: "print à sa soulde"; literally 'took into his pay' as mercenaries.</note> to fight against Cetus, who was defeated and put to death. This event is what gave rise to the fable.

It is incredible how such greatness could have been represented in such a small volume. *This refers to what Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of Natural History.</note> says in book 35, chapter 10, concerning Timanthes, one of the most inventive and ingenious of the ancient painters. Timanthes possessed a marvelous spirit; and by his hand is that Iphigenia <note>A famous lost painting of the sacrifice of Iphigenia, noted for the painter's clever way of depicting different levels of grief.</note> so celebrated by the—*

From **Ariston** came another **Sophocles**, also a tragic poet, who composed 40 tragedies and won seven victories: plus another of the same name, a tragic and lyric poet, who came after the **Pleiades** <term>Pleiades: a group of seven tragic poets in 3rd-century BCE Alexandria, named after the star cluster</term>, as they call those seven poets who all emerged at the same time.

**To show him how to draw the bow.** *Leto had two children by Jupiter: Apollo and Diana, both of whom were excellent archers. This is clearly shown by the opening of the Hymn to Apollo in Homer:*

From which bow he was also accustomed to let fly, in the manner of arrows, incurable diseases and other discomforts and ruins upon mortals, which Plutarch calls "solar" ailments; those who are afflicted by them are called "struck by Apollo" <note>original Greek: Ἀπολλωνοβλήτοι (Apollonobletoi)</note> or "sun-struck" <note>original Greek: ἡλιοβλήτοι (heliobletoi)</note>. It first invaded the horses and the dogs, then the people. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Apollo’s divine nature, moving from the physical instruments mentioned on the previous page to the metaphorical harmony Apollo creates as the sun and the leader of the Muses.</meta>

# HYACINTH.

The sun, which is nothing other than Apollo, touches and moves every part of the universe very appropriately and in good harmony, creating together a beautiful concert of Music, well-proportioned with many voices and instruments tuned to one another; he introduces himself everywhere in such a way that no discord is found in nature. He furthermore creates the seasons of the year, which follow one another in turn, and through the dryness that his rays cause in the air, the voices of animals and the songs of birds reach our ears more quickly and from further away. *He says this because we see well enough by experience that just as sight extends more clearly and easily through clear and limpid water, in the same way hearing <note>original: "l'oye"</note> functions through pure and serene air more distinctly than if it were murky and thick, heavy with mists and clouds.* By this means, Apollo is made to be the leader and guardian of the Muses, who preside over Music. This Music, according to Plato, was not granted by the gods to men for a voluptuous enjoyment or a delicate tickling of the ear, but rather to be employed in divine service and honor, and afterward to make us more modest, gracious, and well-mannered—as Plutarch cites from him in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*. And in the *Treatise on Music*, he says that the image of Apollo that was in Delos held a bow in the right hand, and in the left the three Graces: one having a Lyre in her hand, the other an Oboe <term>original: auboys; a double-reed woodwind instrument, ancestor of the modern oboe</term>, and the third a German flute that she held to her mouth. Regarding this same subject of Apollo and Music, Plato, at the very beginning of the Dialogue on poetry titled *Ion*, notes that at Epidaurus, prize games were celebrated every year in honor of Aesculapius, son of Apollo, on the day of his feast and solemnity. As for the first inventors of music, they must have been very ancient, for Orpheus and Linus were most excellent Musicians, as these verses from the 4th Eclogue of Virgil mark among others:

> Neither Thracian Orpheus nor Linus shall defeat me in song, 
> Though the mother be present for the one, and the father for the other. 
<note>original Latin: "Non me carminibus vincet nec thracius Orpheus, / Nec Linus, Huic mater quãuis, atque huic pater adfit." Virgil refers to Orpheus's mother, the Muse Calliope, and Linus's father, Apollo.</note>

->*Orpheus has Calliope; the beautiful Apollo has Linus.* <note>original Latin: "Orphei Calliopea, Lini formosus Apollo." A reference to the divine parentage or patronage of legendary musicians.</note><-

For by "songs" <note>original: "carmes"; from the Latin *carmina*</note> one must understand the verses that were recited aloud in song accompanied by an instrument, as can be gathered from the first book of the *Aeneid*:

->— *Long-haired Iopas makes the golden lyre resound.* <note>original Latin: "Cythara crinitus Iopas Personat aurata."</note><-

And then afterward:

->*He sings of the wandering moon, and the labors of the sun.* <note>original Latin: "Hic canit errantem lunam, solisque labores." In classical poetry, the "labors" of the sun often refer to eclipses.</note><-

Plato, therefore, in the third book of the *Laws*, attributes the invention of that which concerns Music to Marsyas and Olympus; and the Lyre to Amphion, to whom Pliny in Book 7, Chapter 56, refers it quite resolutely. Nevertheless, he details it in this manner: Amphion invented Music; Pan, the flute with nine holes; the *monaulos* <note>a single-pipe flute</note> or the reed-pipe of a single tone, Mercury; the German flute (the Italians call it the *traversa* <note>transverse flute</note> in imitation of the Latin *obliqua tibia* <note>slanting pipe</note>), Midas in Phrygia; two flutes coupled together, Marsyas; Amphion the Lydian air; Thamyris of Thrace, the Dorian; Marsyas the Phrygian. Amphion again the Cithara <note>original: "Listre"</note> and the Lyre—or Orpheus according to others, and some say Linus. Terpander added up to seven strings, Simonides the eighth, and Timotheus the ninth. But for simply playing the Lyre without accompanying it with the voice, Thamyris was the first author; with the voice, Amphion, or Linus according to some. To sing in intervals while playing the flutes was established by Trezenus the Dardanian. This is how Pliny speaks of it. But the interpreters of Homer on the penultimate book of the *Odyssey* attribute to Mercury the invention of letters, Music, wrestling, and geometry. For this reason, in the schools of exercise <note>the gymnasia</note> he was represented in square form, or with four faces, as seen in certain boundary stones <term>original: "termes"; statues consisting of a head or torso atop a square stone pillar</term>, of which Plutarch speaks in the *Life of Alcibiades* and of *Nicias*, calling them Herms <note>original: "Hermes"</note>, images of Mercury, which Pausanias in the *Messenian* books claims were the invention of the Athenians, from whom others learned to make them square in this way.

# HYACINTH.

Apollo was held in paganism to be the god of predictions and divinations <note>original: "deuienemens"</note>, because of his oracle at Delphi where people flocked from all parts of the earth to seek counsel and obtain advice concerning the past, the present, and the future: As the Poet says;
> *Those things which are, those which were, and those which are drawn toward the future.* <note>original Latin: "Quæ sunt, quæ fuerint, & quæ ventura trahuntur." A common classical phrasing of total prophetic knowledge.</note>

And this oracle lasted in its strength and reputation for nearly three thousand years according to Plutarch in his treatise on the Pythia, until the time of Lucan <note>OCR reads "Lucron," likely referring to the Roman poet Lucan</note>, some fifty years before the birth of the SAVIOR, when it began to decline, as he says in the second book *On Divination*:
> *Such force and vigor the light of truth already possessed, even before its physical arrival, against the darkness of the father of lies who reigned in these false oracles: just as the first herald rays of the Sun—even before its luminous globe begins to appear on the horizon and seems to graze the surface of the earth—dissipate and drive away the foul humors and vapors that night is accustomed to produce in its absence.*

But regarding this science of divining that Apollo promises here to the beautiful Hyacinth, it is said that this god, having once fallen in love with Cassandra, daughter of King Priam, for her excellent beauty, gave her the choice of anything she might require from him in exchange for his enjoyment of her. Having only asked to know how to predict future things, after he had granted it to her, she mocked him and would not keep her promise. Irritated by this, because he could no longer take back what he had once given, he decreed that no one should ever believe her predictions. This was partly the cause of the ruin of her homeland. But concerning this oracle and what depends upon it, it has been discussed sufficiently before in the description of the painting of Phorbas, and other types of divinations <note>original: "deuinemens"</note> in that of Hercules in the cradle. To which may still be added this verse from the *Hymn to Apollo* in Homer;
> *I shall declare to men the infallible will of Zeus.* <note>original Greek: "χρήσω τ' ἀνθρώποισι Διὸς νημερτέ α βυλή."</note>

And furthermore, that it was Apollo who instituted the first oracle on earth:
> *Or how, seeking the first place of prophecy for men, you went through the land, far-shooting Apollo.* <note>original Greek: "Ἡ’ ὡς τὸ πρῶτον χρηστήριον ἀνθρώποισι Ζυτευών κτ’ γαῖαν ἔβης ἑκατηβόλ’ Α’πόλλων."</note>

ambiguous deceptions. Nevertheless, as **Cicero** says very well in the aforementioned passage: In this matter, one must rather regard the events and seek them out, than the causes:

> *For there are many things that are similar which are not the same;* <note>original Latin: "Multa enim sunt similia quæ non sunt eadem;"</note>

than the rules and canons of **Astrology**, which commonly strike more at generalities than at particular instances.

# HYACINTH.

...And to make him excellent above all others in wrestling. The Greek text uses the word *palaistra* <note>original: "παλαίστρα"</note>, which indeed signifies wrestling; but this word extends to several other meanings and is generally taken for all bodily exercises designated by the *pentathlon* <note>original: "πένταθλος", the five-fold contest</note>, which were anciently practiced in the solemn games of Greece: namely running, jumping, wrestling, the discus, and boxing with fists. All of these have been discussed at length in the descriptions of the pictures of Arrichion and Phorbas, and will be again in the *Heroics*. The word "Palaestra" is also used for the place where one went for combat. The Greeks call it a *gymnasion* <note>original: "γυμνάσιον"</note>, from *gymnazesthai* <note>original: "γυμνάζεσθαι"</note>, meaning to strip oneself entirely naked, because it was necessary to undress both to learn and to perform in earnest. This can be seen in the fifth book of Vitruvius, where he demonstrates its architecture, and in the *Bacchides* of Plautus. Cicero, furthermore, in the first letter of the third book to his brother Quintus, and in the second book of *The Laws*, describing the place of pleasure he had at Arpi, calls it a "Palaestra"; and Virgil likewise in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*:

> Some exercise their limbs on the grassy wrestling-grounds. <note>original Latin: "Pars in gramineis exercent membra palestris."</note>

As does Geta in the *Phormio* of Terence:

> Look, he comes forth from his own wrestling-ground, <note>original Latin: "Eccum à sua palestra exit foras"</note>

wishing by this to denote the lodging of the mistress whom his young master was supporting, which was his entire exercise and occupation. Suetonius also touches on this in *Domitian* 22, speaking of his lust:

> Being of excessive lust, he called the persistence of sexual intercourse a kind of exercise, "bed-wrestling"; <note>original Latin: "Libidinis nimiæ, assiduitatem concubitus velut exercitationis genus, clinopalen vocabat." The term "clinopale" is a pun on the Greek words for bed and wrestling.</note>

namely, the exercise of Venus within four bed-curtains. The term is also taken for the elaborate pleadings of lawyers in Cicero, he having followed the ancient poet Lucilius in this, from whom we have this verse cited by Porphyrio, the interpreter of Horace:

> The wrestling-ground of the judge Hortensius was born for that matter. <note>original Latin: "Iudicis Hortensi est ad eam rem nata palestra." Here, "palaestra" refers to forensic skill or rhetorical training.</note>

And Plato, at the very beginning of the *Charmides*, takes it for the place where men of letters were accustomed to assemble to dispute and confer about their studies. But Plutarch, in the second book of the *Symposiacs*, fourth question, restricts it only to the floor where the athletes practiced wrestling. This he calls the "rolling pancratium" <note>The *pancratium* was a no-holds-barred combat sport; "volutatoire" refers to rolling on the ground.</note>, where they wallowed and tumbled in the dust, biting, weighing down, scratching, and doing the worst they could to one another. Plato, in the seventh book of the *Laws*, states that Antaeus and Cercyon were the first authors of it.

Others attribute it to **Theseus** after he had overcome **Cercyon** <note>Theseus was a legendary king of Athens; Cercyon was a cruel king who forced travelers to wrestle him to the death until Theseus defeated him using skill over strength</note>, and this as a preparation for war. Regarding this, **Suidas** <note>The *Suda*, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia formerly attributed to an author named Suidas</note> says: "Palaestra, having found a slope in a certain place which seemed suitable to him for arranging cavalry and infantry in battle, had it leveled and hollowed out to serve for the exercises of war and arms." Some believe it serves to strengthen the body and for health: but what health could one have in this violent exercise, so arduous and so dangerous? Nevertheless, there was perhaps some more moderate wrestling, of which it seems that **Clement of Alexandria** <note>An early Christian theologian, c. 150–215 AD</note> wishes to speak in the 3rd book of his *Pedagogue*, where he calls it, "accompanied by decency and honesty" <note>original Greek: "μετ’ εὐσχήμονος"</note>. By which means **Hercules** (he says) was the first to institute that when wrestling, men should cover their private parts with a loincloth <note>term: "brayer" — a primitive form of athletic trunks or a loincloth used for modesty</note>. This is what these hendecasyllables <note>eleven-syllable poetic lines</note> from the first book of **Martial** intend to strike at:

Whatever its origin, it was the second part of gymnastics or exercising with a naked body, which **Plato** in his books of the *Laws* divides into two: namely, *dancing* <note>original Greek: "ὄρχησις"</note> or the saltatory art <note>term: saltatory — relating to jumping or dancing</note>, which includes all sorts of dances, ballets, *mattachins* <note>term: mattachins — a traditional sword dance performed by masked dancers</note>, the Cubistic art or acrobatics of somersaults, and the "Feats of Hercules" <note>likely referring to staged displays of strength</note>, the ball game played in cadence so exactly represented by **Homer** in the 6th book of the *Odyssey*, the Pyrrhic dance or armed dance, which is very close to what jesters dance with shields and swords: and many other such exercises which are not relevant here. 

The other was wrestling, in which one practiced within the place called the **Xystus** <note>term: Xystus — a covered portico or gallery where ancient athletes practiced in winter</note>, where the wrestlers, their bodies completely naked and anointed with oil to make grasping them more difficult—then sprinkled over with a very fine dust in order to absorb the sweat—came to seize one another as best they could, by the arms and the hollow of the waist <note>original: "fau du corps"</note>, trying by infinite turns of dexterity and strength, leg-hooks, traps, *clinquets* <note>term: clinquet — a specific wrestling maneuver or "click" involving the feet</note>, and similar terms of the art used in **Brittany** <margin>Brittany was (and is) famous for its traditional style of wrestling called Gouren</margin>, to throw each other to the ground on their backs; for falling on the belly, which is called "giving the paunch," counts for nothing. 

The Greeks called these maneuvers *the charge* <note>original Greek: "ἐμβολὴ"</note>, the first approach and meeting when one comes to grips; *the entanglement* <note>original Greek: "παρεμβολὴ"</note>, the links, hookings, and interweaving of arms and legs; *the positioning* <note>original Greek: "διαθέσις"</note>, the approaches and sizing up of one another before grappling and seizing; *the engagement* <note>original Greek: "σύστασις"</note>, the ruses, feints, ambushes, deceptions, and schemes one sets up to floor the other. And other such devices, which aimed primarily at wrapping the legs of one's adversary to trip him, because these are what support the body, as pillars and columns support the arches and vaults resting upon them. This is what **Plautus**'s *Pseudolus* <note>A Roman comedy by Titus Maccius Plautus, c. 191 BC</note> aims at in Act 5, speaking of the wine with which he has become drunk, that it acts like a cunning wrestler who addresses the legs first, because in drunk people, they are the first to begin to falter.

...is nothing other than that the Sun is the author of life; "the Sun and man beget man," says the *Philosopher* <note>A common Renaissance reference to Aristotle, specifically his *Physics*</note>. By the *Swan*, on the other hand, is represented the sweet and graceful departure from this life, especially for good people, who leave the life of the body not with regret, but with a great joy of spirit, to go find the life of the soul. This soul proceeds from that other *Sun*, which the *Kabbalists* call *Tiphereth* <term>Tiphereth — in the Jewish Kabbalah, the sixth Sephirah (emanation), symbolizing beauty, compassion, and the spiritual Sun</term>, the source of all ornament and beauty in the intelligible world, of which the sensible *Sun* is the true type and exemplar. For as soon as they sense their hour has arrived—if they have ever sung well in all their life—they then strengthen their melodious harmony with all their power, rejoicing that they will soon see that god whose *Ministers* and servants they were here below." 

But men, because they fear and abhor death, have also invented lies against these excellent birds, alleging that they sing because they deplore their own end, and that from the anguish they feel and the pains that come to prick them, they force themselves to sing thus more vehemently than usual. In this, they do not consider that there is no bird that sings when it is pressed by hunger, or when it feels the cold, or is bothered by some other languor that afflicts it. Neither the nightingale, nor the swallow, not even the *Hoopoe* <note>original: "Huppe"</note> itself, which they say is accustomed to sing, or rather groan, out of grief. 

By which means, that which the *Swans* warble so sweetly when they are on the point of giving up the ghost is, in my opinion, because they are consecrated to *Apollo*, and therefore provided with a certain instinct for divination, when they foresee the blessings that are in the af— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "l'autre" (the other life/afterlife)</note>

### HYACINTHE. ###

...[past] century: This is what causes them to strengthen their music at the hour of their passing, in which they rejoice much more than in all the rest of their past life. *On this subject, Ovid, at the very beginning of the Letter from Dido to Aeneas,* <note>Referring to Ovid's *Heroides*, VII</note>

> Even so, when the fates call, the white swan, cast down upon the wet grass by the waters of the Meander, sings his song. <note>original: "Sic vbi fata vocant vdis abiectus in herbis / Ad vada mæandri concinit albus olor."</note>

As if they wished to give thanks to the divinity for stripping them of this hindering carcass, in which their spirit remains entangled—*though this leans somewhat toward the Pythagorean philosophy of the transmigration of human souls into animals* <note>The belief that souls move from one body to another after death, a core tenet of Pythagoras</note>—as if in a dark prison. For according to Cicero in his *Tusculan Disputations*, swans are attributed to Apollo, who is the god of divination, because among all others, they most clearly foresee their approaching end and rejoice in it, receiving it with great contentment and pleasure, as if they foresaw by an occult divine inspiration the good that is in death. These are the words of Cicero, which he must have borrowed from Plato, as he did many other things. Furthermore, swans are a mark and symbol of the Poets, who have that god [Apollo] as their Patron. And this is what Horace intends to address in the 20th Ode of the second book of his *Odes*, already previously cited in the argument of the painting of Orpheus, where he says he must be transformed into a swan, which with its song will fill the whole circle of the earth.

> Now, even now, rough skin settles on my legs, and I am changed into a white bird above; smooth feathers grow on my fingers and shoulders. <note>original: "Iam iam residunt cruribus asperæ / Pelles, & album mutor in alitem / Superne, nascunturque leues / Per digitos, humerósque plumæ."</note>

But this is an allusion he makes to old age, by which he feels himself now affected; it produces rough skin on his legs and turns his hair white. Plutarch, in his interpretation of the word **Ei** <note>Referring to Plutarch's essay *On the E at Delphi*, which discusses the mysterious inscription at the temple of Apollo</note>, says that Apollo delights in Music, the song of swans, and the sound of the cithara. And in the treatise *On the Cleverness of Animals*, [he writes] that it was the swans and nightingales who invented Music. This conforms to what Phurnutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher who wrote on Greek mythology</note> writes in the chapter on Apollo and Diana: that the swan is

...dedicated to Apollo, because it surpasses all other birds in the sweetness of its song and the whiteness of its plumage; this has a certain affinity with the light of day which comes from the Sun and is white, as are all luminous things. By contrast, the shadows and the night are black and dark, like the Raven, which Apollo holds in hatred and detestation. For the Raven’s gossip was the cause of Apollo, seized with jealousy, killing his most beloved *Coronis*, who was pregnant by him with *Aesculapius*, as is recounted in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*. Consequently, he turned the bird black, though it was white before.

Regarding the places where Apollo took the most pleasure, and which he promised to have *Hyacinthus* visit while mounted upon a *Swan*, *Homer* in his *Hymn* <note>The Homeric Hymn to Apollo</note> specifies the greater part, providing a catalogue of them: "All those that Crete contains within, and the land of Athens," etc. <note>original Greek: ὅσσας κρήτη ἐντὸς ἔχει, καὶ δῆμος Ἀθηνῶν</note> From all these places and many others, he acquired various epithets, which must be examined here in a bit more detail; leaving aside others that are not relevant to this topic and which depend—according to *Macrobius* <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and philosopher</note>—on the force and virtue of the Sun. This deity is called "the Sun" in the Heavens; *Liber* and *Bacchus* <note>Names for the god of wine and theater, here linked to solar energy</note> on the Earth; and Apollo in the underworld. However, *Plato* in his *Cratylus* <note>A dialogue by Plato on the philosophy of language and names</note> wishes to derive the name "from the brandishing of rays," <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν τὰς ἀκτῖνας</note> meaning the darting of his beams. But there are infinite other etymologies.

HOMER, then, first lists the island of *Crete* or *Candia*, a kingdom belonging to the *Lordship of Venice*. <note>At the time of the author's writing, Crete was a major colony of the Republic of Venice.</note> Then *Athens*, a city so famous in ancient times, both for the practice of the arts and sciences which flourished there more than in any other part of the earth, and for their great power upon the sea. But today, it is stripped of all its ancient ornaments and reduced to a few poor, miserable little shacks for fishermen, set among great piles and heaps of stones—an inhabitancy for snakes, lizards, and similar vermin.

AEGINA, an island with a city of the same name, near the shore of the *Peloponnese* and the coast of *Attica*. For it was separated from the famous port of *Piraeus* at the foot of *Athens* by only four leagues; it was named after *Aegina*, daughter of *Asopus*, King of *Boeotia*...

And in one of its hands it would hold a city capable of ten thousand inhabitants, and in the right hand a large cup in the form of a lake, into which a great river would flow, and from there discharge into the sea. ### HYACINTHE. ###

**50**

**CLAROS**, a city of Ionia, formerly very renowned for the oracle of Apollo, who from there was surnamed Clarius; for there was a certain water, by drinking of which the Priests gave their responses, though they lived but a short time. Pliny, in Book 2, Chapter 6, refers this to the city of Colophon: *In the cave of the Clarian Apollo at Colophon there is a pool, by the drinking of which miraculous oracles are given, though the life of the drinkers is shortened.* <note>original Latin: "Colophone in Apollinis clarij specu lacuna est, cuius potu mira redduntur oracula, bibentium breuiore vita."</note> And Strabo in Book 14 writes that the seer Calchas, after the fall of Troy, while returning by land with Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus, found another in Claros more excellent than himself. For when Calchas, to test him, asked what he thought of the litter of a sow that was there ready to farrow, Mopsus replied that she had only three piglets—namely, two males and one female. This was found to be the case. And Calchas in his turn, having been unable to answer truly how many figs were on a small fig tree laden with fruit, Mopsus guessed it exactly without being off by a single one. Calchas, vexed to see himself surpassed in his art, died there of displeasure. Nearchus wishes to derive this word "Claros" from *kleros* <note>original Greek: κλῆρος</note>, meaning "lot" or "inheritance," because it fell to Apollo's share by lot. Others derive it from *klaiein* <note>original Greek: κλαίειν</note>, meaning "to weep," because Manto, daughter of the seer Tiresias—to whom they attribute the first founding—fled there from Thebes after the Epigones <term>the "descendants" of the Seven Against Thebes who finally conquered the city</term> had ruined it; there, she made a fountain from her tears, from which the place took its name. It is also an island of the Myrtoan Sea in the Archipelago, between Tenedos and Chios, dedicated to Apollo. Ovid in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> The Delphic land and Claros, and Tenedos, and the realm of Patara serve me. <note>original Latin: "Mihi delphica tellus / Et Claros, & Tenedos, pataraeaque regia feruit"</note>

And Callimachus in his Hymn:

> O Apollo, many call you the Helper,
> Many call you Clarius, etc. <note>original Greek: Ω' πόλλων, πολλοί σε βοηδρόμιον καλέυσι / Πολλοί δὲ κλάριον, &c. Boedromios translates to "the Helper" or "one who runs to a war-cry."</note>

**MICALE**, a city of Caria according to Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary</note>; so named because it was situated in a "cale" or nook of the Carian sea, which is called *mychos* <note>original Greek: μυχός</note> in Greek. Herodotus identifies it as a promontory; Didymus as a mountain which the same Stephanus says is opposite Samos, from which the Nymphs were said to have taken the name of...

# HYACINTHE. 94 #

...Mycalessians. There was also a city of Boeotia so named <note>Mycalessus</note>, where Ceres <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter, associated here with the harvest.</note> was revered, and from there she was likewise called "Mycalessian," in a temple built on the seashore. There, according to Pausanias in his *Description of Boeotia*, Hercules used to perform the duty of closing and opening the doors. Every year, people offered all the fruits that are produced in autumn, which were preserved there throughout the year as fresh as if they had just come from the tree.

**Miletus**, likewise a city of Caria, called *Melaxo* in the common tongue, was very famous for the philosopher Thales—one of the Seven Sages of Greece—who was a native there; also Anaximander, and other excellent personages. But it was more famous still for the oracle of Apollo surnamed Didyma <note>Referring to the great temple of Didyma near Miletus.</note>, as has been mentioned above.

**Cos**, or *Stancou*, an island of the Archipelago <note>The Aegean Sea.</note> and one of the Cyclades, was highly renowned for Hippocrates, the Prince of Physicians, and for Apelles, the most excellent painter who ever lived, both of whom were natives. There was a very beautiful temple of Asclepius <note>The god of medicine</note>, son of Apollo.

**Cnidus**, a city facing Asia at the tip of the Carian peninsula; it was in great vogue in ancient times for that incomparable marble Venus which was previously described in the section on the "Venus Elephantine." <note>This refers to the famous Aphrodite of Cnidus by the sculptor Praxiteles.</note> There was also a temple of Apollo with a small grove of tall timber trees; because Turulius took it upon himself to have them cut down to build ships, he was put to death by the command of Augustus, as recorded by Cassius Dio in Book 50.

**Carpathus**, or *Scarpanto*, is an island halfway between Crete and Rhodes; it sits opposite the coast of Egypt and has given the name "Carpathian" to the surrounding gulf.

**Naxos**, an island of the Archipelago and one of the Cyclades, but rising higher than all the others, otherwise called *Dia*. Today it holds the title of an archbishopric, though the Turk <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire's control of the region at the time of writing.</note> possesses it. This was where Theseus left Ariadne sleeping, in order to go away with her sister Phaedra, as was mentioned in the entry on the painting of Ariadne.

**Paros**, another island of the Cyclades, was in great renown in ancient times for the excellent marble quarried there, which was ideal for making statues because it had the color of flesh without any spots or veins.

**AMYCLEAN.** From *Amyclae*, a city of Laconia, of which *Hyacinth* was a native, as could be seen in his other entry <note>original: "tableau"—referring to a previous section or illustrated plate in this work</note>.

Before it had taken this name, which comes from "appearing" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ δηλοῦ"—from the Greek *delos*, meaning manifest or visible</note> because it appeared amidst the waves, it was called *Ortygia*, *Asteria*, *Gythie*, *Lagia*, *Chlamydia*, *Cynethus*, and *Pyrpile*, from the fire that was first found there.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a classical mythological scene with a seated figure in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>OENEUS, King of Calydonia <note>An ancient Greek region; the city of Calydon was famous in myth for the hunt of the Calydonian Boar.</note>, had by his wife Althea, daughter of Thestius and granddaughter of Parthaon, a son named Meleager. Althea, as soon as she knew it, setting aside her merciful love as a mother for that of a sister, went in her spite to burn the fatal wood-brand <note>The piece of wood the Fates had linked to Meleager's lifespan.</note>; and as it was consumed, Meleager ended his days, devoured by a burning fire within, without any remedy being found. It is told differently elsewhere, but that will be detailed later in the annotation of the painting.

So much so, that it killed a great number of men and maimed others before being brought to bay <note>In the myth, the Calydonian Boar was a monstrous creature sent by Diana (Artemis) to punish King Oeneus for forgetting her in his harvest sacrifices.</note>.

These Curetes, as long as Meleager remained in the fight, always had the disadvantage, until Meleager came into a dispute with his mother Althaea on account of his brothers <note>The text says "brothers" (*freres*), but the myth traditionally specifies that Meleager killed his mother's brothers—his maternal uncles—during the argument over the boar's hide.</note> whom he had put to death with his own hand. Consequently, he no longer wished to go out against those Curetes, but remained quiet and idle at home to enjoy the company of his very dear and well-beloved wife Cleopatra, daughter of Marpessa and of Idas—the most valiant man of his time. It was Idas who had the boldness to pursue the god Apollo with arrows for having carried off his wife; when Marpessa could not be recovered, her mother changed her name to that of Alcyone <note>Also known as the Halcyon, a bird associated with grief and the sea.</note>, for her misfortune was quite similar to that of the other Alcyone, wife of Ceyx. 

Meleager, therefore, indignant against his mother for the imprecations <note>Curses or ritual prayers for vengeance.</note> she made against him for the homicide of his uncles, stayed with his wife, with whom he was also desperately in love for her excellent beauty. He ignored whatever prayers were made to him to take up arms again, whether from the Priests, his father, his mother, or his sisters. He even refused the offers to give him a great number of acres of arable land and vineyards—the best in all the surrounding region—until the Curetes had entered Calydon by force. They had already begun to put everything to fire and sword when Cleopatra, putting before his eyes the piteous disasters and calamities that ordinarily follow such seizures of cities—when they are taken by assault, where all the men are massacred, the fire converts the buildings to ashes, and the women and children are led away into captivity and servitude—by these remonstrances and others like them, she knew how to coax him so well that he took up arms again, and

->## M E L E A G E R.<-

...strong and valiant. And Atropos <note>One of the three Fates (Moirai) in Greek mythology, specifically the one who cuts the thread of life.</note>, taking a firebrand from the hearth, said: "This creature shall live only until this brand is entirely consumed." The mother <note>Althaea, the mother of Meleager.</note>, having heard this, suddenly threw herself out of bed and went to extinguish it. Then she hid it in the middle of the Palace, for fear that it should be consumed by fire. 

And in the following chapter, the same Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Roman mythographer whose work *Fabulae* is a primary source for these myths.</note> specifies name by name—as Ovid also does in the 8th book of the *Metamorphoses*—all the young Lords of note who were present at this hunt of the Boar <note>The Calydonian Boar, a monstrous creature sent by Artemis to ravage the lands of Meleager's father.</note>, of each of whom we shall provide a short summary here, just as we did in the preceding plate regarding the places pleasing to Apollo. This will serve as a relief for those who have not had the opportunity or means to unearth their deeds from Greek and Latin poetry.

**FIRSTLY, Castor and Pollux:** Jupiter, having become enamored with Leda, wife of Tyndareus, enjoyed her company transformed into a Swan, she being already pregnant by her husband. Thus, at the end of nine months, she produced two eggs: from one of which were hatched Pollux and Helen, immortals, as having been procreated from divine seed; and from the other Castor and Clytemnestra, who was the wife of Agamemnon. The two brothers, having reached the age to bear arms, cleared the sea of Pirates, for which reason they have ever since been invoked during storms. They are those two twin fires which, when the sea wishes to calm itself, are accustomed to come and rest upon the yardarms of ships; we commonly call them Saint Elmo’s fire <note>original: "Sainct Herme." A weather phenomenon involving luminous plasma seen on ships during storms, historically viewed as a divine omen by sailors.</note>. They were present on Jason's voyage to Colchis, and in several other enterprises, as was mentioned in the plate concerning Glaucus.

**JASON, son of Aeson and Alcimede:** of him and his deeds, much has been said in the aforementioned plate of Glaucus.

He incurred a very great danger to his life while still a young boy due to the machinations of his stepmother Medea. But after the death of his father, having ascended to the Throne, he did many noble things, as may be seen in his life within Plutarch <note>Referring to Plutarch's *Parallel Lives*, which includes a biography of Theseus.</note>. ### IOLAUS,
Son of Iphicles, who assisted Hercules in exterminating the Hydra: for as Hercules cut off a head, Iolaus would cauterize it with a hot iron, for fear that others might regrow in the same place. One of the Centaurs, whom Hercules put to death for having pursued Deianira in marriage, who had been promised to him. Hyginus, 31.

### ECHION,
One of the Argonauts, and a very fast runner.

### NESTOR,
Son of Neleus, King of Pylos, and of Chloris. In his youth he was present at this hunt, and at the wedding of Pirithous along with Hercules, where he did his brave duty against the Centaurs. ### LAERTES,
Son of Arcesius, King of Ithaca, and father of Ulysses, which is his most illustrious quality.

### ANCAEUS,
There was one who was the son of Neptune and Astypalaea.

they are called *miry boars* <note>original: "sangliers mirez." A term for older boars whose tusks have begun to curve back or "mirror" toward their eyes.</note>. Until the age of eighteen months, they remain with their mothers; and because they then travel in great troops, they are called *beasts of company*, belonging to the *black game* <note>original: "au noir"</note>, that is to say, among the black beasts. But among the *tawny game* <note>original: "au faulue," referring to red or fallow deer</note>, otherwise called the red and gentle ones—also because they have no gall <note>A common historical belief that deer lacked a gallbladder, making them symbols of gentleness.</note>, such as stags, roe deer, and fallow deer—this is called a *herd of beasts*. At two years old, when their teeth or tusks begin to emerge from the young boars' mouths, they are called *Rafaux*; and they keep this name until, feeling strong enough on their own, they separate from the company and henceforth go about their business alone, except when they go to the *rut*, which is to say they enter into their mating season and go in search of the *lees*, which is the name given to their females or *sows*. This *rut* usually begins in Advent, around the feast of St. Andrew <note>November 30.</note>, and their great heat lasts until Christmas, so that their piglets are born in the month of March toward the Spring Equinox. The rut for stags lasts the whole month of September for the oldest ones; then the young ones, who do not dare approach during that time, enter it in their turn. And the hinds give birth in April.

NOW, for as much as the text follows afterwards concerning *the tread of the foot* shown by the tracks, it is better to set down here, all at once, some other terms of *venery* <note>The traditional art and language of hunting.</note> for both *black game* and *tawny game*, to see the difference between them, for one speaks differently of the one and the other. The foot of the black beasts, then, is called the *trace*, referring both to the print of a black beast’s steps and to the entire foot and leg up to the joint. And when these tracks are marked in soft earth that clearly expresses their shape—which is called the *turf* <note>original: "le Gazon"</note>—hunters have sometimes been accustomed to bring it to the assembly when they come to make their report, to demonstrate thereby the size of the boar. But for the stag, this is not done. Furthermore, what are called *dewclaws* on a domestic pig are called *guards* on a wild boar, and *bones* on a stag. In *tawny game*, the foot is called the *foot*, and the steps or vestiges are called the *ways*; but if they are in a meadow or upon the grass, they are called *foilings*. The branches that it breaks and scatters while passing through a *stronghold*—that is, a thicket—are called *bearings*. The head of a boar is the *hure* <note>A culinary and hunting term for the boar's head, still used today.</note>, which is held in higher esteem than all the rest of the black beast; for the stag, not at all. Its teeth are called *tusks*. The horns...

<meta>This page continues the technical glossary of venery (hunting terminology), specifically detailing the specialized vocabulary used to describe the anatomy and behaviors of the stag and the wild boar, following the general distinctions between "black" and "tawny" game established on the previous page.</meta>

-># MELEAGER<-

...of a stag, the head: the <term>forks</term> <note>original: "cornichons"</note> and the <term>tines</term> <note>original: "andoulliers," the sharp branches of the antler</note>. The beam or stalk of which they speak is the <term>main shaft</term> <note>original: "marrein"</note>. The long ridges running lengthwise are the furrows; the small grains with which this shaft is sprinkled are the <term>pearls</term>, at least one says a "well-pearled head" or a "well-pearled shaft." And when there are many tines or forks, it is called "well-pegged." It is "well-sown" when there are as many tines on one side as on the other, and "ill-sown" if there are more on one side. Those large rings where the shaft attaches to the skull are the <term>burrs</term> <note>original: "meulles," the coronet at the base of the antler</note>. If, when a stag is dead, one forcibly and violently separates his antlers from the head while still attached to the skull or cranium, that is called the <term>trophy</term> <note>original: "massacre"</note>. If they fall off by themselves—as they do every year once a stag is five or six years old—and are renewed while increasing in size and number of tines, these are the <term>cast antlers</term> <note>original: "mues"</note>. Between the neck and the shoulder of a boar, where one aims to spear him, is the <term>shield</term> <note>original: "Escu," referring to the thick, tough skin in that area</note>. As for the stag, one never approaches him from the front because of his high-set antlers, which would be no less dangerous to a man on horseback than on foot; rather, one gains the rear if possible to strike him in the hock or the flanks. The dung of a boar is called the <term>scumber</term> <note>original: "layes"</note>, and the droppings of a stag are the <term>fewmets</term> <note>original: "fumees"</note>. The feeding of "black beasts" <note>boars</note>, of which there are several kinds, is called "eating"; for "tawny beasts" <note>deer</note>, it is <term>grazing</term> <note>original: "viander"</note>. Sown fields are called <term>feeding grounds</term> <note>original: "gaignages"</note>. The testicles of a boar are called the <term>pursuits</term> <note>original: "suittes"</note>; those of a stag, the <term>dousets</term> <note>original: "dintiers"</note>. The place where the boar lies down is the <term>wallow</term> <note>original: "baulge"</note>. For a stag, it is the <term>bed</term> <note>original: "lict"</note>, or more commonly the <term>harbor</term> <note>original: "reposee"</note>. And the spot where he stops to take a short pause before going to lie down in the thickest part of the forest is the <term>drying-off spot</term> <note>original: "Ressuit"</note>. Where the beasts—both black and tawny—leave the woods in the evening to go to their foraging, it is called the <term>unharboring</term> <note>original: "desembucher"</note>; where they enter, the <term>re-harboring</term> <note>original: "rembuchement"</note>. The small branches that hunters on the quest throw here and there to serve as markers are <term>broken branches</term> <note>original: "brisees"</note>. When one goes to rouse the beast with a lime-hound <note>a scent hound on a leash</note> held by the strap, it is called <term>starting the track</term> <note>original: "frapper à routte"</note>. When the beast is up and the dogs are unleashed afterward to hunt, it is the <term>slip</term> <note>original: "laisser courre"</note>. Those sent to various points with fresh dogs to hasten the chase are the <term>relays</term> <note>original: "Relaiz"</note>. Skinning a stag is to <term>dress</term> <note>original: "defaire" or "despouiller"</note> him; as for the boar, because one does not skin him but rather burns and flames him like a pig, it is called <term>singeing</term> <note>original: "fouailler"</note>.

There are infinite other terms and ways of speaking in this trade and profession, which would require a separate volume; for these, you may consult the book of **King Modus and Queen Ratio** <note>original: "le liure du Roy Modus, & de la Reyne ratio," a famous 14th-century allegorical treatise on hunting</note> on the pleasures of the chase and falconry, and another by the **Count of Foix, called Phoebus** <note>Gaston III, Count of Foix, author of the renowned *Livre de chasse*</note>. **Le Fouilloux** <note>Jacques du Fouilloux, a 16th-century author whose work modernized hunting techniques</note> has followed them more recently and has refined many things, just as **Orlando Lassus** did for the music of **Josquin**, **Conseil**, **Adrian Willaert**, and other ancient musicians; but for the little experience I have been able to have in this art, I would prefer to stick to the ancient fashion, and I am quite certain that fewer stags would be lost that way than by Fouilloux's method.

There remains here what **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> records in his *Arcadica*, that **Augustus Caesar** took from the temple of Tegea in Greece one of the tusks of that **Calydonian Boar**, which was half an <term>ell</term> <note>original: "aulne," a historical unit of length</note> long, and hung it in the temple of Bacchus within his gardens in Rome. For my part, I suspect that this was not a natural thing, but rather a counterfeit created by artifice, like the **Griffin’s foot** hanging in the **Sainte-Chapelle** of this city of Paris, and the head or antlers of the stag in the **Chapel of the Château d'Amboise**; both are imitated so perfectly that one would take them for products of nature, even though these antlers are of such disproportionate size that an animal would have to be far more enormous than an elephant to carry them upon its head. Furthermore, animals have always been of the same size throughout time, though it is true that there is some difference and disproportion between certain individuals, and even more so in dogs and horses than in others. There are also regions where they are larger or smaller in one place than in another: for instance, in **Brittany**, boars are far smaller and less dangerous than in **Nivernais**, where I have seen very large and furious ones. In the cabinet at **Nevers**, there is a portrait of one taken in the woods of **Decize** some fifty years ago, measuring fourteen <term>spans</term> <note>original: "empans," the width of an outstretched hand</note> in length from the <term>snout</term> <note>original: "bouttouer," the specialized term for a boar’s digging nose</note> or muzzle to the end of the rump where the tail begins; however, the tusks do not project three inches out of the jaw. Therefore, one must understand this "ell" of which Pausanias speaks according to how **Suetonius** <note>A Roman historian</note> restricts it to a <term>cubit</term> <note>original: "couldee"</note>, which is equivalent to a foot and a half, or eighteen inches, and...

<margin>Numbers 35. Deuteronomy 19.</margin>
As for *Hyllus*, he was the son of *Deianira* and *Hercules*. After the death of his father, he married *Iole*. Having been driven out of his kingdom along with his brothers by *Eurystheus*, King of *Argos*, he withdrew to *Athens*. There, he built the Temple of Clemency or Mercy in memory of the grace the *Athenians* had shown him by receiving him into their city against the persecution of his adversary. Consequently, since that time, this place served as a refuge for all those who went there to seek sanctuary <note>original: "franchise"</note>, much like the *Asylum* of *Romulus* in *Rome*, and the seven cities of *Palestine* called the cities of refuge for criminals <note>These biblical "cities of refuge" allowed those who committed accidental manslaughter to claim protection from retribution</note>. *Pausanias*, in his *Attica* <note>original: "ses Attiques"</note>, writes that this *Hyllus*, having come to a man-to-man duel against *Etheon* son of *Aeropus*, was killed there and buried at *Megara* with his grandmother *Alcmene*. He also writes that near a small town in *Lycia* called the Gates of *Temene*, a mound split and opened up due to a great flood of water, revealing the bones of a man buried there in former times. These bones were fifteen feet long, which the sacrificers and diviners declared to be those of the Giant *Hyllus*, a son of the Earth, from whom the nearby river took its name, and which has since been called the *Phrygian* according to *Strabo* in his 13th book. For this reason, *Hercules*, remembering the acquaintance he once had in those quarters with *Omphale*, who was Queen there, named the son he later had by *Deianira* *Hyllus*.

They saw him thus afflicted by cruel and unbearable pains <note>The original French text "douceurs" (sweetnesses) is a clear typesetting error for "douleurs" (pains), given the context of his agony.</note>, lying on the ground upon down and moss mixed with tree leaves and fern, from which he had made himself a makeshift bed to protect himself at night from the cold.
