And at night, dragging himself back into his cave, he spent the whole time without closing an eye, lamenting the piercing agonies he felt and the discomforts to which he was reduced in a most miserable state of wasting. He was so wasted and gaunt that his skin clung to his bones, into which the violence of the venom had penetrated even to the marrow; this had made the wound so corrupt that all the air was infected by its stench, and he himself was so poisoned that he could hardly bear it. His eyes were sunken into his head, with eyebrows so overgrown that they covered them, and his complexion was dull and leaden. 

Such was the misfortune to which the bite of the pernicious viper had reduced him—a creature which, constantly flowing with a mortal, pestilential venom, had foully stained the threshold and entrance of the cavern. This cave was hollowed out not by the skill of human hands, but by the long passage of time and the sea waves that came to strike against this rock. At the entrance hung the bow made by Hercules’ own hand, along with his ample and wide quiver full of arrows. Some of these were intended for hunting to provide himself with game and venison, but the others, which were stained with the incurable venom of the Hydra <note>The Lernean Hydra, a multi-headed monster slain by Hercules; its poisonous blood made Philoctetes’ arrows instantly fatal.</note>, he reserved for cruel beasts and those who might have dared to attack him. For all the Greeks, and the Atrides <note>The sons of Atreus: Agamemnon and Menelaus, the leaders of the Greek expedition.</note> themselves among the others, were very sorry for his misfortune, which they said should be blamed only on the fates, whose determined rigor no person can avoid, whether they incline toward good or toward evil.

In short, they coaxed him so with their fine speech that he forgot his resentment. And after they had washed him with seawater and cleaned his wound with a sponge, he felt some relief. Then they had him sit at the table, for he was almost perished with hunger, as they had brought many provisions and refreshments with them. This being done, as the night began to become sleepy and heavy, they slept on the shore until the next day at the appearance of dawn, when, raising anchors, they set the sails to the wind; and Minerva gave them a favorable wind at their stern. Thus, setting their prow on its true course, they furrowed the sea waves, the billows of which foamed all around the vessel along with the dolphins, which gambolled ahead of them as if they wished to clear the route they were to take. At last they arrived in the Channel <note>original: "Lanal"; a probable printer's error for Canal.</note> of the Hellespont <note>The narrow strait now known as the Dardanelles, connecting the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara.</note>, so fertile in fisheries, where the Greek fleet had remained anchored for ten years already. Which was filled with a marvelous...

For he could hardly walk, no more nor less than an oak or a beech tree <note>Original: "fousteau," an archaic term for a beech tree.</note> that a woodcutter has half-cut through; and he leaves it still standing on its base until some squall comes to finish bringing it down. Or, as when long slashes and incisions are made in a pine tree to extract its resinous pitch, it wobbles and staggers in the wind, now to one side, then to the other, ready to fall if it had not been propped up beforehand. Such was the gait of Philoctetes as these two valorous heroes led him to the tent of Agamemnon, where all the chiefs of the Greek army had assembled to receive him honorably. And as he passed, the soldiers—having compassion for him to see him so feeble compared to how he used to be—pointed him out to one another.

But the expert surgeon Podalirius <note>Podalirius was a son of Asclepius and the healer for the Greek forces during the Trojan War.</note> applied such remedies to his wound that he soon set him on his feet, for which the Greeks gave great applause and affection to this learned son of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>. And they rejoiced with a marvelous tenderness of heart with Philoctetes, whom they washed and anointed with oil, so that his disconsolate affliction—with which divine providence had willed to visit him so harshly—vanished to make way for the joy that came to seize him, banishing from his sad face the pale languor that had tarnished it for so long. Thus, in its place, there came to be imprinted a ruddy complexion, fresh and serene, and in all his limbs a renewal of strength and vigor, which one could see growing before one's eyes. It was just like a field full of ears of grain ready for harvest, which, having been flattened by a storm and a rush of water, soon straighten themselves up again if a pleasant ray of Sun, accompanied by a sweet breath of wind...

Philoctetes loosed three arrows, which followed one another so closely they hardly waited for each other. IN Egypt near the city of Thebes there was a cavern, resembling a pipe <note>original: "fistule"; used here to describe a long, narrow, winding passage resembling a reed or tube.</note>, with several twists, turns, and hollows naturally carved in circles within the earth, which wound one into the other like the volute of an Ionic capital, or the shell of a snail. For its paths did not extend in a straight line, such that they would branch out directly from one side to the other; rather, by curving from the entrance at the foot of the mountain, they went from there turning in oblique entwinings and spiral revolutions underground, where they hid themselves in several and various detours that it was quite difficult to keep without going astray. There at the bottom was placed a figure of a Satyr made of marble upon a base of the same material, in a place somewhat apart. This figure was, moreover, very well arranged, raising the sole of his foot backward: And in his fist he held a flageolet <note>A small woodwind instrument of the flute family, popular in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note>, at the sound of which he raised himself up right from the start: But the music of this player did not reach the ears of the beholders, nor was the flageolet of such a kind that one could play it; rather, art had imprinted upon the marble such an action as if the Satyr were truly playing. <meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of the two Philostrati to the work of Callistratus. It serves as a scholarly introduction to the art of sculpture, which the author feels necessary to include as a preamble to Callistratus's descriptions of statues.</meta>

# CALLISTRATE.

This is why, despite the fact that in the Greek copies he <note>Referring to Callistratus, an author of the 3rd or 4th century AD known for his "Descriptions" of statues.</note> is placed after the *Heroics* <note>original: "l'Heroique"; referring to the *Heroikos*, a dialogue by Philostratus.</note>, because they are by the same hand, I have nevertheless chosen to thread him immediately following their descriptions of paintings <note>original: "tableaux"; referring to the *Imagines* of the Philostrati.</note>, as the subject matter is more similar than the lives of the ancient heroes. And because Callistratus does not use any preamble here as the others have done, it will be necessary to discuss—since it is so fitting to do so—something about sculpture or statuary, otherwise called <term>imagerie: The art of making images, specifically statues or carvings.</term>. This art is divided into two main techniques: <term>relief: Carving where the figures project from a background.</term> (or "the boss") and the hollow <note>original: "le creux"; referring to intaglio or engraving where the image is cut into the surface.</note>, which are directly opposite one another.

Of relief, there are two kinds: one called full relief <note>original: "plein relief"; also known as sculpture "in the round."</note>, when the image of whatever object is in its perfect state, rounded on all sides, without being attached to anything. Such are all the ancient heads and statues seen in Rome and elsewhere; and also the vases commonly called Corinthian <note>original: "Corinthiaques"; highly prized ancient bronze or ceramic vessels.</note>. The most beautiful of these in Rome are the Adonis or Meleager belonging to <term>Messere Francisque de Norche: Francesco da Norcia, a 16th-century Italian physician and prominent collector of antiquities.</term>; the Apollo Belvedere; the Laocoon with his two children, carved from a single piece of marble; the Cleopatra; the Hercules of Echion the Athenian, which stands in the courtyard of the <term>Farneze Palace: A prominent High Renaissance palace in Rome that housed a massive collection of ancient sculpture.</term>; and several others.

Very few are seen in bronze, except for the Hercules of the Capitol and the Marcus Aurelius mounted on horseback; yet even that is made of assembled pieces and not cast as a single piece, like the four horses harnessed to a chariot above the portal of the Chapel of St. Mark in Venice. The other kind of relief is what is called <term>bas-relief: Low relief, where the figures project only slightly from the background material.</term> (half-boss or low-cut), depending on whether the sculpture is raised more or less from the background to which it is attached. Examples include the two historiated columns of <term>Trajan: The Column of Trajan in Rome, featuring a spiral frieze of low-relief carvings.</term> and Antoninus Pius, and the decorations of all the triumphal arches; also many <note>original: "piles"; here referring to sarcophagi or large stone basins.</note> or marble coffins; furthermore, medals of gold, silver, and bronze; and the <term>camaieux: Cameos; gemstones carved in relief to show a figure against a background of a different color.</term> made of agate and other fine stones.

Regarding the hollows or engravings, some are likewise carved more or less deeply than others, as can be seen in countless onyxes, carnelians, lapis lazuli, agates, <term>chalcedonies: A translucent variety of quartz.</term>, amethysts, jaspers, crystal, and so on. Among these, onyx and carnelian were the ones in which the most excellent craftsmen most willingly employed their labor, because they are firmer and more uniform, and can be carved more cleanly than any others...

# CALLISTRATE.

...of the others. I have seen—and I am not sure if I have already mentioned it elsewhere—a diamond valued at five or six thousand crowns, upon which were engraved the coat of arms of Portugal. And another of far greater importance in Rome—for its value exceeded thirty thousand crowns—on which was most exquisitely engraved the entire coat of arms of the King of Spain. This was a task of extreme labor and patience, due to the many quarters <note>original: "quartiers"; divisions of a coat of arms representing different noble lineages or territories.</note> and all the minute details of which it consists. Furthermore, it is well known that a diamond can only be cut by itself; thus, the most excellent engraver among the moderns spent a good five or six years upon it. It is true that, to refresh his spirits, he worked at intervals on other things. 

But to return to statues, which are our principal topic and subject here—for we have spoken sufficiently of medals in our annotations on Livy <note>Referring to Titus Livius, the Roman historian; the author, Blaise de Vigenère, published a well-known translation and commentary on his works.</note>—the material and substance of <term>imagerie: The general art of creating figures or statues.</term> consists of bronze, gold, silver, ivory, ebony, wood, marbles, and hard stones of all kinds, as well as clay or potter’s earth, and wax mixed with pitch, white lead, lime, and similar materials, at the discretion of the craftsmen. 

Now, there is no doubt that statues of clay were the very first of all. (Whether painting preceded sculpture, or vice versa, is a separate question; but I would estimate that simple drawing came before both). This is because no statue of importance is made, of whatever material it may be, without first preparing a model. The Greeks call this <term>modeling: <note>original: "πλαστική" (plastikē); the art of molding or shaping plastic materials like clay or wax.</note></term>, as one might say "shaping" or "forming," representing natural things in relief. Pliny speaks of this quite extensively in Book 35, Chapter 12. Dibutades, a potter of Sicyon, was the first who, by means of his daughter in Corinth, invented the art of <term>terra cotta: <note>original: "terre cuitte"; literally "baked earth."</note></term> sculpture. For she, being enamored with a young man who was to travel far away, had attempted to represent his face from his shadow cast by candlelight against a wall, where she traced the profile in broad strokes. And the father, coming upon it, applied clay to it, so that he made a model which he put to bake in the furnace with his other pottery works; once it had hardened, it was thereafter kept in the <term>Nymphaeum: A monument or shrine dedicated to nymphs.</term> until...

As for the first invention of statues, there is no doubt that it was very ancient, as Eusebius discusses in the 3rd book of his *Evangelical Preparation*; for Moses having forbidden making them—for the purpose of adoring them, it must be understood—that sufficiently presupposed that there had been some before then. And Pliny, book 34, chapter 7, notes that from the time of Evander, many years before the foundation of Rome, there was a Hercules dedicated in the cattle market <note>original: "marché aux bœufs"; the *Forum Boarium* in Rome.</note>, and a Janus later by King Numa. However, Plutarch in his *Life* <note>Referring to the *Life of Numa*.</note> writes that for more than one hundred and sixty years after <note>After the founding of Rome.</note> there was no image, neither sacred nor profane, whether in relief or flat painting. Herodotus in his *Clio* <note>The first book of his *Histories*.</note>, and Strabo in the 15th book of his *Geography*, write that the Persians also were not accustomed to using statues. And Muhammad since then, wishing like an ape to imitate the Mosaic traditions, expressly forbade—what all those of his Sect observe very strictly—the making of any image whatsoever of a thing produced by nature; it not being (as he says) permissible for the creature to counterfeit the works of his Creator. Macrobius, in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 11, notes after a certain Epicadus that Hercules, having defeated Geryon in Spain and brought his herds of horned beasts to Italy, had as many wicker effigies <note>original: "simulachres de clisse"; figures made of woven twigs or wickerwork.</note> dressed in clothing made as he had lost of his principal men in that journey and enterprise, and threw them down the Tiber to be rolled from there into the sea, as if the waves were bound in good faith to carry each to his own country to receive burial. But Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in the first book of *Antiquities*, records that the Pelasgians, having brought a most inhuman superstition to Italy of sacrificing living men to Pluto (called Dis) and offering human heads to Saturn, Hercules, interpreting the oracle, changed this into little figures called *oscilla* <note>Small figures or masks hung on trees as ritual offerings to replace human sacrifice.</note>: and regarding the heads, he demonstrated that one should read *phota* <note>original: "φῶτα"; meaning "lights."</note> which signifies lights or candles, and not *phota* <note>original: "φωτὰ"; meaning "men."</note> meaning head or person. Diodorus in the 4th book attributes the first invention of images to the Ethiopians, from whom the Egyptians received them; and Lactantius, in the 2nd book of *The Origin of Error*, chapter 11, to Prometheus, who made his Pandora from clay, and to animate her, went to steal fire from heaven, for which he was punished

There are, then, several manners and means of drawing and depicting, such as with charcoal, black or red crayon, and the pen, which is the most laborious, difficult, and bold of all. Those who draw and portray from life are very accustomed to using this, so that upon their chalk sketch—which they reshape and correct as they please using white breadcrumbs <note>Breadcrumbs were the primary tool for erasing charcoal or chalk before the invention of rubber erasers.</note>—they can later elaborate and finish a portrait complete with its natural colors; for this sketch serves them just as a model serves for sculpture <note>original: *imagerie*</note>. And since design <note>original: *dessein*</note> is but the shadow, so to speak, of relief <note>The three-dimensional form of sculpture.</note>, and flat-painting is a design accompanied by its colors, consequently, relief shall be rightly esteemed as the principal foundation of both. Thus, one could hardly ever succeed in being an excellent painter without being versed in sculpture, which provides the skill and dexterity to well represent foreshortenings, depths, and projections on a flat surface; and as they say in painting terms, to make what is represented entirely flat, without any physical protrusion, appear to be in relief and to stand out from the work—which is one of the greatest perfections of this art and the highest praise one can give to flat-painting. 

Pliny, on this subject in Book 35, Chapter 10, speaking of that excellent portrait of Alexander that Apelles made in the temple of Diana at Ephesus, bearing the likeness of Jupiter holding lightning in his hand—and this for the price and sum of one hundred and twenty thousand crowns <note>original: *six vingts mille escus*</note>, if the copies do not lie: *He also painted Alexander the Great holding a lightning bolt in the temple* <note>original Latin: *Pinxit & Alexandrum magnum fulmen tenentem in templo*</note>.

The image-makers <term>imagiers: a term used in the Renaissance for sculptors or carvers of images</term>, moreover, guide themselves in arranging their models in this way, which have four principal views: the front, the back, and the two sides. The drawing, which is traced by the aforementioned shadow represented on the wall, greatly assists this, as the person taken as the specimen and pattern is made to turn according to various suitable positions. And from this, several beautiful concepts can come into the craftsman’s imagination, sometimes in one way, then in another, until finally one settles on the one that is most pleasing. I have said four principal views, which are subdivided into four others in between, so that they make eight, and not only eight, but more than forty or fifty, according to the diversity of the muscles and their movements, which vary the appearance of each limb. There, everything moves and diversifies in infinite ways even if the person moves but a little, or changes their seat and posture. For this reason, one can hardly assign any particular rules for this, but only some general maxims and rough estimates by sight <note>original: *à veue de pays*; a French idiom meaning to judge something roughly or at a glance without precise measurement</note>, where neither the rule nor the compass would suffice to guide a craftsman's hand in sculpture or panel painting <term>plattepeinture: literally "flat painting," referring to two-dimensional art as opposed to the three-dimensional relief of sculpture</term>, although the main part depends on them, especially in large measurements, because all sorts of straight and curved lines are guided by them. 

Furthermore, just as it is well required that in arranging one’s model, one looks at it carefully and at leisure, without being too hasty or holding too firmly to one’s first opinions; and even to take the counsel and advice of experts in the art, and of people of learned spirit and judgment. For even if they do not know how to paint or draw, they nevertheless often provide fine insights and resolutions, because the human understanding is very universal, and the dexterity of its conjectures extends everywhere. On the other hand, to always want to amuse oneself by changing and re-changing projects and opinions, without finally settling on one, would be an error and a fault no less than the first. They turned the lively naturalness <note>original: *naifueté*; in this context, it refers to the spontaneous, life-like quality or "inner life" of an artwork</note>—which should spring from a cheerful, bold, and alert readiness—into something duller, more listless, and heavy. Now, that sculpture is more difficult and hazardous than painting can be seen, among other things, by the works of Michelangelo <note>original: *Michel L'ange*</note>, the most accomplished of the moderns in both arts. For although he excelled in both almost equally, and balanced his time between them as if on a scale, he nevertheless made a hundred painted and well-colored figures for every one marble statue. One can see this in the *Last Judgment* in the Sistine Chapel <note>original: *chapelle Sixte*</note> at the Palace of St. Peter, and in the Prophets on the vaults, which are much larger than life-size and which the great masters prize more than the *Judgment* which is on a flat surface. This difficulty of sculpture <term>imagerie: the art of making statues or "images"</term> does not come solely from the labor required by the hardness of marble, but also from the care that must be taken in observing the diversity of views in a statue of full relief <note>original: *plein relief*; a sculpture that is fully three-dimensional and can be viewed from all sides</note> that is fully rounded. This is not the case for flat painting, which does not require so many viewpoints. Another excellence of sculpture over painting is that it showed the way and gave the law to all the proportions and measurements of architecture, which were borrowed from the human body and took their origin and foundation there. Thus, a sculptor has a great advantage in this regard and will be much more suited to it than a simple painter—though a painter may still understand it to some extent because of their knowledge and practice of design <term>dessein: a Renaissance term encompassing both the physical act of drawing and the underlying conceptual plan or "design" of a work</term>, as could be seen in Raphael of Urbino <note>original: *Raphael d'Vrbin*</note>. ...[man], and of an animal, it is even more possible to design a building, whose outlines are better suited to the ruler and the compass than the features of the aforementioned animals. But insofar as one only imitates them after nature, from which the first design proceeds, and because the ordering and arrangement of a building—which the Greeks call architecture <note>original Greek: *οἰκοδομία* (oikodomia), meaning house-building or structural arrangement</note>—depends on the imagination of the architect, who is like a new creator regarding its form and figure, the difficulty therein is much greater. This is because it is harder to invent than to imitate, and especially to appropriately assign the parts to their proper placement; for they correspond to the members of the human body. 

And in fact, just as the painter or sculptor varies them to create diverse figures, and adapts these figures in different ways for the representation of some historical subject—whether on a flat surface or in relief—the architect must do the same with the pieces of his building. Thus, there is a very great affinity between them; for this reason, it would be very difficult, even almost impossible, for one to be a good architect if one does not understand design and portraiture, and to make it more perfect, something of sculpture <note>original: *imagerie*; the art of carving figures or statues</note> as well.

The most excellent French sculptor, then, or any other on this side of the mountains <note>original: "deçà les morts"; likely a transcription error or archaic variant for "deçà les monts," meaning the French side of the Alps</note>, was Master Germain Pillon, who died in the year 1580, of whom infinite masterpieces can be seen in marble, bronze, and terracotta, both in full-relief and low-relief <note>term: bassetaille; carving where the figures project only slightly from the background</note>. As for marble, it truly brings with it not only more difficulty than clay, wood, and similar soft materials that are easier to handle—due to the mass which weighs four to five pounds <note>the author is likely referring to the weight of the hammer or the resistance of the material</note>, and the point or chisel which must be sharpened anew at the forge at every turn—but also because of the cunning and practice one must have to know the grain <note>original: "le fil"; literally the thread or natural alignment of the stone</note> of the marble, and from which angle <note>original: "biez"; bias or slant</note> it must be struck. On this subject, I can say I saw Michelangelo, although he was over sixty years old and no longer among the most robust, knock off more scales <note>note: "escailles"; stone chips or flakes</note> from a very hard marble in a quarter of an hour than three young stonemasons could have done in three or four—a thing almost incredible to anyone who did not see it. And he went at it with such impetuosity and fury that I thought the whole work must go to pieces, knocking to the ground with a single blow large chunks three or four fingers thick, so precisely...*

As for **wood**, and **ebony**, and **ivory** too, they are all softer and more tractable, and less rebellious and coarse; but such is this dexterity and assurance of the hand which is acquired by a long experience and practice. So much so that he who is accustomed to making figures of stone or wood is much more capable of crafting them from metal than the simple metalworker <note>term: imagier metallaire; a craftsman specializing in casting metal figures rather than carving stone</note> is of striking indifferently upon marble. It is true, however, that regarding the design and the models—which are common to both, whether they be of earth, wax, or other similar material—there remains for the latter only the practice of casting it well into his molds.

NOW, since we are on the subject of marbles, it will do no harm to touch upon them all at once, for there are several sorts and species, some harder and more stubborn under iron tools, and more difficult to handle than others. In the first place is **Porphyry** <note>a hard igneous rock, typically deep red or purple, highly prized in antiquity for imperial monuments</note>, the hardest of all except for **Serpentine** <note>a dark green stone with mottled patterns resembling a serpent’s skin</note> which surpasses it: the former is a dark red stone speckled with white spots, and Serpentine has a green field similarly dappled with white, with some blackness mixed in. Modern artists, seeing the difficulty of "biting" into it with iron tools, wanted to persuade themselves that the ancients possessed some secret for softening it, but there was nothing but their long patience and the expense of infinite tools which were re-steeled and tempered at almost every blow, and their points renewed. For in our time we have seen a certain **Francesco del Tadda**, a Florentine <note>Francesco di Giovanni Ferrucci (1497–1585), known for rediscovering the technique for carving porphyry</note>, who made several heads from it—indeed, even entire statues, though small, but clothed in compensation, where there are more details to seek out than in the nude, even if the science of it is not so great. He was the first of whom there is memory who, since the ancients, had the boldness to attack the hardness of this disobedient stone. However, this was by the favor of the late great **Cosimo de' Medici**, the first Grand Duke of Tuscany—a prince of immortal praise—who gave him the courage for it, providing him the funding. Furthermore, due to its speckles and spots, it has not been at all suitable for making statues, and so no one has spent any time on it.

**FOLLOWING** next in hardness is what is called **breccia** <term>breccia: a rock composed of broken fragments of minerals or rock cemented together by a fine-grained matrix</term>, of which there are several kinds, all very hard and varied with diverse colors; and therefore no more suitable for imagery, but only for making pillars, columns, tables, doorframes, chimneys, windows, entablatures, and other similar works. The marble called "noble" <note>original: "gentil"; meaning refined or high-quality</note>, because it is uniformly white without any veins, is good for this, and many heads and entire figures are seen made of it; but because it is very hard and difficult to handle, the great masters have not wanted to dwell on it, but have all preferred **Parian** marble <note>from the Greek island of Paros, famous for its translucent white marble</note>. This is as much because it resists all the injuries of the weather very well, without altering or decaying, and it is sufficiently hard to receive a polish yet not stubborn; furthermore, it has a certain luster and color that approaches that of human flesh <note>original: "charneure"</note>, and there is never a stain or defect to be found in it, however large the pieces one wishes to extract, for it has no beds or layers <note>original: "banc ny d'estages"</note> like our stones from these parts. Whereas **Carrara** marbles, whether white or black, and likewise those from the **Pyrenees** mountains, are all or for the most part scattered with stains and veins of colors other than their base. Nevertheless, it is found in places to be uniform, such as that from which **Michelangelo** <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564)</note> made all the figures that are in the **Medici Chapel** in **Florence**, in the Church of **San Lorenzo**.

There is, moreover, another species of marble much softer than those mentioned above, which is called *Mischio* <note>Italian for "mixed" or "medley"</note> or "mixed," in the manner of **jasper**, because of its diverse colors, of which there are infinite kinds. This was not used for making figures either, for it would not be suitable, and it is used for no other purpose than the breccias. One sees nothing else in **Rome** but people busy cutting and sawing ancient pillars and columns of these mixed and jasper-like marbles, which are easier and more obedient to work than the breccias. Next there are chisels of several widths: small ones for working on the surface, and large ones for the hollows; these chisels are toothed <note>original: "brettez"; notched or serrated chisels used to remove material quickly while leaving a textured surface</note>, some with one tooth, others with two or three, like those used by stonemasons. Many other tools and instruments are invented by workers from day to day, according to what suits them, the subject they must treat, and their own whims; for one proceeds by one way, another by another, following the saying of Geber the Arab <note>likely referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous alchemist and polymath</note>:
> There are many ways to one intent and one end. <note>original Latin: "Multæ funt viæ ad vnum intentum, & vnum finem."</note>

THE WORKER, therefore, must first of all firmly establish his model, by which he must guide and bring his work to completion, having it always before his eyes as his example and pattern, raised in relief <note>original: "en bosse"; a 3D model, likely in clay or wax</note> after his first project and design. Otherwise, if he were not well-resolved by mature deliberation and were to strike the marble inconsiderately, he might make great blunders <note>original: "pas de clerc"; literally a "clerk's step," meaning a foolish or clumsy mistake made through lack of experience</note> that he could not later repair, as one might easily do in a flat painting, or with stucco, or clay. This would cause a useless loss of time, effort, and material. On the other hand, to receive advice from no one would be a great rashness and a sign of arrogance. But there would be no less danger in amusing oneself with the diverse opinions of everyone; for besides the fact that one would never finish, it would be a completely disjointed work, whose parts would not correspond to the whole, which must proceed from the same thread and the same vein, so that it would turn out like a piece of writing by several different hands: or like those two statues by Lysippus <note>A celebrated Greek sculptor of the 4th century BCE, famous for his realistic style and for being the personal sculptor of Alexander the Great.</note> of the same subject and invention, one of which he made in secret by himself from his own imagination, and for the other he displayed the model in his workshop to the view of all passersby, who each said their bit about it, and with clay he reworked it at every suggestion. Nonetheless, he said to them: "This one that you reprove comes from your opinions and advice, and the other from mine." By which means, in this as in all other things, one must maintain moderation and discretion.

...from several people that which will be most beautiful and best proportioned, as is read of *Zeuxis* <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE known for his realism.</note>, who, in order to create his *Venus* in panel-painting <note>original: "platte-peinture"; referring to two-dimensional painting on a flat surface as opposed to a sculpture in the round.</note>, chose the five most beautiful and accomplished young women from the whole territory of *Croton*, so that by taking what each had most beautiful and exquisite in herself, he—being a most excellent master—could create an image in which nothing could be found wanting; for the perfections required can hardly all be found in a single subject. 

Therefore, based on nature—but nature well-chosen—the craftsman should form his design and model, and upon this model guide his work toward the goal he intends. For to follow the invention of another entirely is not a way to acquire much glory or reputation; and to take an arm from here, a head from there, and a leg from there <note>referring to a disorganized borrowing of parts without a unified plan.</note> would be to fall into the error that *Horace* <note>The Roman lyric poet and critic.</note> mentions at the very beginning of his *Art of Poetry*:

> ->If a painter should wish to join a horse's neck to a human head,<-
> ->and to spread feathers of various colors over limbs sought from everywhere, etc.<-
<note>original: "Humano capiti ceruicem pictor equinam / Iungere si velit, & varias induere plumas, &c." Horace uses this image to mock art that lacks organic unity.</note>

Above all, the <term>image-maker<gloss>A term for a sculptor or artist who creates representational forms.</gloss></term> must be well-instructed and versed in anatomy, and the proportions and measurements of the human body. He must know how to discern what he should choose as a pattern for what is beautiful and praiseworthy, and properly relate all the individual limbs, as well as their gestures and movements, to the action he wishes to represent in his statue, so that the parts are, in turn, coherent.

As for the model, it is most reliable if it is of the same size as the intended statue; however, it is customary to first form a smaller one—about a foot and a half, more or less—and to enlarge the other, which must serve as the exemplar, based on its measurements. This follows the technique and practice used to enlarge <term>Colossal<gloss>Statues of exceptionally large size, far exceeding life-scale.</gloss></term> statues from small models. ### ->CALLISTRATE<-

I i

...entire roundness, and the plurality of viewpoints all around and from every side, are more difficult to observe and more dangerous to lose one's way in, the best course—even for the most confident masters—is to make the model of the same size that the statue is meant to be. This cannot be practiced in the patterns and models of architecture, nor in great colossi, unless perhaps they were in bronze, which is safer to handle than marble: because the actual model can be used there to serve as a mold and means <note>In bronze casting, the original model is used to create the mold, whereas in marble, the model is merely a guide for carving.</note>, whereas a mistake made in marble can no longer be patched up. 

The model thus determined and finished in all respects, one will first trace with charcoal or black stone upon the Block, or the roughly-hewn mass of marble, the form one wishes to give it. One traces the principal view of it as exactly as possible, using curved calipers <note>original: "compas croches & recourbes"; tools used by sculptors to measure the thickness of a 3D object.</note> to take the measurements of the extremities, and squares for the hollows and protrusions. 

Then, with the sharpened point <note>original: "poincte aceree"; a punch tool used for roughing out the stone.</note> and the mallet, one will begin to remove the excess, holding the point tilted sideways, and not directly plumb <note>At a 90-degree angle.</note>, so as not to enter further than necessary. Thus, one proceeds wisely, discovering the form bit by bit with patience and discretion, until reaching the "penultimate skin," as it is called in this art, just as if one only intended to make a figure in low relief or "half-round" <note>original: "demy bosse"; referring to high relief where figures are attached to a background but deeply carved.</note>. 

This done, one must move further with the chisel to smooth the rest down to the "final skin." From there forward, one proceeds with half-round rasps, knife-shaped rasps, and curved scrapers of various sorts. Files are, as has already been said before, more for works in bronze, though they can also be used here at times. So too are the bits or drills, and the braces—an instrument common to carpenters and locksmiths, but which are turned in various ways. But beyond the fact that all these tools are well enough known and common, all their shapes and sizes can hardly be strictly defined, as workmen vary them as they please according to their intentions and projects.

When these works are brought to their final perfection, they are glazed and polished by means of finely crushed sandstone passed through a sieve, then...

Once everything is well-smoothed, one gives it its polish with putty powder <note>original: "pottée"; a traditional polishing compound made from metal oxides.</note>, which is made of lead and tin calcined <note>Burned to a powder.</note> together and soaked with water; rubbing the marble with this composition using a cloth until the luster is to your liking. ## ARGUMENT.

<image-desc>Decorative initial I featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

HERE is described with great artistry the figure of a *Bacchante*—these were women dedicated to the service of the god *Bacchus* <note>The Roman god of wine, fertility, and ritual madness; known as Dionysus in Greek mythology.</note>, where they practiced many execrable ceremonies and placed themselves, both through the wine they took in excess and by other extraordinary means, into such a furious alienation of mind that they became enraged, running with a strange madness through the fields, mountains, and valleys, in the most remote wanderings of inaccessible rocks and trackless forests. But beneath this were committed infinite and excessive misfortunes <note>original: "malheuretez"; implying the tragic or violent acts often depicted in the myths of the Maenads/Bacchantes.</note>, as can be seen more fully below in the annotation, in addition to what has been touched upon previously regarding the paintings of *Semele*, *Pentheus*, the *Tyrrhenians*, *Andrians*, and the *Islands* <note>References to other chapters in this work describing the myths of Dionysus/Bacchus.</note>; this statue, moreover, is by the hand of the most excellent sculptor *Scopas* <note>A famous Greek artist of the 4th century BCE known for his ability to render intense emotion in stone.</note>. *Callistratus* <note>A Greek author known for his "Descriptions" (Ekphraseis) of statues.</note> strives to demonstrate tacitly the affinity that exists between the vehemence of oratory—especially that of *Demosthenes* <note>The preeminent orator of ancient Athens, known for his powerful, "sinewy" style.</note>, the most forceful and persuasive orator of all—and the action represented by the gestures and expressions that skilled craftsmen introduce into their figures, so that even though they are inanimate in themselves and made of a completely dead and senseless material, they nevertheless do not fail to appear alive. From this, it does not stray far from what is read of *Cicero* <note>The source text prints "Licorum," likely a corruption or variant referencing Cicero.</note> and *Roscius* <note>Quintus Roscius Gallus, the most famous comic actor of Rome.</note> the sovereign comedian, who very often entered into dispute as to which of them could express the same thing in more ways: he, *Cicero*, with his plentiful eloquence, or the actor with his silent and mute gestures and actions.

beholding her is not at all devoid of its proper movement, for she dominates entirely and preserves the figure given to her by her own maker, and in her form as a **Bacchante** <term>Bacchante: a female follower of Bacchus, the god of wine and ritual madness</term>, she keeps the passion that transports her.

# ANNOTATION.

Bacchus and his mysteries have already been spoken of sufficiently before in the works of the **Philostrates** <note>Philostratus the Elder and the Younger, Greek authors known for the *Imagines*, descriptions of artworks</note>. It remains here to say something also of his ministresses: the **Maenads**, **Bassarids**, **Thyiads**, **Mimallonians**, **Lenae**, and other such names. One of these is described here, almost in imitation of the one in the "Painting of the Islands," where we brought in the passage from the *Chiliads* of **Tzetzes** <note>Johannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine scholar</note>, which characterizes her very naturally; therefore, there will be no need for repetition here. The **Maenads**, then, were so called from the Greek *to be mad* <note>original: "μαίνεσθαι" (mainesthai)</note>, which signifies to be frenzied, to rage, or to act with wild abandon. **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century grammarian</note> names them otherwise as *Potniades*, after the city of **Potnies** in Boeotia, where it is said that **Glaucus**—son of Sisyphus and Merope—was born. He was the father of **Bellerophon**, which will be relevant hereafter regarding the **Chimera** <note>A mythical monster; here the author links the name of the beast the Bacchante holds to the legends surrounding Glaucus and his son</note> that this Bacchante holds in her arms in place of a victim. Glaucus used to nourish certain mares he owned with human flesh to make them more furious and emboldened against his enemies; but when this fodder came to be lacking, they fell into such a rage that they devoured their own master, as the commentators of **Virgil** <note>The Roman epic poet</note> state regarding the third book of the *Georgics*.

> *Truly, the madness of mares is notable above all others,*
> *And Venus herself gave them this spirit in that time when the*
> *Potnian four-horse team tore apart the limbs of Glaucus with their jaws.*
<note>original Latin: "Scilicet ante omnes furor est insignis equarum, / Et mentem venus ipsa dedit quo tempore glauci / Potniades malis membra absumpsere quadrigæ." — Virgil, Georgics 3.266-268.</note>

Regarding this, **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> says in his *Boeotica*: About half a league from the city of **Thebes**, when you have passed the river **Asopus**, you will see the ruins of Potnies, with the sacred grove of **Ceres** and **Proserpine** <note>Demeter and Persephone</note>, whose images...

...villages that are near the water are called the Potniades, and there every year on a certain day they perform I know not what sacrifices, where among other things, they sacrifice little newborn piglets, but the reason for this is hardly well clarified. Nearby there is also a temple of Bacchus surnamed **Aegobolus** <term>Aegobolus: Greek for "goat-shooter," a title of Dionysus/Bacchus reflecting the transition from human to animal sacrifice</term>, because once, as the inhabitants of the place were sacrificing, they became so drunk that they put his minister to death; for which reason, having been infected by the plague, the oracle admonished them to sacrifice a handsome young boy to him every year; but some years later, he commuted this cruel and inhuman offering to a sacrifice of goats. *As for the **Bassarids**, of whom **Persius** says in his first satire: "The Bassarid who will carry off the head cut from the proud bull calf" <note>original Latin: "Et sectum vitulo caput ablatura superbo Bassaris"</note>, they were so called after the long robes they wore down to their heels, according to **Pollux** and **Hesychius**, which were made in the city of Bassare in **Lydia**, as **Acron** notes on this passage of **Horace** in the 18th ode of the first book: "I will not shake you against your will, O bright Bassareus" <note>original Latin: "Non ego te candide Bassareu invitum quatiam"</note>. But **Phurnutus** <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher often referred to as Phurnutus in older texts</note> prefers to derive it from the Greek "to cry out" <note>original: "Βάζειν" (bazein)</note>, and writes it with only one 's,' Basaris. The **Thyiads** were so called, as **Pausanias** writes in his *Phocics*, after **Thyia**, daughter of Castalius and mother of Delphus (whom Apollo begot upon her), the first of all mortals to sacrifice to Bacchus and who instituted the **Orgies** <term>Orgies: secret ritual acts and festivals dedicated to Dionysus, characterized by ecstatic worship</term> of which more will be said hereafter. The **Mimallonians** or **Mimallonides** [were named] after Mount **Mimas** in Asia Minor, not very far from **Colophon**, or rather a cape that projects quite far into the sea, continually covered with clouds by which one predicts the coming weather: and there every year the Bacchantes went to celebrate the Orgies, as **Strabo** records in the 10th book. # OF A BACCHANTE.

...to shorten by that much the circuitous route of navigation one is forced to take when doubling it <note>This likely refers to Bacchus's legendary travels or the crossing of an isthmus</note>, but he desisted from it. Some also wish to derive this word from "to imitate" <note>original Greek: μῑμεῖσθαι</note> because in these orgies and sacrifices, the **Bacchantes** represented the journey that **Bacchus** made to the Indies, attaching little horns to their heads, along with garlands of vine-shoots, ivy, and fig tree leaves; for the leaves of these three have a great resemblance and affinity. This was done in memory and for the love of the nymphs: **Staphyle**, who was changed into a vine; **Syce**, into a fig tree; and the beautiful youth **Cissus** <note>The text reads "lisse," likely a corruption of the Greek name Cissus, meaning ivy</note>, into ivy. For this reason, their javelins <term>thyrsi: ritual staffs tipped with a pine cone and wrapped in ivy or vine leaves</term> were adorned with these, along with such other equipment as **Ovid** <note>original: "Omian," likely an OCR error for "Ovidien" or "Ovidius"</note> describes in his discourse on **Bacchis**. The **Lenae**, named from the surname of Bacchus **Lenaeus**, of whom it is said in the fourth book of the *Metamorphoses*: "With Lenaeus, the festive planter of the grape" <note>original Latin: "cum lænæo genialis confitor vuæ"</note>, a name taken from the Greek word for "wine-press" <note>original Greek: ληνὸς</note>, where the vintage is pressed. The 27th *Idyll* of **Theocritus** conflates them with the Bacchantes.

**Orgies**, as **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil</note> writes, were originally understood as all kinds of sacrifices, as well as ceremonies, so named from the verb "to sacrifice" <note>original Greek: ὀργιάζω</note>, or "to consecrate" <note>original Greek: ὀργιάζομαι</note>, from which the priests were also called *orgeones* <note>original Greek: ὀργεῶνes</note> from "to stretch out" or "to raise" <note>original Greek: ὀρέγω</note>, because in celebrating divine service they raised their hands on high. But afterwards, this word "orgies" was particularly restricted to the sacrifices of Bacchus, as **Strabo** testifies in his tenth book: "Most of the Greeks have attributed to **Father Liber**—whom they otherwise call **Bacchus**, **Iacchus**, and **Dionysus**—the entire practice of the ceremonies called the Orgies, the **Bacchanalia**, the Choral dances, and the mysteries of the sacrifices; and he is the leader of those of **Ceres**, of sacred dances and ballets." His ministers include the **Sileni**, **Satyrs**, **Bacchantes**, **Lenae**, **Thyades**, **Mimallonians**, **Naiads**, and **Nymphs**, along with those called **Tityri**. The Orgies were also so named from "impetuosity" and "fury" <note>original Greek: ὀργὴ</note>, as was present in all those people while they celebrated them; or from "mountain" <note>original Greek: ὄρος</note>, because they were held principally in mountainous places covered with solitary and remote woods. This occurred every three years—at least the most solemn ones, which were thus called **Trieterica** or "triennial," as **Virgil** mentions in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*.

of Apollo, who went to bury them at Mount Parnassus; but the Corybantes, otherwise called the Cabiri, had stolen the genitals, which they carried into Tuscany. from where he departed, accomplishing by this means the revolution of the offices and functions of this world, without departing from the secret mysteries of nature: but Phurnutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, often called Phurnutus in older texts, was a 1st-century Stoic philosopher known for his allegorical interpretations of Greek mythology</note> allegorizes in this way. We find in Greek fictions that Bacchus, having been dismembered by the Titans, was once again gathered into one by Rhea, under which veils the authors of this fable intended to presuppose nothing else but that the laborers and vine-growers, who are like children of the earth, have gathered and mixed together the clusters of grapes from which has come this precious liquor of wine, reduced into one body, which before was spread out in several parts separated from one another. *But how much better does our religion, which according to the teachings of its* Redeemer *reduces all these allegories of bread composed of many grains and ears of wheat, and of wine expressed from many seeds and clusters of grapes, to the Communion of the faithful: who, being separated according to their individual selves, come to unite together into a single body of the* Catholic Church, *and in the Sacrament of this Communion under the species of bread and wine, transformed really into the body and the blood of our* SAVIOR.

It is taken up, and the path of a freer life [begins]. <note>original: "Sumitur, & vitæ liberioris iter." This Latin quote refers to the transition into adulthood and the "freer life" celebrated during the Roman festival of the Liberalia.</note>

But the Bacchanalia <term>Bacchanalia</term> <note>Roman festivals of Bacchus, based on the Greek Dionysia but later suppressed for their perceived immorality.</note> were celebrated every month, until they were finally abolished entirely for the reasons we will bring forward later from the 39th book of Livy <note>Titus Livius, the great Roman historian who documented the rise and fall of various Roman customs.</note>. And the Dionysia or Orgies were held only every three years, for which reason they were called Trieteric <term>Trieteric</term> <note>From the Greek 'tri' (three) and 'etos' (year); though occurring every two years by modern reckoning, the ancients counted the starting year, making it a "three-year" cycle.</note>, as has been said above. Furthermore, there were three kinds of these festivals in Athens: one in the open country and the countryside, in the towns and villages, held in the month of Poseideon <note>An ancient Greek month roughly corresponding to December.</note>, which corresponds for the most part to our December; the second in the month of Lenaeon, otherwise called Gamelion, which falls in January and February and is the last month of winter—from which the name Lenaea <term>Lenaea</term> <note>An Athenian festival focused on dramatic competitions and the "Lenae," or frenzied women who served Bacchus.</note> was given to the priestesses of Bacchus; and the third, which were the Dionysia in the month of Elaphobolion or February <note>Modern calendars usually place this month in March, but the author aligns it with late winter.</note>. Thus, all three of these festivals followed one after another, back-to-back, during the three months of winter. 

However, Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer whose *Saturnalia* is a treasure trove of ancient lore and philosophy.</note> in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 18—where he proves by vivid and authentic reasons that Bacchus is the very same thing as Apollo—states that the Bacchanalia were celebrated every two years on Mount Parnassus, which is consecrated to Apollo and the Muses. There, it was said that large troops of Satyrs <term>Satyrs</term> <note>Mythological companions of Bacchus, typically depicted with the features of goats or horses, representing the wild forces of nature.</note> were often seen during this solemnity, and that one could even hear their cries, along with the echoing of cymbals, drums, and other such Bacchic instruments, which often reached the ears of many people who heard them distinctly.

The Bacchanalia, therefore, were anciently in very great vogue and devotion among the pagans; but as all things become depraved and deteriorate with time—which causes them to be destroyed—a very great scandal arose from these Bacchanalia in Rome in the year 567 from its foundation <note>Approximately 186 BCE.</note>, under the consulship of Spurius Postumius Albinus and Quintus Marcius Philippus. Indeed, this scandal affected all of Italy, leading to a very strict and rigorous inquiry. Several thousand people were executed for the execrable abuses and crimes committed there, as Livy describes at length at the beginning of his 39th book. This passage deserves to be brought forward here in its entirety, even though it is a bit long, because nothing could be cited that would better clarify this whole affair.

These mysteries, therefore, were taught to only a few people at the beginning; but shortly thereafter, they were spread little by little among both men and women. All of this was accompanied by enticing baits and lures of delicious pleasures, including wine and feasts, to attract more and more followers. 

And as drunkenness and the night perverted their understanding—men mixed pell-mell with women, and those of a tender age with the more advanced and robust—they erased and banished from themselves all shame and fearful respect. Every kind of depravity and debauchery began to be practiced there, as each person found carnal pleasures prepared according to whatever lust their nature was inclined. 

And yet, all their wickedness did not consist solely of lewdness <term>lewdness</term> <note>original: "paillardiſſes," referring to sexual immorality or fornication.</note>, which was practiced there without any distinction toward women, daughters, boys, and others of free condition; rather, from this same shop <note>A metaphorical "workshop" or "source" of crime.</note> came false witnesses and depositions, forged signatures, and falsified judgments. Callistratus <note>Callistratus was a Greek sophist of the 3rd or 4th century CE, known for his "Descriptions" (Ecphrases) of fourteen statues.</note> uses here a very ingenious conceit in presupposing that the craftsman of this statue, having encountered a lead-colored vein in the marble from which he intended to work it, had so skillfully utilized it as to suit a dead chimera <note>A mythical monster, usually depicted with a lion's head, a goat's body, and a serpent's tail.</note> that this Bacchante <note>A female follower of Bacchus, the god of wine, often depicted in a state of ecstatic frenzy.</note> held in her hands. And in truth, it was a most delicate touch, for it expresses at the same time very naturally the insane alienation of mind of this frenzied woman: that she had taken this foul, stinking, and corrupt monster as the first thing she had encountered on her path to offer to her God, without thinking further of it. 

This reminds me of a very strange and striking act performed in the past by a Gentleman around the year 1543, when Monsieur de Boutières <note>Guigues Guiffrey, Seigneur de Boutières (1497–1545), a French military commander who served Francis I.</note> was Lieutenant General for King Francis I in Piedmont: this gentleman, having suddenly lost his wits without anyone noticing it yet, went one morning to the residence of the said Lord where everyone was accustomed to gather to pay their respects. He had hidden under his cloak the body of a child who had very recently died of the plague, and said these words: *"There are many brave men here who make threats beneath the chimney-piece, but I shall see now if there will be any so bold as to try and snatch from me what I hold,"* and immediately went and threw it into the middle of the room. From there you can imagine how they struggled to challenge him to strip him of his booty; he thought he had performed a fine feat.

<meta>This page continues the rationalist (Euhemerist) critique of the Chimera myth, likely drawing from the work of Palaephatus. It transitions from the physical impossibility of the monster to a historical explanation involving a ship and a volcanic mountain.</meta>

# OF A BACCHANTE <note>The header appears to be a misprint or a vestige from a different section of the original manuscript, as the text continues the story of Bellerophon and the Chimera from the previous page.</note>

...heads only of these three animals: which would be an absolute impossibility, for they all require different types of nourishment. Furthermore, that it was mortal and breathed fire from its mouth is also a fabrication; for which of these three so dissimilar beasts would have had the governance and direction of the body? Therefore, the matter goes like this. Bellerophon was a young man born in Corinth, exceptionally handsome and of a very good nature. Having found the means to equip a galley <term>fuste: a light, fast-sailing vessel often used by corsairs</term> which he named Pegasus—just as it is common to give names to all vessels—he went to scour the coast of Phrygia, where at that time a man named Amisodarus reigned near the river Xanthus. Along this river there was a very high mountain called Telmissus, which one could climb from the plain by two access points; and at the front of the city of the Xanthians there were many good pastures, but the back toward Caria was deserted and inaccessible. In the middle of all this there was a great chasm and opening in the earth, from which great flames of fire and smoke exhaled at intervals, near which there was another mountain called Chimera. Now at that time, as the inhabitants of the place recount it, a lion frequented the front of this plateau, and a great serpent frequented the back, both of which greatly harassed the shepherds who led their flocks there to graze. But Bellerophon, having arrived with his galley, seized this mountain of Telmissus which was covered in woods and set fire to it; by this means, the lion and the serpent perished. This was the reason the people of the country said that this valiant young man, having arrived there on the Pegasus, had put to death the Chimera of Amisodarus.

But Fulgentius, in the third book of his *Mythologies*, allegorizes this much more deeply. He suggests that Bellerophon—who mounts Pegasus (who was produced from the blood of the Gorgon) and who put the Chimera to death—is so named as if he were a "Bringer of Counsel" <note>original: *βουληφόρος* (boulephoros)</note>, full of good advice and fit to give it. But whose wife was this Antia? She was the wife of Proetus, whose name in the Pamphylian language is equivalent to saying "filthy," "dirty," "vile," or "sordid," because lewdness is the true wife and spouse of the filthy and the infected.

On the other hand, Bellerophon, who represents good and prudent judgment, what horse does he mount if not Pegasus, whose name comes from "fountain" <note>original: *πηγή* (pege)</note>, implying an everlasting spring? For wisdom is the living, eternal source. He has wings because contemplation penetrates in an instant the nature and disposition of the entire universe through its prompt meditations. By this means, he is said to have opened the fountain called the Hippocrene <term>Hippocrene: literally "the Horse's Spring," located on Mount Helicon</term> with a strike of his hoof. This spring was sacred to the Heliconian Muses, who receive it from wisdom.

For this reason, he is imagined to have been procreated from the blood of the Gorgon, which signifies "fright" and "terror." This is why she is displayed on the breastplate of Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom, often depicted with the head of the Gorgon Medusa on her aegis (shield or breastplate).</note> upon her chest, as Homer mentions in the 5th and 11th books of the *Iliad*. By this, he means nothing other than that after fear has passed, wisdom is born—just as Pegasus was born from the blood or the death of the Gorgon. For folly is always uncertain and fearful. Or rather, according to our Holy Scripture: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord" <note>A reference to Proverbs 9:10 or Psalm 111:10.</note>, because wisdom is born and grows within us from the respect we owe Him and the fear of offending Him. And whoever fears losing his reputation will be wise; therefore, he will put to death the Chimera, so named as if it were a "fluctuation of love" <note>original: *χῶ μ' ἔρωτος* (cho m' erotos)</note>. For this reason, she is depicted...

This is what Hesiod intended to imply by the fiction of his Echidna, mother of the Chimera, who is interpreted as <term>having a versatile and multifaceted mind</term> <note>original Greek: *ποικιλόνουν, καὶ πολυειδῆ* (poikilonoun, kai polyeidē).</note>, an understanding adorned with many different disciplines.

For this God is tender and polished, without any majesty or haughtiness, having an action suited to the bronze, and appearing to grow as if before one's very eyes. 

And even though he is deprived of the faculty of movement, he nevertheless shows himself quite ready to set off at this very moment; standing, moreover, upon a firm pedestal, he looks upward, as if he had the administration of the course of the stars and the heavens: and he delights in laughing, his eyes sparkling with something both burning and benign at once. For you can see how the **Bronze** obeys these emotions, and receives within itself, quite naturally, the appearance of a laugh. There he is then, raised on high, his right arm slightly bent, and with the other hand he raises his bow, leaning toward the left side to serve as...

It is this Theodorus <note>Theodorus of Samos, a 6th-century BC architect and sculptor credited by ancient sources with inventing bronze casting.</note> who engraved the emerald that Polycrates, the Tyrant of Samos, took such pleasure in <note>This refers to the legendary ring of Polycrates, which he threw into the sea to appease the gods, only for it to be found again inside a fish.</note>. There are, moreover, more considerations regarding metal than marble, such as their wax layers, their tunics and coverings of tin; the earth from which one must make the models and <term>cores</term> <note>Original: "moyeux," the internal structural support for a hollow-cast statue.</note>; the plaster for the hollows and molds; the armatures of iron bands and hoops to hold them; and the furnaces where the cores and hollow molds must be fired; and finally, the melting of the metal to pour them.

As for the earth, one should not take fatty and smooth clay like that used for making pots—which is dug up in several places around here in Paris, mainly at Gentilly—for it is too prone to cracking and expanding. Instead, one uses another type that is somewhat sandy; one of the most excellent kinds that can be found anywhere is that from the suburb of Saint-Honoré, which is taken to build the ovens of bakers and pastry cooks, and also in the Arsenal for artillery, and likewise for casting bells. If one had only clay, it would have to be tempered with ashes and <term>molding sand</term> <note>Original: "sablon d'estampes," a fine sand used in foundry work.</note>, or something similar, fine and smooth as flour. 

Once this earth is well-dried, it is ground fine and passed through a sieve or strainer to separate out stones and other foreign or uneven impurities. This done, one mixes in half as much <term>shearman’s flocks</term> <note>Original: "bourre de tondeurs de draps," the waste wool fibers from cloth production, used as a binding agent to prevent the clay from shrinking or cracking during the heating process.</note>, soaking the whole with water and incorporating them well together by beating it with an iron rod. Then it must be left to cure and mature for a period of three or four months, until the wool is well-decomposed and blended with the earth, and the whole is reduced to the consistency of a soft and tender ointment. This long curing makes the composition better suited to receive and withstand the intense heat of the metal without altering or splitting. 

And with this earth thus prepared, you will first form your figure in its perfection and the state in which it must remain. Then, you will fire it very gently over a slow fire, as if halfway, where it will shrink slightly—about the thickness of a finger, more or less. Therefore, you will retouch it again with the same earth in the appropriate places that have narrowed, in order to fill the void of the wrinkles and shrinkages, if any...

Then, apply a layer <note>Original: "chemise," literally a 'shirt,' referring to a coating or skin of material.</note> of wax about a finger’s thickness, or slightly less; and you shall build it up wherever necessary using suitable wooden and iron tools, also removing any excess. Incorporate these with water in which dried cow or horse dung has been steeped and finely ground, the whole mixture being gently passed through a strainer <note>Original: "estamine," a fine cloth mesh used for sifting.</note> without squeezing it, until the water remains tinted and no more, and no dregs or residue are left behind. 

With this liquid composition—much like the colors used by painters, or like a green primer <note>Original: "fausse vert."</note>—you will apply a coating over the wax using a pig-bristle brush (turning the bristles toward the side where they are attached to the leather so they are softer), smoothing it well and letting it dry. Then, apply another coat and let it dry in the same way, repeating this until this crust reaches the thickness of the back of a knife. Then apply another layer of the aforementioned earth from which the figure was built, half a finger thick, and let it dry. Once more, you will double this with another layer of the same thickness on top.

There is another way to proceed with these layers and coatings: for once the earthen model or figure has been brought to its final perfection and refired as described above, one must take equal portions of wax and turpentine and melt them together in a pan or an earthen pot, mixing them very well. Then, using the aforementioned brush, gently coat the figure and lay over it leaves of tin, commonly called <term>orpel</term> <note>From "or" (gold) and "peau" (skin); thin metal foil or tinsel used here to create a separation layer or to smooth the surface.</note>, as if one intended to silver it. However, this layer for applying the tin can also be made with a paste of fine flour, such as that used by booksellers <note>Meaning bookbinders, who used starch pastes.</note> and shoemakers. Once this is done, one allows it to flow at its own pace: and towards the end, it must be helped along with iron shovels and rakes until the mold is filled.

As soon as the pit is filled with earth <note>Founders packed the pit with earth around the mold to support it against the immense pressure of the heavy liquid bronze.</note>, one must light the fire in the furnace without further delay, for fear that the mold might attract some new moisture; the craftsman must have an eye for all these details, because the slightest mistake in this case would be to his great detriment. Regarding the channel or canal through which the metal must pass, it should be made almost half a foot wide, more or less according to the quantity of metal, and the walls on both sides just as high, all made of raw bricks. But these must be very dry, joined with the aforementioned earth, and very well fired by lighting a charcoal fire all along it to heat it while the Bronze melts. When one is ready to cast, all the coals must be removed, and the channel cleaned thoroughly of its filth, even removing the ash with a bellows so that it does not mix with the Bronze. The rest of the furnace—both the walls and the covering—can be made of small bricks <note>original: "thuillots"</note> laid with the same earth. Regarding its proportions and measurements, these vary according to the quantity of metal one wishes to melt, both in its width and height, and in the opening of its mouths. There are two of these at the sides through which the flame emerges, and another at the back joined to the small oven where the wood is placed through a hole at the top. Through this, the flame enters the large furnace where the bronze is kept, acting like a reverberatory wind-furnace <note>A reverberatory furnace is designed so that the heat is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the metal, rather than the fuel coming into direct contact with it.</note>. This causes the flame to swirl around seeking an exit; since the exit is denied to it by the top hole (for it is blocked with an iron lid as soon as the wood is thrown in), and because fire by its nature always tends to rise, the flame is forced back down onto the bronze, which it heats and melts. It then flows at its determined time, sooner or later depending on the quantity of metal and the heat that has been duly administered without any interruption. This is vital, as such intervals usually make the metal more stubborn to melt and create a hard crust on top, which is often the cause of many difficulties for foundrymen. Indeed, sometimes the metal, instead of flowing, calcines <note>Oxidizes into a powder due to excessive or improper heating.</note>; this is remedied with tin that is thrown in, and other skills and remedies well known to those who handle metals and fire, whose actions are very difficult to limit. There are also air vents <note>original: "souspiraux"</note>, four in number, through which the smoke escapes, wide enough to fit half a fist. And finally, there is the tap-hole <note>original: "pertuys"</note> through which the metal must exit into the channel <note>original: "coullouere"</note>; this is hollowed out of a brick firmly set into the masonry on both sides. Grind it finely and sift it, to make it even more firm and solid. And because all clay is subject to loosening and cracking when fired, the best course is to join the pieces as closely to one another as possible, so that there is less space in the joints and assemblies; for when the Bronze is in a bath and melted, it could escape through there, and seeking some escape, ruin the furnace floor. The rest of the furnace—both the walls and the roof—can be made of tiles <note>original: "thuillots"</note> masonry with the same clay. 

Regarding its proportions and measurements, they vary according to the quantity of metal one wishes to melt, in its width and height as well as in the opening of its mouths. There are two on the sides through which the flame exits, and another at the back joined to the small furnace <note>The firebox or "petit four" mentioned previously</note> where the wood is added through a hole at the top. Through this, the flame enters the large furnace where the Bronze is kept, as in a wind-driven reverberatory furnace <term>reverberatory furnace|a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof down onto the material being heated, preventing the fuel from touching the metal directly</term>. This makes the flame swirl to find an exit; since the top hole is denied to it (for it is blocked with an iron lid as soon as the wood is thrown in), and because fire naturally tends to rise, the flame is forced back down onto the Bronze. 

It heats and melts the metal until it flows at its determined time, sooner or later depending on the quantity and the heat that has been duly administered without any interruption. Such intervals usually make the metal more resistant to melting and create a hard crust on top, which is often the cause of several inconveniences for the founders. Indeed, sometimes the metal, instead of flowing, calcines <note>Turns into a powdery ash or oxide due to excessive heat without melting properly</note>; this is remedied with tin <note>original: "estain"</note> thrown in amongst it, and other skills and remedies well known to those who handle metals and fire, whose actions are very difficult to limit. 

Then there are the vents <note>original: "souspiraux"</note>, four in number, through which the smoke escapes; they are wide enough to fit half a fist. And finally, the tap-hole <note>original: "pertuys"</note> through which the metal must exit into the channel <note>original: "coullouere," the trough leading to the mold</note>. This is hollowed out in a brick firmly set on both sides. However, this tap-hole must be a bit wider on the inside than on the outside, as must the plug <note>original: "tampon"</note> that blocks it, in order to better seal it against the force <note>original: "impetuosité"</note> of the metal, which, when melted, comes to bear against it, just as...

...the water of a pond at the sluice of a dam, owing to the slope of the bottom. One must join this plug to the hole in the brick using finely sifted ash diluted with water, so that it does not offer too much resistance against the blow of the tapping bar <note>original: "periere"; a long iron tool used to break the clay seal of the furnace to let the metal flow</note>. In front of this brick, another must be placed, pierced in the same way, but in reverse; for the opening must be wider on the outside toward the channel <term>launder|the "coullouere," a trough or gutter that directs the molten metal from the furnace into the mold</term> than on the inside toward the furnace brick.

Next is the other, smaller furnace where the wood is thrown, as was said above; but its floor, which is somewhat lower than the mouth through which the flame enters the large furnace, must be floored with a grate of iron bars spaced one inch apart. In this way, the ash and embers fall into the pit that will have been dug beneath it, from where they can be removed with an iron rake <note>original: "rable de fer"</note>, for fear that the pit might fill up and consequently stifle the air that must rouse the action of the fire.

Furthermore, one must not forget to season <note>original: "recuire"; to pre-fire the furnace to remove moisture</note> all these furnaces for twenty-four hours, providing the fire little by little and by suitable degrees until they are thoroughly dry and no longer cast off smoke or vapors, which would prevent the bronze from flowing clean and liquid as is necessary. 

When placing the metal into the furnace, care should be taken to arrange the pieces upright and not flat upon one another, so that there is air between them. If one must add additional pieces after the metal in the furnace is ready to melt, these should be heated beforehand at one of the furnace mouths, lest they chill the rest and thus delay the work.

There are enough other considerations regarding this matter, which we shall touch upon more fully in our treatise on artillery within the *Military Art* of Onasander <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher whose work on military strategy was translated and annotated by many Renaissance humanists</note>, a Greek author translated by us into the French language with annotations. Therefore, we shall finish this discourse here, after stating that figures of gold and silver are made from sheets, which are made to take the desired form over bronze models that have been cast from plaster molds. These sheets are beaten upon the models with flat and blunt iron tools until they have achieved the closest possible resemblance to the model; then they are finished by chasing <note>original: "cizellant"; the process of detailing metal with a hammer and chisel</note> them as required, and finally, the pieces are soldered together. ## NATION OR SOLDERING.

There are doubts and controversies in this matter among the legal scholars, who get stuck on words that they perhaps do not well understand. For words, being very subject to ambiguity, need to be specifically distinguished for the understanding of that to which one wishes to apply them; this serves as a guide and correction to keep them on the right path. Cassius, in the writings of Paulus, states: *<term>Ferrumination|the process of joining two pieces of the same metal together without using a different alloy</term> with the same material creates a blending; but <term>soldering with lead|original: "plumbatura"</term> does not achieve the same.* <note>original Latin: "Ferruminatio per eandem materiam facit confusionem: plumbatura uero non idem efficit."
