In the first place, therefore, one must delve deeper into the interpretation of this word <term>Ferrumination</term> <note>From the Latin *ferruminatio*, a term used by Roman authors and jurists to describe the joining of metals; the author is arguing it means more than just iron-working despite its root in *ferrum*, iron</note> than what it sounds like on the surface. For one can clearly see that it is not restricted only to iron, from which it takes its name, but also extends to silver, and consequently to all the rest of the metals—indeed, even to several things that lie outside their range, as will be seen by the following authorities. Pliny, in Book 10, Chapter 33, speaking of the manner in which magpies transport their eggs from one nest to another: *A twig being placed over two eggs and cemented with glue from the belly, they carry them elsewhere, balanced equally on both sides with the neck placed underneath.* <note>original Latin: "Surculo ſuper bina oua impoſito, ac Ferruminato alui glutino, ſubdita ceruice medio æquè vtrinque librato deportant aliò."</note> There, it is undoubtedly taken as a form of glue. In the eleventh book, Chapter 37, giving the reason why the bones of dogs and horses cannot be "ferruminated"—that is to say, being broken, they cannot knit back together—which he attributes to the lack of marrow: *and the marrow seems to have been discovered for this purpose, being red, and turning white in old age: it is only found in hollow bones, and not in the legs of beasts of burden or dogs; which is why, when broken, they do not knit back together [ferruminate]; which happens because the marrow flows away.* <note>original Latin: "& medulla ex eodem videtur eſſe iniuenta rubens, & in ſenecta albeſcens : non niſi cauis & oſſibus: & cruribus iumentorum aut canum ; Quare fracta non Ferruminantur: quod defluente euenit medulla."</note> In Book 27, Chapter 4, for soldering: *I consider those things fabulous which are added concerning the nameless herb; that when fresh, if it is burned, iron or bronze is soldered.* <note>original Latin: "Fabuloſa arbitror quæ adiiciuntur de herba anonymo; For a hardening, in Chapter 26 of the same book: *The glass of the tomb, having been cooked, is hardened [ferruminated] into stones.* <note>original Latin: "Vitrum ſupulchri concoctum, ferruminatur in lapides."</note> And finally—

But here we are concerned only with that of metals: where we must first inquire why this word "Ferrumination" took its name from iron—the vilest metal of all—rather than from any of the others. For it is not to be believed that this was done haphazardly and without reason; especially since in ancient, primary words there is a certain emphatic property that carries with it the reality of the thing they represent. Iron, then, despite the fact that at first glance it seems outwardly cold and dry (being very earthy in nature), is nevertheless in its hidden nature—and from within—adhesive and viscous. 

Let us hear what the aforementioned <term>Rhasis</term> <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential figures in the history of medicine and alchemy.</note>, an excellent Arab philosopher, says in the *Book of the Perfect Mastery*: *Iron in its exterior is hot and dry; in its depths it is cold and moist like tin; on one side, hot and moist like gold; on the other, cold and dry like lead.* <note>original Latin: "Ferrum in altitudine sua est calidum & siccum: in suo profundo frigidum & humidum ut stannum, in uno latere, calidum & humidum, ut aurum: in alio frigidum & siccum ut plumbum."</note> 

But this concerns more the chemical considerations and the "anatomies" of metals through their transformations from one quality and nature into another state. For there is nothing that receives more alterations without being entirely cast out from its being—to which it can always be restored—than metal does. We shall expand upon the above words of Rhasis with this passage from the *Book of Vapors* by <term>Avenzoar</term> <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162 AD), a renowned physician from Al-Andalus (modern-day Spain).</note>: *The nature of iron is hot and dry; yet some have said that it is cold and moist, and that it is both masculine and feminine. Its manifest part is hot, dry, and hard; its hidden part is the opposite of these. Nor is there anything in any body harder than its manifest part. Similarly, its softness is revealed when it is converted into its hidden state.* <note>original Latin: "Ferri natura calida & sicca est... Similiter eius mollicies manifestatur, cum in eius occultum convertitur."</note>

But to what purpose are these authorities—and rather difficult ones at that? It is to show that the nature of iron in its interior is very sticky, more so than any of the other metals; for this reason, it is most suited for soldering, and consequently for giving its name to solders, cements, and glues, especially because of its hardness, which these substances must resemble. For in the first place, we see that there is no metal whose pieces rejoin and consolidate more easily when forged and hammered while red-hot—to join and unite them together—than does iron, without the addition of outside materials, as we shall see below in its first method of soldering.

They will be converted into a powder more impalpable than fine flour, and red as blood. That, mixed with powdered bricks and glass, coal-stone, lime, and sand, will make a cement to last almost for eternity. Rust and iron ore, finely beaten, produce the same effect—all because of its gluey viscosity.

Place it upon half-extinguished coals until the verdigris is burned and consumed by means of the saltpeter, for the sal ammoniac will dissipate into smoke. And to this end, using tongs <note>original: "mollets," small pincers or tongs</note>, you will take glowing coals and pass them over the areas where the composition remains too thick, so that it burns off as quickly and evenly as possible and does not dry upon the work, as that would hinder the coloring. Once this is done, remove it from the fire and let it cool in a leaded bowl. When it is cold, clean it with a brush and set it to soak in the urine of young boys aged ten to twelve years <note>Historical metalworkers used the ammonia in urine as a cleaning agent and to enhance the color of gold alloys.</note>.

For this removes all the foul fumes and vapors that the gold might have drawn from the copper, which blacken and infect it to some degree. Furthermore, what is called "annealing" for gold is "brazing" for silver: namely, passing them briefly over the embers.

The subsequent manner of restoring its color is with verdigris <note>A green pigment or crust (copper acetate) formed on copper, brass, or bronze.</note> and sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, used here as a cleaning agent.</note>, equal parts of each, and a twentieth part of saltpeter <note>Potassium nitrate, often used as an oxidizing agent in metalwork.</note>, the whole reduced to powder on a marble slab. Temper this composition with enough distilled vinegar to form an ointment; with this, you will coat your gold work to the thickness of the back of a knife, using a brush. Place it over half-extinguished coals until the verdigris is burned and consumed by means of the saltpeter, for the sal ammoniac will vanish in smoke. For this purpose, using small tongs <note>original: *mollets*</note>, you shall take glowing coals and pass them over the places where the composition remains too thick, so that it may burn equally as soon as possible, and so that it does not dry out upon the work, because that would hinder the coloring. This done, remove it from the fire and let it cool in a lead-glazed bowl. Then, being cold, you will clean it with a brush and set it to soak in the urine of young boys ten to twelve years old <note>In historical metallurgy, urine was a readily available source of ammonia and urea used for pickling and cleaning metal surfaces.</note>.

Silver solder is made with seven parts of silver and one of copper, if the silver being worked is fine at eleven deniers <note>A traditional unit of purity for silver; 12 deniers was considered pure, so 11 deniers is roughly 91.6% purity.</note>. If it is of a low alloy, brass <note>original: *letton*</note> must be taken instead of copper. Melt the copper first, because it has a harder fusion <note>A higher melting point.</note> than silver, and then put the silver inside, and make them play well together—

❦ It remains now to examine the passage in Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author whose "Natural History" was a primary source for Renaissance scientists</note> concerning solders, Book 33, Chapter 5, where he says thus: "Goldsmiths claim chrysocolla <term>chrysocolla: from the Greek 'chrysos' (gold) and 'kolla' (glue); historically identifying various green minerals or soldering agents</term> for themselves for gluing gold; and from this, all who use it similarly call it by that name." <note>original: "Chrysocollam auri artifices sibi vendicant adglutinando auro: Et inde omnes appellatam similiter utentes dicunt."</note> (Because this word signifies gold-solder). "It is tempered, however, with Cyprian verdigris, and the urine of a prepubescent boy, with nitre added." <note>original: "Temperatur autem ea Cypria ærugine, & pueri impubis urina, addito nitro."</note> It seems that he intends to treat therein the artifice we have set out above for giving color to gold—because of the verdigris, the nitre, and the urine of young children—and not of soldering. For since chrysocolla is undoubtedly borax, it cannot be made without metal filings; so that the word *tempered* <note>original: "temperatur"</note> could not be taken to mean the making of the said solder, but rather for the thinning <term>thinning: "destrempement," the process of mixing a dry substance with a liquid</term> of the chrysocolla or borax with the verdigris (which he calls *Cyprian ærugo* <note>Cyprian verdigris</note>) and the nitre. These three together would not be able to glue or solder gold without the solder described above, unless perhaps by the first method called "hot soldering." And yet, Pliny does not intend by this word *tempered* to teach the composition of chrysocolla, nor of solder, as some have believed, but only the manner of using it to solder gold.

[Bo]rax, which the Arabs call *Atincar*, and Pantheus <note>Giovanni Agostino Panteo, a 16th-century Venetian priest and alchemist, author of the *Voarchadumia contra alchimiam*</note> in his *Voarchadumia* calls *oleum vitri* (oil of glass) <term>oleum vitri: literally 'oil of glass,' an alchemical term for a liquid preparation of borax or similar fluxes used to aid melting</term>, because it is artificial and not natural, it must first be understood that it is the true means to facilitate the fusion of all metals: and to reduce their calxes <term>calx: the powdery residue (oxide) left after a metal has been roasted or burnt</term>, however much they may be altered, into a metallic body; By "silvery gold," he means gold alloyed with silver, which is called "alloying with white"; and by "coppery gold," he means that which is mixed with fine copper, because gold cannot be well joined to **brass** <term>letton</term> <note>an alloy of copper and zinc</note>, rather they reject each other; and this is called "alloying with red." 

But for the rest, I do not quite understand what **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 1st-century Roman encyclopedia *Natural History*</note> means in this place, for gold alloyed with either silver or copper is soldered indifferently with the solder called the **alloy** <term>ligue</term> <note>original: "ligue," the specific mixture used to join pieces</note>, by means of **Borax**, which he calls **santerna** <term>santerne</term>. Furthermore, goldsmiths work more willingly with gold alloyed with copper than with silver, both because it is firmer and withstands **engraving**, **cutting**, and **chiseling** better, and because it takes on a more beautiful color than the other, which is alloyed with white and remains more pale and dull. 

The **standard** <term>tiltre</term> <note>the purity of the gold</note> with which they commonly work is twenty-two **carats** <term>caracts</term>: that is to say, twenty-two parts of fine gold and two parts of copper or silver, to reach the twenty-four carats which is the highest graduation and standard of gold, though one never reaches it quite precisely. As for example, **gold solder** [made] of two parts gold and one of silver, of three of gold and one of silver, etc. Up to seven of gold and one of silver: which is what he <note>Pliny</note> means to say here. But the true solder for gold which is called the **alloy** <term>ligue</term> <note>original: "la ligue"; here referring to the standard mixture used for joining gold</note>, is made of eight parts fine gold, three of silver, and as much of copper. That of **silver** of low alloy is [made] of five parts silver and one of **brass** <term>letton</term>, at eleven **deniers** <note>a unit of fineness; pure silver is measured at 12 deniers</note>, for the fine reaches twelve, which is what they work with in some places, particularly in the mints; for the **Paris hallmark** <term>poinçon de Paris</term> <note>the official standard mark of the Paris goldsmiths' guild</note> is only ten and a half, that is to say, ten and a half parts silver and one and a half of copper. The solder, then, for silver at eleven deniers, is seven parts silver and one of copper or brass: but copper is firmer, and consequently endures and allows for cleaner **chasing** <term>cizellage</term> <note>the art of detailing or refining the surface of metal with small chisels</note>. That of copper [is ...] and one of silver. But one solders candlesticks, **fire-dogs** <term>chenets</term> <note>ornamental irons for supporting logs in a fireplace</note>, and the like with solder made of **lead** and **tin**: what the legal scholars call **Plumbatura** <note>original: "Plumbatura"; a Latin term for soldering with lead</note>, which does not mix with the metals they solder, but here serves only as mortar or cement does for stones, or glue for wood. And one must be advised that in all the aforementioned solders, one must always mix in a third part of **Borax**, made into a paste with a solution of **tragacanth gum** <term>gomme de draghant</term> dissolved in common water.

It follows consequently in **Pliny**: *“The glue of gold is such as has been said: clay for iron; cadmia for copper masses; alum for sheets; resin for lead and marble; but black lead is joined to white, and white to itself, with oil; likewise tin to copperwares; silver with tin.”* <note>original Latin: "auri glutinum tale est quod dictum est: Argilla ferro cadmia æris massis : alumen laminis: Resina plumbo & marmori, sed plumbum nigrum albo iungitur, ipsumque album sibi, oleo: item stagnum æramentis; stagno argentum." Note: Pliny refers to lead as "black lead" and tin as "white lead."</note> Pliny tells us of wonderful things here, and in few words, having been satisfied with what he could hear superficially of infinite things he touched upon as if in passing, without having experience of them. ...place all the clay in the world, it would be of no use in **soldering** <term>soulder</term> iron, unless by accident, such as to hold two pieces of iron steady while waiting for them to be joined: and to prevent **scorching** <term>adustion</term> <note>damage caused by excessive heat during the forge-welding process</note> during that time. For what compatibility can there be between clay and metal? *And that which does not penetrate, does not alter* <note>original Latin: "Et quod non ingreditur non alterat"</note>, says Gelée <note>likely Jean Gelée, a 16th-century commentator or apothecary</note>. As for the **cadmia** <term>cadmie</term> <note>a term used for zinc ores or cobalt, but here specifically calamine</note> which he says solders bronze in a mass, why did he not also immediately mention plates and similar pieces, as he says it is **alum** <term>alun</term> that produces this effect? There are, moreover, several types of cadmia: but he means **calamine**, a mineral found in copper mines, which is common in Germany and in the Duchy of Milan. It is with this that one reduces copper into **bronze** <term>airain</term> or **brass** <term>letton</term>, melting them together, a layer of one upon a layer of the other, in a large furnace. **Tutty** <term>tuthie</term> <note>zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</note> has the same effect, or nearly so: but it does not serve to solder copper or bronze, whether in a mass or otherwise, any more than alum serves for copper plates—besides the fact that there cannot be a great difference between soldering plates or bars of the same material.

*Resin for lead and marble* <note>original Latin: "Resina plumbo & marmori"</note>. In truth, **plumbers** and **pewterers** <term>pottiers d'estain</term> use **rosin** <term>poix resine</term> in their **solders** <term>souldeures</term> which are made of lead and tin, as was said above, to heat and make the metal flow so that it bonds better. It also serves for marble and similar hard stones: and this is called **masticating** <term>mastiquer</term> <note>joining or filling with a cement-like adhesive</note>, because one similarly employs mastic, pitch, and other such gums for it.

Regarding the *black and white lead* <note>original Latin: "plumbum nigrum & album"; in antiquity, "black lead" referred to lead, and "white lead" to tin</note> of which he speaks here, here is what he touches upon more fully in Book 34, Chapter 16: the origin of lead is twofold: for it either occurs in its own vein and mine separately without producing anything else of itself, or it is born with silver, and the two veins are melted together. From this, the first liquid that comes to flow in the furnaces is called **tin** <term>estain</term>; the next after is silver; and that which remains in the furnace is **galena** <term>galene</term>, which is a third portion and species of the vein. <header>OF SICYON.</header>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring an ornate frame with scrolled foliage and a central figure in a dynamic classical pose.</image-desc>The ancients of pagan times left nothing behind—as **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> says—of everything that could fall under human understanding, feelings, and actions, without making it into some kind of deity. They did not forget the "occasion" or "opportunity" that presents itself to do something at the right time. The Romans, who treated the word as feminine, called it *occasio* <note>original: "occasio" — the Latin root for "occasion," meaning a favorable juncture of circumstances.</note>; and the Greeks, using the masculine, called it <term>kairos</term> <note>original: "καιρὸς" — a Greek term representing the "opportune moment" or the "crucial time" for action.</note>, which **Festus** <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> defines as a convenience of time that offers itself by chance. And **Cicero**, in the first book of *On Invention*: "Opportunity is a portion of time, having within itself some fitting chance to do or not do a thing." Furthermore, in the first book of *On Duties*, the opportune and suitable time for action is called <term>euchairia</term> <note>original: "εὐχαιρία" — Greek for "good timing" or "fitness of occasion."</note> by the Greeks and *occasio* in Latin. This opportunity arises and mingles with human actions, which do not prevent an outcome; it is like a young boy who, by falling asleep, might provide an opportunity for thieves to help themselves to his goods.

For the rest, she was depicted entirely naked, with wings on her feet and standing upright on a fast-turning wheel to show her unstable lightness, which constantly turns and varies. All her hair is spread over her face in the front, but she is bald behind. This denotes that one must seize her when she offers herself; for she suddenly passes by, and one cannot afterwards reach back or grab hold of her. From this follows repentance and the regret one has for having let her escape in vain; thus, Repentance is always placed behind her, as the one who ordinarily follows her. **Callistratus** <note>A 4th-century Greek sophist and rhetorician known for his descriptions of statues.</note> describes her as **Lysippus** fashioned her in a bronze figure—for his art was in casting—and he gave it as a gift to the city of **Sicyon**, of which he was a native. But **Ausonius** <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310–395 CE), a Roman poet and teacher.</note> attributes another to **Phidias** <note>The OCR reads "Pfidias," a misspelling of the famous Greek sculptor Phidias.</note>, which he describes very elegantly in this Epigram. We have rendered this into English and placed both versions opposite one another so that they may be better compared.

# THE STATUE

Whose work is this? Phidias’ <note>Phidias (c. 480–430 BCE) was a renowned Greek sculptor, though this specific poem is traditionally attributed to the Roman poet Ausonius.</note>, who [made] his statue of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom.</note>,
And who made Jupiter: I am his third masterpiece.
I am the goddess Opportunity, rarely known to many.
Why do you stand on a wheel? I cannot stay in one place.
Why do you have winged sandals? I am swift; [even those] whom Mercury <note>The messenger god, associated with speed and luck.</note>
Is accustomed to bless, I delay when I wish.

You cover your face with hair: I do not wish to be recognized.
But look here,
You are bald at the back: lest I be held back as I flee.

Who is the companion joined to you? I ask you to tell me.
I am the goddess to whom even Cicero himself gave no name.
I am the goddess who exacts punishment for what is done and not done:
Indeed, so that one may repent, I am called <term>Metanoia</term> <note>original: "metanæa" — a Greek term for repentance or a change of mind.</note>.
Now tell me, what does she do with you? If 
ever I fly away,
She remains: those whom I have passed by hold onto her.
You too, while you ask questions, while you 
delay in changing [your mind],
Will say that I have slipped from your hands.

# ON OPPORTUNITY

I wish also to represent to you in words one of the masterpieces of Lysippus, which this ingenious sculptor, having designed in his mind as the most excellent of all his statues, displayed to the view of the Sicyonians <note>The Sicyonians were the inhabitants of Sicyon, an ancient Greek city-state renowned for its school of bronze sculpture.</note>. It was the image of Opportune Time <term>Kairos</term> <note>original: "temps oportun" — in Greek mythology, Kairos is the personification of the "right moment" or opportunity, distinct from Chronos (linear time).</note> made of bronze, in which art contended with nature: namely, a young adolescent, flourishing from head to foot with a joyful youth; beautiful to behold and most agreeable, the soft down of his first beard which covered his chin like cotton, abandoned to the wind to curl at its pleasure, and otherwise letting his locks hang in liberty on whichever side they wished: of a pleasant color, which clearly manifested by its luster the delicate complexion of his body, for the most part resembling a Bacchus <note>Bacchus, the Roman god of wine and theater, was often depicted in art as a beautiful, soft-featured, and slightly effeminate youth.</note>.

For his face shone with attractive grace, and his cheeks were colored with a natural, deep-pink vermilion, resembling a rose—certainly beautiful to see—from which a very delicate scarlet <note>original: "escarlatin" — here used to describe a vibrant, healthy flush or glow.</note> beamed into the eyes of the onlookers. Furthermore, he was positioned upon a ball where he supported himself on the tips of his feet, which were equipped with winged heels <note>original: "eslerons" — small wings on the heels, representing the speed and fleeting nature of opportunity.</note>. Regarding his hair, it was not according to the usual order of nature, but was instead all thrown forward

# THE STATUE

Towards the eyebrows, [the hair] spread from there down the length of the face, so that the back part of the head was entirely bare, with only the roots of the hair visible <note>This specific hairstyle—long locks in front and bald in the back—is the classic iconography of Opportunity (Kairos). It signifies that one can seize the "right moment" by the forelock as it approaches, but once it passes, there is nothing left to grab from behind.</note>. At the sight of this spectacle, we were struck with a certain amazement and remained there suspended, seeing this metal—a product of nature—worked in such a way that it exceeded the order nature had established for it. For although it was bronze, it nonetheless appeared to blush; and despite being so hard and solid in itself, the image nonetheless yielded delicately to everything the art had wished to portray. Endowed with all sense and life, one would have firmly believed that there was something—I know not what—enclosed within it.

It was thus positioned so that it rested upon the very tips of the toes; and while standing still, it nonetheless appeared to have the power of motion, so that it deceived the sight, as if it had within its power all sorts of gestures and movements received from its maker—even to making its way through the air, cleaving it with its wings if it so pleased. We found it truly admirable that it should be so. 

Now, if any man expert in the arts and sciences, who knew well how to seek out with the subtlety of his senses the industrious wonders of skilled craftsmen, and through the liveliness of his reasoning <term>ratiocination</term> <note>original: "ratiocination" — the process of logical or methodical thinking.</note> discern the effectiveness of the occasion...

### ANNOTATION.

If one looks closely at **Callistratus** <note>A Greek writer, likely from the 3rd or 4th century CE, famous for his *Descriptions* (Ekphraseis) of statues, which this text is likely translating or commenting upon.</note>, he seems to always repeat the same thing, though in somewhat different terms, as if he were playing on a single string, varying only the tones by the keys or frets where the fingers strike, making the string shorter or longer. For he only aims to show through his descriptions that the marble and bronze of which these statues consist are so well crafted that they display a sense of life in an inanimate material, imprinted there by the skill of the craftsmen. Everything else concerning the subject of this image, as well as its details, has been touched upon at such length earlier in several places—as could be seen in the statue of the **Maenad** <note>original: "Bacchante". A female follower of Bacchus, often depicted in a state of ecstatic dance.</note>—that it would only be a tedious waste of time for readers to use repetition here. Similarly with the works of **Daedalus** <note>A mythical architect and craftsman, legendary for creating statues so lifelike they had to be tied down to prevent them from walking away.</note>, in the painting of **Pasiphaë**...

### A N N O T A T I O N.

This Memnon was not a statue carved in the figure of a man, but rather a large, shapeless stone casting forth a certain cheerful sound at the rising of the sun—at least if what is told of it is true—and toward evening something plaintive and lamentable. Aesculapius was the son of Apollo and the Nymph Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas and Larissa, according to Ovid in the 2nd book of the *Metamorphoses*. After she later gave herself to a young man named Aemenius (otherwise called Ischrys), Apollo, out of spite and jealousy, put her to death with arrows just as she was ready to give birth; but having felt regret afterward, he had her opened, and from her the child was pulled out alive. He named him Aesculapius and gave him to be raised and instructed by the Centaur Chiron, from whom he learned Medicine and Surgery, along with the properties of herbs and other simples <note>In historical medicine, "simples" were individual medicinal plants or minerals used as remedies before they were combined into complex mixtures.</note> from which medications are composed. Having greatly profited from this knowledge, at the request of Diana he restored Hippolytus to life—who had been dismembered by his horses through the trickery of his stepmother Phaedra. Because of this, Jupiter struck him with a thunderbolt, as recorded by the commentators of Pindar on the 3rd Pythian Ode to Hieron, where the entire life of Aesculapius is recounted at length, including how Apollo, after the death of the mother, saved him from the fire where her body was being burned. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Aesculapius (Asclepius), the Greek god of medicine. The previous page detailed his mythological birth and his education under the centaur Chiron. <header>THE STATUE</header>

...attributed to the nature of the *Sun* and the *Moon*, because of their courses which they complete obliquely in a circle like serpents; and that *Aesculapius* is the efficacy and healthy virtue originating from the substance of the *Sun* to assist the spirits and the bodies of mortal men; and health is one of the effects of the lunar nature, by which the limbs of animals come to be reinforced by a salutary temperament <note>In ancient medicine, a "temperament" was the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined health.</note> here below. For this reason, images of serpents are commonly applied to their statues, because they are both the cause and the means by which human bodies—as if they were shedding a skin of infirmity and disease—return to their original convalescence and vigor, in the same way that serpents renew themselves each year, their old age having been cast off and laid down. *Apollodorus* in the *Book of the Gods* states that *Aesculapius* also presides over divinations and predictions, because a physician, according to *Hippocrates* in his treatise on *Prognostics*, must be able to give an account of his patients: what their disease is, what it was, and what it will be; just as *Homer* in the first book of the *Iliad* says of the seer *Calchas*: "who knew the things that were, those to come, and those that had been before" <note>original Greek: "ὃς ᾔδη τά τ' ἔοντα, τά τ' ἐσσόμενα, πρό τ' ἔοντα"</note>, which *Virgil* translated word for word: "what is, what has been, and what is drawn forth to come" <note>original Latin: "quae sunt, que fuerint, & quae ventura trahuntur"</note>. So much so that this art is very difficult, as the same *Hippocrates* testifies at the beginning of his *Aphorisms*: which is denoted by the knotted staff that *Aesculapius* holds in his hand <note>The knots on the staff of Aesculapius represent the "knotted" or difficult problems a physician must solve.</note>. The dogs that were usually kept in his temple show that he had been nursed by a female dog; and the fact that these temples are everywhere outside of cities and in high places is because the ancients, according to *Plutarch* in the 94th *Roman Question*, considered dwelling in the fields to be healthier than in cities. Concerning which *Pliny* in Book 29, Chapter 1, writes: "The ancients did not condemn the practice of medicine, but the art itself; they especially refused that it should be a trade conducted at the immense price of a life. Therefore, they are said to have built the temple of Aesculapius outside the city, even when he was accepted as a God, and again on an island" <note>original Latin: "Non rem antiqui damnabant, sed artem (speaking of Medicine) maximè vero quæstum esse immani pretio vitæ recusabant, ideo templum Æsculapij, etiam cum reciperetur is Deus, extra urbem fecisse, iterúmque in insula traduntur."</note>. We should not believe that the image to which Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note> committed such great virtues, etc. That is to say, regarding the efficacy and power that can exist in things inanimate and dead by their own nature—I am not speaking here of "occult properties," such as those found in medicines, or in the magnet <note>original French: *l'aymant*</note>, which is more admirable than anything else in its attraction to both iron and the North Pole—but rather as in images made of wood, stone, or metal, fashioned under certain constellations and applied with characters <note>In this context, "characters" refers to magical symbols or astrological signs inscribed on an object.</note>, along with exorcisms, incenses, sacrifices, and similar superstitious ceremonies, all of which depend upon Magic. 

As for the images of our Saints and their relics, that is a separate case, which depends immediately upon the grace that it has pleased God to impart to them; just as one sees that nature places stronger powers and virtues in certain "simples" <note>A "simple" is a medicinal herb used on its own, as opposed to a compound medicine.</note> than in others, and that these remain imprinted in them for a very long time after their death—that is to say, after they are plucked from the earth from which they took their being and sustenance.

Now, most Philosophers, and especially the Platonists, agree on this: that the lower things of this elementary world correspond by a certain analogy to the celestial ones, and that everything done here below, as Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) who was one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> specifies, must first have been sketched out—indeed, preformed—in the movements and conceptions of the stars and their spheres. To this, the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of thought in Jewish mysticism.</note>—who have surpassed the philosophers in matters of mental speculation—have gone further, stating that everything likewise corresponds to the intelligible world, where the Ideas of all forms of the sensible world exist. From that world, these forms derive and are drawn down as if through channels brought from afar from a living spring underground to water a garden. This occurs by means of the ten Sephirots <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself and continuously creates the universe.</note> which all proceed from the source of the divine essence, which Rabbi Eliezer <note>Likely referring to Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, a prominent Jewish sage, often cited in mystical and midrashic literature.</note> and the other Hebrew doctors call the "Throne of the Glory of God" <note>original Hebrew concept: *Kiseh HaKavod*</note>. This Throne, through the mediation of His Angels, the Heavens, and the Stars, spreads all virtues here below that can be seen in the three types of individuals: animals, vegetables, and minerals; and not only in things...

And if the rays departing from the stars can in an instant penetrate the globe of the earth to its center—where there are more than a thousand leagues in a straight line from its surface—they can much better and more strongly imprint them upon certain suitable and proportionate things, which are exposed to them quite naked and openly without any hindrance or obstacle. For there being nothing but the air between them, their light and power can more easily penetrate there than through water; and water more easily than glass; and glass more than crystal; and crystal more than the condensed earth along with the hard and solid stones enclosed therein. This is why, among other things suitable for forming images, wax <note>original: "cyre"</note> has been chosen on many occasions for being so soft, flexible, and obedient to all the figures and qualities that one wishes to imprint upon it, and consequently susceptible, even in its melting, to the influences and faculties of the celestial bodies. # OF ASCLEPIUS

And I seem to have read somewhere that near Cairo there was found, some five or six hundred years ago, a leaden image in the likeness of a Crocodile; which, having been broken into pieces by the command of the <term>Caliph</term> <note>A title for a supreme Muslim civil and religious ruler.</note>, because the Muslims detest all figures of any natural thing whatsoever, immediately afterward those pernicious animals began to reappear in that part of the river Nile, and to infest the banks as they used to do before that leaden figure had been placed there—during which time, within the memory of man, not a single Crocodile had been seen, at least none that did harm, from the sea where the mouths of this river are, for more than a hundred leagues upstream.

But if our religion does not permit their use, nor that of any other kinds of charms, even for some good and charitable effect, and thus requires that one rely entirely upon the virtue that God has imprinted in natural things without departing from them; for even stronger reason, one could use them even less without a very great offense to harm and damage one’s neighbor, or any other person whomsoever, even if he were a heretic, a miscreant, and in all other ways detestable, since we have been given other ways.

### ANNOTATION.

*This entire low-relief scene made of stucco is quite intelligible in itself, for it is well known what is meant by the wind of **Zephyrus** and the **Ocean**, whom the poets imagine to be the son of Heaven <note>Uranus</note> and **Vesta** <note>likely representing Gaia or the Earth here</note>, and furthermore the husband of **Tethys**, and the great superintendent of the sea—indeed, the sea itself. From him proceed not only all the gulfs that make their way into the land, such as the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea, the Persian Sea, and many others, but also all the rivers and streams, and the springs from which they originate, only to return once more to him. Regarding **Amphitrite**, the poets imagine her to be his daughter, so named from the Greek word "to surround" <note>original: $\dot\alpha\mu\phi\iota\tau\epsilon\iota\beta\epsilon\iota\nu$ (amphitribein)</note> because she encircles the earth on all sides where it is bounded. They say that when **Neptune** sought her in marriage, she wished to preserve her virginity and went into hiding from one place to another without him being able to find news of her; he then dispatched a **Dolphin** who searched so far that he finally found her at the foot of Mount Atlas. There, the dolphin acted in such a way that she yielded to the suits of Neptune, by whom she had **Triton**. This is the point **Callistratus** <note>Callistratus (4th century BCE) was a Greek sophist who wrote descriptions of statues, known as *Ekphraseis*</note> intends to make here when he describes the dolphins frolicking around her. But since she encircles the earth just as the Ocean does, what harm would there be in bordering this scene with their Hymn from **Orpheus**, accompanied by that of Zephyrus, who makes the waters peacefully navigable? He writes as follows: but understand that the Ocean, Tethys, Amphitrite, Nereus, and other such names are but one and the same thing—namely, the Ocean Sea, diversified by all those different names.*

<meta>Continuity: The Vinedresser is explaining his history to the Phoenician traveler. Having previously mentioned how the hero Protesilaus helped him secure his land, he now describes his transition from a city-dwelling student of philosophy to a rustic laborer under the hero's guidance.</meta>

### OF PHILOSTRATUS.

To tell the truth, in our younger years we made our residence in the city, occupied with the study of **Philosophy**: where we had very good teachers. But our affairs did not go well in the countryside, for being constrained to rely on servants <note>original: *vallets*. Here referring to hired farmhands or domestic workers who managed the estate in his absence.</note>, they were not accustomed to bringing us anything back to the house, so that we had to take out money at interest upon our estates, or be oppressed by necessity. 

Now, I used to have **Protesilaus** <note>The first Greek hero to die at Troy, who, according to local legend, continued to live as a "hero" or spirit on the Thracian Chersonese.</note> for my counsel in all things; but having then become indignant against me for a just cause—namely, that I had left him to retire to the city—he remained quiet, no longer wishing to give me any advice or instruction. But when I had pressed him importunately, and alleged to him that if he misdirected me in this I was in danger of being lost, he said: *"I shall change my dress,"* <note>original: *ie changeray d'accoustrement*. A cryptic, oracular response typical of Greek heroes or deities.</note> which I did not understand at the time; but having thought about it more closely, I recognized that by this he commanded me to change my way of life. 

Whereupon, having clothed myself in a <term>goatskin</term> <note>original: *peau de chieure*. The traditional attire of a rustic laborer or peasant, signaling his abandonment of urban sophistication.</note>, and armed with a good spade, I have not since then found the way back to the city; for all things abound for me in the fields. And even if one of my sheep should fall ill, or my beehives, or if some accident should happen to a tree, I consult **Protesilaus** in all these matters.

...Tutelary patrons of the place, a virgin girl of noble race, in such a way that all those of the most prominent houses had already passed the step <note>An idiom meaning they had faced their turn to be sacrificed.</note> each in her turn according to what happened by lot, except for his, which had not yet been included, until it came to the turn of one of the greatest named Mastusius. He flatly refused to submit his own daughter to this hazard if those of **Demiphon** did not come into play: who, indignant at this, had Mastusius's daughter immolated without even casting lots. The father hid his feelings for the hour, claiming he had no occasion to complain since it was for the public safety; nevertheless, he would have borne it with less regret if it had passed by the ordinary way. And he knew so well how to feign his feelings that the King gradually forgot about it, thinking that Mastusius would have done so on his part as well. But some time later, he invited Demiphon and his daughters to one of his solemn sacrifices and feasts; having sent them ahead while he cleared up some business, Mastusius had them massacred and mixed their blood with wine that he presented to Demiphon, and then confessed the whole affair to him. Demiphon immediately had him thrown into the sea with the cup from which he had drunk; for which reason the sea was thereafter called the **Mastusian**, and the harbor "The Cup" <note>original: "la couppe"</note>: which the ancient Astrologers have represented by a number of stars up there in the sky in a constellation of the same name <note>The constellation Crater, known as the Cup.</note>, to serve as a warning to mortals not to do injustice nor wrong to anyone: or if one does, to seek to repair it, or to stand on one's guard, thinking that those who have received the outrage will not want to forget it.

Philostratus, moreover, describes here a certain <term>palingenesis<note>From the Greek, meaning 'rebirth' or 'regeneration.' In this context, it refers to the hero returning in a semi-divine, physical form.</note></term> and revivification of **Protesilaus** in a spiritualized body, following what Plutarch cites from the poet Hesiod regarding the "Cessation of Oracles." He established four types of natures that participate in rational discourse: the gods, the <term>daemons<note>Not 'demons' in the modern evil sense, but 'daimones'—intermediate spirits between gods and men.</note></term>, the demigods, and men; for the **Heroes**, he says, are among the number of demigods. And upon this, some argue that a mutation of bodies occurs as well as of souls; for neither more nor less than water is gendered from earth, air from water, and fire from air, so do good souls also undergo mutation, turning from men into demigods, and from demigods into daemons, and from daemons finally coming to participate in divinity. But those who cannot restrain themselves, but rather let themselves go and involve themselves once more in mortal and corruptible bodies, live a somber and obscure life, like a murky smoke.

...seven hundred thousand combatants is described quite fully by **Herodotus** and several others; this occurred around the year of the world 3480, and some 270 years after the founding of Rome. As for the two other disasters, one of fire and the other of water—following the example, as philosophers and physicians suggest, of the two ways in which a man's life naturally ends (if his life is not cut short by accidents): one through fevers and heats that consume the **radical heat** <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, "radical heat" was the vital internal fire believed to sustain life and digestion.</note>, and the other through the suffocations and choking of **catarrhs** <note>Catarrh refers to an excess of bodily fluids or phlegm; here, it is used as a metaphor for "drowning" from within.</note>—the first of these two disasters in the world (which is the "great man" <note>The "Macrocosm," or the universe, which was thought to mirror the "Microcosm" of the human body.</note>, for there is an analogy between the one and the other) was by fire under **Phaeton**, King of Ethiopia, during the time of Abraham or shortly after.

Having set out for Italy to conquer it, many places there were set ablaze, such as Mount Vesuvius near Naples, and Mount Etna in Sicily, and many others—indeed, a great portion of the earth and the heavens, if one wishes to believe the poets, who expand upon this with infinite fictions, Ovid himself among others in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*. But Pliny, in book 37, chapter 2, following Theophrastus, says that he died in the Ethiopia of Ammon. Regarding **Deucalion**, son of Prometheus, there was another, entirely opposite disaster: namely, a deluge and flood of waters that submerged a portion of the earth some 700-odd years after the universal flood of Noah, specifically in Thessaly. He and his wife **Pyrrha**, having saved themselves in a small boat on Mount Parnassus, went to seek counsel from the Oracle of the goddess **Themis** after the waters had drained and settled, to learn how they might restore the human race. She commanded them to return, throwing the bones of their "great mother" behind them. They interpreted this as pebbles, which are like the bones of the earth—our common mother—and they were transformed: those of Deucalion into men, and those of Pyrrha into women.

Virgil also did not forget him in his *Aetna* <note>A Latin poem about the volcano Etna, historically attributed to Virgil but now considered part of the "Appendix Vergiliana"</note>:
> Their nature is such that down to the belly they are human; below, a scaly serpent winds its path through twisted coils. <note>original Latin: "His natura sua est aluo tenus, ima per orbes / Squammeus intortos sinuat vestigia serpens."</note>

Wherefore the Emperor Commodus <note>A Roman Emperor (161–192 AD) who famously competed as a gladiator and believed himself the reincarnation of Hercules</note> in the writings of Lampridius <note>One of the authors of the "Augustan History," a collection of Roman imperial biographies</note> used to call "Giants" those who had twisted legs and feet. This, Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian known for seeking historical or rational explanations for myths</note> takes to mean the crooked wickedness of the malevolent, who anciently oppressed the greater part of the earth. As they still do today: those who never walk straight, but rather windingly, so that they stumble at every turn—especially those who attempt to violate right religion and belief. We must also discuss something of that which concerns the Thracian Rhesus <note>original: "Rhefus." Nevertheless, people do not cease to sacrifice to him while passing through that mountain and Thrace. # PROTESILAUS.

The general of the Athenians, having captured and impaled alive a certain Artayctes, a Persian governor of Sestos, for having perpetrated a multitude of villainies and wicked acts in the temple of Protesilaus at Elaeus <note>Eleonte</note>, bringing women there under the guise of devotion, only to violate them afterward; he <note>the historian Herodotus</note> calls him a Persian, and Philostratus calls him a Median or Mede, but these two provinces being under the same rule, it is very easy for you to mistake one for the other. *Regarding the resurrection of this body preserved in salt, which follows after, I have read nothing of it anywhere else: these are miracles with which this work is entirely stuffed.*

->A Dardanian man slew him,<-
->As he leapt from his ship, by far the first of the Achaeans.<-
<note>original Greek: "τὸ δ᾽ ἔκτανε Δάρδανος ἀνὴρ, Νηὸς ἀποθρώσκοντα πολὺ πρώτιστον ἀχαιῶν."</note>

And he emits a voice that is distinct and easy to hear, like a soft mute <note>fourdine; likely referring to a "sordino" or damper used to soften musical instruments</note>, sounding from a weak and small mouth. *Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine monk and philosopher known for his work on demonology</note> on this subject states that Demons <note>In the classical sense of 'daimones' or spirits</note>, being highly spiritual as they are, approach our imaginative spirit and remind it of what they wish, and not by emitting a resonating voice that strikes the air: but by introducing their thoughts to us without speaking or making any noise. And in fact, those who speak from a distance need to shout louder than if they were close: and if someone spoke in your ear, it would be so low that those present would not think anything was said. They believe this character is so strongly imprinted that, after being separated from the body, the soul's operations and passions do not remain entirely extinguished and erased. In this way, notwithstanding that the organic body is corrupted and dissolved from its former being, the operation will not cease for all that; rather, some traces of its affections will remain, just as when fire is taken out of a hearth or a furnace, the heat does not absent itself all at once, but there remains what the Greeks call* <term>empyreuma <note>original: ἐμπύρευμα. This refers to the "embers" or residual heat and sparks left behind after a fire is gone; here used metaphorically for the soul's lingering earthly habits.</note></term>. Virgil was not ignorant of this either, when in the 6th book of the *Aeneid* he says thus:

> *The same pride in chariots and arms that they had while living, the same care to feed shining horses, follows them now that they are laid in the earth.*

From which Saint Augustine also does not distance himself at all, for he confesses that souls separated from the body still retain for some time a memory of the inclination they had in this temporal life...

Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and occultist famous for his theories on nature spirits.</note> therefore establishes a kind of men whom he calls "spirituals," because their bodies are much more subtle than ours. He is moved to this by that philosophical consideration that one cannot pass from one extreme to another except by a middle disposition: so that between man, who is mortal and has a corruptible body, and the Demon <note>The term "Demon" here refers to the Classical *daimon*—a spirit or minor deity—rather than necessarily a malevolent entity.</note>, who is immortal, it was thought there must be a third nature participating in both, being neither the one nor the other. That is to say, they have a body just as man does, but incomparably more rare and subtle, in the manner of an air less thick than clouds, without any earthly solidity; for which reason our eye could not discern them except as it pleases them.

Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine philosopher whose works on demonology were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> says on this matter: "The nature of demons is not without a body; rather, they possess them and have commerce with physical things, so much so that they can even be touched. They are subject to passions, especially the Subterranean ones, so that they can feel fire and sometimes leave ashes from their burns." <note>original French: "la nature des Demons n'est pas sans corps..." summarizing Psellus's *De Operatione Daemonum*.</note> Paracelsus continues afterward, saying that although they are subject to death and dissolution, they are nevertheless of much longer duration than we are. 

And just as the Demon is the middle point between men and the gods (who are entirely abstract and separate from bodies, because men inhabit the earth and the gods the heavens), these "spiritual creatures" or "spiritual men" are positioned between men and Demons on one side, and men and brute beasts on the other, because they have no rational soul; rather, at their death, everything in them perishes. He classifies them into four types, according to the number of the Elements, and based on which one they primarily inhabit. Namely: the Pygmies or Gnomons <term>Gnomons: now usually called Gnomes; earth-dwelling spirits in Paracelsian lore.</term> as he calls them, who reside in the bowels of the earth and in the hollowest cavities of the mountains; the Nymphs, Naiads, or Undines in the water; the Sylvans <note>Often referred to as Sylphs in later occult traditions.</note> and Giants in the air, in the most remote and deep forests—and these are the least approachable of all to people, except for...

Nevertheless, not all <term>Demons</term> <note>In this context, the author uses "demons" in the classical sense to mean spirits or supernatural beings, rather than exclusively evil entities.</note> do so, but only those who are closest to matter, such as the Subterranean and Aquatic ones. The second, the aerial; the third, the terrestrial, where they cause infinite inconveniences and disasters; the fourth, the Aquatic and Marine, who live along lakes and rivers where they cause many people to drown and perish; the fifth, the Subterranean, who reside in the depths of the earth, where they molest those who dig wells and mine for metals; the sixth are those who entirely hate the light and make themselves unapproachable. *Furthermore, the difference between the male and female sexes is not truly within them, but they manifest it in appearance; however, this is hardly stable, no more than the shapes formed in clouds, whether in form or color, which dissipate just as quickly—and the same occurs in water. And insofar as the flesh and all the rest of our bodily substance that we have taken from Adam is coarse, massive, and earthly, like wood or stone, theirs—on the contrary—which does not come from our first father but from a separate creation, is incomparably more subtle and more impalpable to the touch, almost in the manner of air, so that it easily penetrates everywhere there are pores, small vents, and conduits: like the vapor of a <term>thunderbolt</term> <note>original: "fouldre"</note> which will break a sheathed sword without harming the scabbard, and will reduce coins to powder inside a leather purse or other fabric, without any damage to it. *because these creatures are not made of earth, they penetrate all solid things quite easily, such as doors and walls, without breaking them or making a breach; and they yield to nothing at all, no matter what resistance there might be, which is why they have no need of doors, windows, or any other opening to enter anywhere.*

For the rest, they are much like <term>Adamic man</term> <note>A term used by Renaissance philosophers and occultists to refer to humans as descendants of Adam, defined by a physical body and an immortal soul.</note>, composed of flesh, nerves, bones, and blood: whereby they differ from <term>simple spirits</term> <note>Purely non-corporeal entities, such as angels or demons, who lack any physical matter.</note> who have neither flesh nor bones, as the Savior himself says in the final chapter of Saint Luke <note>original: "S. Luc dernier"; refers to Luke 24:39: "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have."</note>: and they engender children among themselves who are similar to them; they speak, drink, eat, and walk, participating in all these things like Adamic man. But on the other hand, they differ from him in agility, speed, promptness, swiftness, and sudden disappearance: in which qualities they more closely approach the nature of spirits: so much so that just as a body composed of two or more substances—or a color made of two or three—produces only a single form, these creatures are likewise intermediate between men and spirits. There is yet another difference: it is that man has a soul, and they have none; rather, they consist only of body and spirit, from which they nonetheless differ in that they come to an end and die, whereas spirits do not. And just as among the brute beasts, one excels the other the more it approaches the nature of man, so these creatures surpass all animals that lack a <term>rational soul</term> <note>In Aristotelian and Scholastic philosophy, the "rational soul" is the highest level of soul, unique to humans, which allows for reason and immortality.</note>, specifically because they approach man more closely than animals do, and they possess all the functions of man, whom they surpass in terms of spirituality while he is accompanied by his earthly body in this temporal life.

*But since the <term>Redeemer</term> <note>Jesus Christ.</note> died only for men endowed with a rational soul, which grants them a perpetual existence, the merit of his passion and the salvation that depends upon it do not extend to this class of spiritual people; though their life is much longer than ours, when they come to pass away, everything dies and is annihilated with them, as they possess no rational soul—*

They possess great discretion in the conduct of their affairs, and in their justice and policy, which they observe very exactly. In them, there is a certain natural instinct like that of brute beasts, but incomparably more excellent. This is why they have no concern for religion or divine worship, as the rational creature does.

->Of their habitations and dwellings.<-

THEIR dwellings are diverse, as has been touched upon above, according to the quality and disposition of their nature. Those closest to our own nature—though very little approachable and indeed quite wild—are the **Sylvans**, because they live in the air as we do, and their death is more similar to ours: for they can suffocate in water, stifle in the earth, and burn in fire. The **Undines** live in the water, which does them no more harm than the air does to us. The **Gnomes** live in the earth, like moles; and since their Element is more foul and coarse than any of the others, their corporeal composition is all the more delicate, so that, like a very subtle vapor, they pierce through everything. *And just as our habitation is in the air, between the heavens and the earth which sustains us, the same is true for the Sylvans; to the Undines living in the water, the bottom of the water is to them what the surface of the earth is to us (which is the bottom of the air), and their heaven is at the surface of the water. In such a way, just as our Sphere is between the heavens and the earth, theirs is between the earth and the air, which serves as their heaven. For the Gnomes, the bottom is the water; their habitation or Sphere is the earth, the surface of which is their heaven. For the Vulcans, otherwise known as Salamanders, the bottom is the air, their dwelling is the Sphere of fire, and their heaven is the ethereal region. All of these take their nourishment and maintenance each in their own place according to their nature: so that for the Vulcans, those flaming exhalations called falling stars, and other such airy fires, serve them in place of meat.*

As for their sizes and statures, the Gnomes <note>original: "Gnomons"</note> barely exceed a cubit <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches</term> in height; the Undines <note>original: "Vndenes"</note> have a stature conforming to our own; the Sylvans are much larger, like Giants; the Salamanders are longish, thin, lanky, and slender.

The Gnomes build their habitations under the mountains, according to their proportion and size; the Nymphs and Undines keep to the floods and rivers, lakes and ponds, and similar aquatic places, most of the time along the banks to more easily communicate with those they please, and they delight in touching people when they bathe there. The Sylvans inhabit deep forests like wild men; the Vulcans <note>A name for fire elementals, derived from the Roman god of fire.</note> live up there in the Sphere of fire, and down here in volcanoes <note>original: "montgibels," a term for volcanoes derived from the Sicilian name for Mount Etna, "Mongibello."</note> like Etna, and other similar places. ## How they come to us, and make themselves visible.

Just as God has not, on every occasion and to all sorts of people indiscriminately, sent visible Angels; nor allowed Demons to work by possessing people, except for very few persons, as it has pleased him (of which we should not inquire further): he likewise does not allow these spiritual men, thus separated from us, to be seen or to communicate except very rarely, and for occasions known to him alone. *And as we have no knowledge of them, nor of their affairs, so they also have none of us and ours, unless by chance they come to visit and become acquainted with us by a particular grant from the Sovereign God; and then, upon their return, they can tell news of us to their fellow creatures, just as some among us who had traveled to the Indies or China would come back to recount what is done there, and how things are conducted. Furthermore, they cannot draw us into their world; for besides the fact that they have no power over us, we would not be able to live there, being of a dissimilar nature, even though they can live in ours—unless by chance it were in the world of the Sylvans <note>Spirits associated with the element of air.</note>, which consists of air, although it is thicker and slower than our own. ### On their admirable works and ways of doing things.

If one were to take a Nymph or Undine <note>Undine: A water spirit or elemental being; in the folklore of this period, they were believed to be soulless unless they married a human.</note> for a walk in a boat upon the water, and she were to be provoked to anger, she would submerge herself in the waves instantly, never to appear again. And yet, he who had her as a wife must hold it for certain that he has lost her forever without seeing her again; nevertheless, let him take great care not to think that she is dead or drowned, for she cannot perish in her own element. Nor because of this should he think himself delivered from his marriage so as to have the liberty to provide himself with another; for if he does so, he can be sure that he will not live much longer afterward. Inasmuch as their marriage is not dissolved by this absence; for it is just as if a woman departed from her husband, she is not for that reason absolved and delivered from her marriage, nor a man who would leave his wife either; thus they remain bound in the same obligation as before as long as both shall live. *The Undines, therefore, once vanished from their husbands, do not return to them anymore, unless by chance he should marry another woman; for in that case, they would come to him as soon as possible to bring about his death, because since they have left their husbands and the lineage they had by them—which is not, however, of long duration, for it does not pass the second or third generation—they will be held to give an account of it on the day of judgment, having by virtue of this marriage obtained a rational soul <term>rational soul: original "ame raisonnable," the immortal soul that distinguishes humans from animals and elementals in Paracelsian thought</term> as if for a special privileged dowry. But just as those who become acquainted with them, whether in marriage or otherwise, are accustomed to not living long, as Homer makes well enough known in the Hymn to Venus regarding Anchises, who fathered Aeneas by her.*

*The Rabbis, commenting on this passage from the 32nd chapter of Deuteronomy <note>The text refers to Deuteronomy 32:17, which mentions sacrificing to demons.</note>, "they sacrificed to the Shedim," interpret this as referring to evil aquatic spirits. These spirits, they say, were revered by antiquity in place of gods—namely, the Nymphs. They are the most capable of all demons at perverting and debauching man, soaking him in delights, pleasures, and bad morals. Indeed, the word <term>Shedim</term> <note>Derived from the Hebrew root ‘shadad’ (שדד), meaning to overpower, despoil, or destroy.</note> is derived from the concepts of losing, wasting, and corrupting. In truth, the Nymphs, being of the nature of water, are the most dangerous because of their fluid humidity, which flows and introduces itself very easily into the sensuality of persons. This sensuality consists mainly of aquatic humidity, which is the source of lechery. For this reason, Venus is feigned to have been procreated from the sea, of which the poet Virgil, in passing through the country, would have said: the agitated waters swell <note>original: "agitata tumescunt æquora"</note>. Therefore, there are other Nymphs called Sirens who haunt the seas more willingly than fresh waters. They take the form of beautiful young girls, yet their nature is somewhat altered from that of natural women. They do not give birth, as they are of the genus of monsters, procreated by aquatic males and females who, for this reason, banish them from their presence. These Sirens are, moreover, of various appearances—like all monsters who do not keep an immutable order as the regulated things of nature do, being without blemish. They also have diverse ways of behaving, which are not, however, entirely abhorrent to human creatures; for some sing, others whistle, and others weep and lament. There is yet another species of these monstrosities produced from a mixture of <term>Gnomons</term> <note>Gnomes; earth elementals.</note> with <term>Undines</term> <note>Water elementals.</note>, who likewise do not give birth, any more than a male or female mule produced from the joining of a donkey and a mare. All these monsters strongly crave human acquaintance—principally the females, who are in much greater number than the males. -> P R O T E S I L A V S . <-

...often watering the earth, and lower down it is hot and arid, so that the roots, seeking for their maintenance the moisture proper to them, are constrained to spread out in this way, rather than sinking deep where they would find no nourishment. But this wise and prudent Queen <note>Likely a reference to Isabella of Castile or a similar figure from the history of the Spanish Americas.</note>, turning this toward another meaning, remarked: "Certainly, this denotes that in a land where trees take root so weakly, the men likewise must be very light, inconstant, and of little faith": which the result has proven true.

But whatever Philostratus wishes to say here as something rare and paradoxical—that trees must be buried so deep into the earth because they receive their nourishment better there—all naturalists agree that good soil suitable for the production of plants <note>original: "Vegetaulx."</note> usually extends hardly more than six feet into the earth; all the rest being useless, composed of stones, gravel, slime <note>original: "glaires," likely referring to viscous or sticky subterranean layers.</note>, clay, tuff <term>tuf</term> <note>A type of porous rock or solidified volcanic ash.</note>, and other similar substances, more suitable for minerals than for trees and plants. And of all trees, especially fruit trees, the pear tree is the one that sinks its roots deepest into the earth, so that its taproot <term>piuot</term> <note>The central, primary root that grows vertically downward.</note>, which corresponds to its trunk, always seeks the bottom in a straight line. Therefore, it should be buried as little as possible, for fear that, encountering this tuff—since it does not spread out wide along the surface like other trees—it might become "melancholy" <note>original: "melencollier," an archaic term used here to describe a tree failing to thrive or withering.</note> and dry up for lack of nourishment.

It follows after from this same discourse that Homer, by "great, high-raised trees," means those that are buried quite deep in the earth; just as he calls wells "high" and "long" to mean "deep." This is taken from the eleventh book of the Iliad regarding trees: *the trees were tall* <note>original Greek: "τά μὲν δένδρεα μακρά."</note>. And as for wells, from the 21st, speaking of the Ocean.

This corresponds to the saying of Heraclitus: since it is no small labor to converse always on high with the gods, and to work there, being continually subject to them, for this reason the soul—partly from a desire for rest, and partly to be more at liberty—sometimes descends back into the underworld <note>original: "es enfers."</note>. But this is mystical, for the rest of the time, or in its dwelling...

For this reason, when Hercules descended to the underworld to bring back the dog Cerberus, he rescued her from there. Now, Admetus represents courage in us; he is so named because fear—which the Latins call *Metus* <note>original: "Metus"</note>—can indeed approach and seize a person in the face of some imminent danger. Therefore, he desires to marry Alcestis, so named from *alke* <note>original: "ἀλκὴ"</note>, meaning strength, vigor, boldness, and assurance. To this end, he must harness two wild beasts; that is to say, he must seek for his courage the virtues of the spirit and the body—the Lion for the virtues of the spirit, and the Boar for those of the body—and render Apollo and Hercules favorable to him in this matter, representing prudence and strength. Thus, this courageous assurance sacrifices itself for the sake of the soul, as Alcestis did; and since such assurance and boldness often fail in the peril of death, virtuous effort must bring it back from the Underworld, just as Hercules did for Alcestis.

For we must borrow all of this from him, as no one has treated it more specifically: Hyllus of Rhodes having entered the 18th year of his age was rejected by the Eleans from wrestling with the children; nevertheless, as young as he was, he obtained the victory among the men.

...five years in Greece, from which the <term>Olympiads (four-year cycles of the Olympic Games)</term> took their name, because this was sorted out in Olympia within <term>Elis (a region in the Peloponnese)</term>, and all that depended upon it. Sufficient mention was made of this previously regarding the picture of Arrichion <note>Arrichion of Phigalia (d. 564 BC) was a famous athlete who won the Pancratium despite dying during the final match.</note> and others. It remains here to briefly recount that there were five principal types [of events]: the jump, the race, throwing the <term>discus (a heavy circular plate)</term>, wrestling, and <term>boxing (fencing with fists)</term> armed with <term>manopples (leather hand-wraps)</term> fitted with studs or small copper bosses. The <term>Pancratium (a no-holds-barred combat sport)</term> was a mixture of this boxing and wrestling, where they would seize one another, striving to overthrow and cast their opponent to the ground, and there wallowing in the sand, biting, gouging, scratching, untying, breaking, and twisting their limbs, according to what <term>Lucretius (the Roman poet-philosopher)</term> says in his 3rd book: <note>original: "Arma antiqua manus ungues, denteſque fuerunt." This quote is actually from Book 5 of De Rerum Natura.</note> *Ancient weapons were hands, nails, and teeth.* <term>Suidas (the author of a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia)</term> also defines it in few words: that the <term>Pancratiaſtes (athletes of the Pancratium)</term> were the athletes who fought with arms and hands, as well as legs and feet. As for the first three [events], they did not match them man-to-man as in wrestling and boxing; rather there were several [competitors], sometimes more, sometimes fewer. According to how they presented themselves in the ranks—specifically those who were judged most worthy—for first a choice and trial were made to avoid confusion. This was the responsibility of the <term>Hellanodikai (the 'Judges of the Greeks')</term>, which is to say the judges of these solemn prize games and sacred combats; who, according to what <term>Pausanias (the 2nd-century geographer)</term> records in his *Eliaca* <note>Books 5 and 6 of Pausanias's "Description of Greece."</note>, were only two established in the 50th <term>Olympiad</term>, which falls in the year of the world 3385. And from there, the others could be added.

*Some years later they were increased to nine: three of whom oversaw the chariot races and horses in harness; three for the <term>Pentathlon (a five-event athletic contest)</term> which comprised the five trials mentioned above; and three for the other combats. Eight or ten years later, one more was added to complete the tenth. # PROTESILAUS.

...deprived of part of their territory by the Arcadians, and reduced to eight tribes, these Judges were restricted to the same number. But in the 108th Olympiad, they returned to ten, where they have always remained since. The <term>Hellanodikai (the chief judges of the Olympic Games)</term> were required after their election to maintain continuous residence for ten months in a place designated in <term>Elis (the region where Olympia was located)</term>, known for this reason as the <term>Hellanodikeion (the hall of the judges)</term>. There, the <term>Nomophylakes (guardians of the law)</term> or keepers of the statutes instructed them in everything concerning their office and how they should conduct themselves. For it was their duty to award the prizes and to impose fines, and this for various reasons: such as having withdrawn without a legitimate excuse from presenting themselves for the matches if they had been enrolled, as is stated here. Or for failing to appear on the appointed day, as is cited there regarding one <term>Apollonius of Egypt (a boxer)</term> surnamed Rhantis; or for a lack of courage, as did <term>Serapion of Alexandria (a runner)</term>, who was so fearful of his adversaries that he fled secretly the day before they were to compete. 

They were also condemned to a fine for having exceeded the statutes and conditions of the matches, or for having used some charms, as shown in this passage from <term>Suidas (a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia)</term>: these <term>Ephesian letters (mystical incantations used as amulets)</term> were certain obscure verses that involved sorcery, which <term>Croesus (the wealthy King of Lydia)</term> is said to have used when he was placed upon the pyre by the command of <term>Cyrus (the King of Persia)</term> to be burned. And in Olympia, during a wrestling match between an Ephesian and a Milesian, the latter could never get the better of his Ephesian adversary because the Ephesian had certain characters <note>Inscribed symbols or magical formulas.</note> near his heel, until they were discovered and removed. 

Athletes could also be fined for having behaved too viciously and with some trickery. The same <term>Pausanias (the 2nd-century travel writer)</term> writes in his 6th book about that renowned athlete <term>Theagenes (a champion of Thasos)</term>, who was fined six hundred <term>scudi (the author's term for an ancient unit of currency)</term> for having excessively injured <term>Euthymus (a famous boxer)</term>. For these matches did not conclude without serious wounds, as one can see in the 23rd book of the <term>Iliad (Homer’s epic)</term> regarding <term>Euryalus (a Greek warrior)</term>, whom <term>Epeius (the builder of the Trojan horse)</term> treated so roughly with a blow delivered with great force that his companions were forced to carry him away in their arms...

From him [Dolon] they learned all of this. By which means, having put him to death, they proceeded immediately under the darkness of night toward the Thracians, and finding them asleep, they killed up to twelve of them, with Rhesus as the thirteenth, and led away his horses before they had drunk from the Scamander. But this matter is not well resolved among authors, some of whom place **Homer** before and others after; moved by the fact that **Homer**, at the end of the ***Odyssey***, finds his father **Laertes** working in his garden in a manner that **Hesiod** in his *Works and Days* <note>original: "labourages"</note> did not touch upon, from which it would follow that it [Homer's work] came after him. **Plutarch**, in the 5th book of the *Table Talk* <note>original: "Symposiaques"</note>, chapter 2, makes them contemporaries: so much so that they even competed in verse against one another at the funeral rites of **Amphidamas the Chalcidian**; and in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*.
