For it is not to be believed that a poet would be so ill-advised as to follow in the tracks of another who had already done better. However, this matter is not well-resolved among authors, some of whom place **Homer** first, and others after; moved by the fact that **Homer**, in the final book of the **Odyssey**, finds his father **Laertes** working in his garden in a manner that **Hesiod** would not have touched upon in his writings on farming <note>A reference to Hesiod's *Works and Days*.</note>, from which it would follow that the *Odyssey* came after him. **Plutarch**, in the 5th book of his **Table Talk**, chapter 2, makes them contemporaries: so much so that they even composed verses in competition with one another at the funeral rites of **Amphidamas of Chalcis**. Furthermore, in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*, **Aulus Gellius** (book 17, chapter 21) states that almost all authors agree they were both of the same time, or **Homer** was a very short time before **Hesiod**; but both lived before the founding of **Rome**, some one hundred and sixty years <note>original: "huict vingts ans"</note> after the destruction of **Troy**. **Suidas** <note>The *Suda*, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> has him preceding **Homer**; others say they were of the same time; **Porphyry**, and many with him, place him one hundred years after **Homer**; some thirty-two years before the first **Olympiad**, which began around the time of King **Solomon**. **Plutarch**, in the *Life of Homer*, notes that some were of the opinion he was born during the **Trojan War**, others a hundred years after, and others a hundred and fifty. **Herodotus**, who lived more than 740 years after the said destruction, wrote that these two poets lived some 400 years before him and no more; which would be quite far from the dates mentioned above. In short, all of this is very confused and muddled.

It follows afterward that **Homer** <note>The author likely means the commentator or critic comparing the two.</note> had corrected **Hesiod** in the description of the shield of **Cygnus**, for having said coldly, and not poetically enough, that the figure of the **Gorgon** was upon this shield. This is the shield of **Hercules**, and not that of **Cygnus** (the son of **Mars**), whom **Hercules** fought and put to death. Furthermore, it is the backplate of the cuirass <note>Armor covering the torso.</note> that he attributes to **Perseus**, representing him on this shield, engraved in such a way, he says, that he seemed to be held by nothing,

To get her back, the Greeks dispatched an embassy to Troy, which included her husband Menelaus himself. Upon this, the only resolution offered to them was the demand for the restoration of Medea before any justice would be done regarding their complaint; so the Greeks gathered a great army and went to sack and ruin Troy. Herodotus, having briefly set this forth, continues in his second book: that while inquiring one day in Egypt from one of the priests about this matter, the priest came to relate to him how Paris, returning to Troy with Helen and the goods he had plundered in Sparta, was caught by a storm in the Aegean Sea. By this he was cast against his will onto the coast of Egypt, where he was forced to drop anchor in one of the mouths of the Nile called the Canopic branch, at Taricheae. ...was more the act of a lewd and voluptuous concubinary than of a legitimate husband possessed of honesty.

Protesilaüs also does not approve of this in Homer: that having proposed to treat the matters of Troy, he departs from them entirely after the death of Hector, to pass suddenly to another discourse where he describes the deeds of Ulysses. 

Homer, in his poems divided into two great works, the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*—each containing 24 books, just as there are 24 letters in the Greek Alphabet to complete the full revolution <note>The 24 books of each epic are traditionally numbered by the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet, from Alpha to Omega.</note>—wished by this means to depict for us the entire course of human life. This life is nothing other than a racecourse that one traverses, all strewn with caltrops <note>original: "chaussetrappes," spiked metal devices scattered on the ground to puncture the feet of soldiers or horses</note>, nettles, thorns, and thistles of miseries and calamities, worries, vexations, and anguishes that happen to us. These occur both in war (which the *Iliad* concerns) and outside of it in the *Odyssey*—a series of infinite tasks, pains, labors, perils, and disasters, such as Ulysses suffered for ten whole years (matching the duration of the siege of Troy) while returning to his own country. 

Furthermore, through these two works, he wished to represent man, who consists of body and spirit. The latter is represented by Ulysses—wise, prudent, and shrewd, eloquent, constant, and patient in all his adversities; and the body by Achilles—strong and robust, agile and nimble, brave and valiant, but spiteful, angry, and very easy to provoke and "take to the field" <note>original: "se mettre aux champs," an idiom meaning to lose one's temper or become highly agitated</note>. These are passions belonging more to the body, which he excellently portrays for us through the quarrel of the said Achilles and Agamemnon over a girl <note>original: "garce," referring here to Briseis, the captive woman who was the catalyst for the conflict in Book 1 of the Iliad</note>, with which he begins <note>original: "enfourne," literally "puts into the oven," meaning to set a work in motion</note> his work. 

For consider what likelihood there was that Agamemnon—having the charge and superintendency of the Greek army, and consequently so many cares and occupations, and so many people to satisfy—at the height of the affair where he should most fear offending anyone, and especially those of distinction <note>original: "signalez"</note> who had voluntarily followed him in this long and troublesome war, undertaken to avenge the wrong and outrage done to his [brother]...

<summary>The text critiques Homer’s structural choices, arguing that the Iliad and Odyssey serve as allegories for the human condition and the dual nature of man (the spirit vs. the body). It specifically questions the realism of Agamemnon’s quarrel with Achilles over a captive woman.</summary>

...the brother [of] Menelaus <note>Agamemnon, the leader of the Greek forces and brother to Menelaus</note>, for going out of all reason to attack, through arrogance and lewdness <note>original: "lasciueté," referring to the seizure of the maiden Briseis</note>, the most valiant and dreaded member of the army; and he, for his part <note>Achilles</note>, who should have had more consideration for the public safety than for his private passions, becoming so embittered that he nearly brought the whole enterprise to the point of ruin. He refused to bend his will in any way, nor would he listen to any reasonable proposal, being moved neither by prayers, nor remonstrances, nor even by offers that were more than reasonable. Instead, he was moved only by the death of his own dear favorite minion <note>Patroclus, his close companion</note>, whom he showed he held much closer to his heart than either the honor of his Country, his own reputation, or the just vengeance for an injury done to all of Greece in general. Homer, therefore, wishing to represent the transported passions of the body, begins this poem with the word wrath <note>original: *μηνις* (mēnis), meaning a divine or monumental rage</note>—indignation and a fierce, wicked anger; and he ends it not precisely at the death of Hector, as Virgil does with the death of Turnus:

->And life with a groan fled indignant to the shadows,<-
<note>original: "Vitáque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub vmbras," the final line of Virgil's *Aeneid*</note>

having begun his *Aeneid* in the same way with the ire and long-held vindictiveness of a slighted Juno against the Trojans; rather, Homer ends with the funeral of the said Hector, to denote the courtesy and pitiful honesty that the same Achilles showed toward Priam, who had come to him to ask for the return of his son’s body. But on this point, some censure Homer for having represented his Achilles as so sordid, stingy, and avaricious that he only returned the body in exchange for the great gifts and presents that Priam brought him—and even then, only after he had treated the corpse with infinite insults and outrages. Plutarch, moreover, in his life of this Poet, shows through vivid reasoning that there is nothing inept or out of place in his poems; as does Horace in his *Art of Poetry*:

### PROTESILAVS. <note>As noted previously, the header title refers to the hero Protesilaus, but the text continues to provide a prose translation and commentary on Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note>

...even though it be with great evils and hardships, if you can restrain yourself and your companions, when your vessel lands on the Trinacrian Isle <note>modern Sicily, named for its three corners</note> to avoid the sea stirred by tempestuous waves, from the cattle you will find grazing there, and the fat and well-fed sheep, all consecrated to the Sun <note>the god Helios</note> who sees and hears everything; and if, leaving them untouched, you set out on your return, certainly you may still by chance reach Ithaca, though it be with great and troublesome tribulations.

But if you amuse yourself by offending them even a little, certainly I announce to you infallibly your death, and that of your companions, along with the ruin of your vessel. And if by chance you escape, it will nonetheless be late, and having suffered infinite labors, that you will arrive at your home, and moreover in the ship of another.

And you will find at your house much desolation: insolent and proud men who eat and squander your wealth, and pursue your wife to marry her, offering her many rich gifts and presents; but upon your arrival, you shall punish all their outrages. 

Now, after you have put to death all these suitors in your house, whether by cunning or by the fury of the sword, embark then promptly in a ship, and sail until you reach a people who know nothing of the sea, and are not accustomed to salting their meat, nor do they know the ships with oars that serve them as wings.

### PROTESILAVS.

*...the people dwelling thereabout will live in great happiness. However, Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Roman author of the 1st century BC known for his collection of myths</note> writes in chapter 127 that Telegonus, son of Ulysses and Circe, having been sent by her to seek his father, was carried by the fortune of the sea to Ithaca. There, constrained by the necessity of foraging the flat countryside, Ulysses and Telemachus, without knowing who he was, came to meet him with armed hands. In this encounter, Ulysses, through this lack of recognition, was put to death by his son Telegonus, following what had been predicted to him by the Oracle. But Telegonus, having learned who it was, by the command of Minerva <note>the Roman name for the goddess Athena</note>, returned to the island of Aeaea with Telemachus and Penelope. They carried with them the body of Ulysses, whom they buried there. And furthermore, by the admonishment of Minerva, Telegonus married Penelope, and Telemachus married Circe, from whom he had King Latinus, from whose name the Latin language took its appellation, and the Latin people also. From Penelope and Telegonus was born Italus, who gave the name of Italy to the whole country.*

**T**he oldest of all the Greeks who went to the siege of Troy, according to what Protesilaus <note>Protesilaus was the first Greek to die at Troy; in this context, he is the ghostly source of "true" history in Philostratus’s dialogue *Heroicus*</note> says, was Nestor, son of Neleus. He was highly experienced beforehand in many wars and encounters, for the youth of his time made war against him, and there were prize games established there for boxing and wrestling. But in the skillful ordering of battle, for both cavalry and infantry, he was excellent in this above all others. And for the administration of a Republic <note>In this period, "Republic" refers to the general "commonwealth" or "state," rather than specifically a non-monarchy</note>, as well as for everything that might occur there by the will of the High God, he conducted himself in such a way that he did not flatter the people to acquire their goodwill, but rather aimed only to make them more modest and more temperate. This he obtained easily by means of his sweet and ornate eloquence, so much so that his warnings and representations were neither harsh nor annoying; and everything that has been said of him by Homer, Protesilaus assures us is true. Likewise, what another has said regarding the oxen of Geryon <note>Geryon was a three-bodied giant; stealing his cattle was the tenth labor of Hercules</note>—that Neleus and his children took them from Hercules without the knowledge or consent of Nestor—is indeed so, and is not a made-up thing. # N E S T O R.

Hercules gave Messene <note>Messene was a territory in the Peloponnese. In mythology, Hercules conquered the region but spared Nestor when he killed his father and brothers</note> to Nestor, out of love for his integrity and justice, specifically because he had not wanted to make any attempt upon Hercules’s herds of horned cattle as his brothers had done. In this way, Hercules became captivated by his friendship, seeing him as such a noble man <note>The original term "preud'homme" implies a man of both high social standing and proven moral worth</note> and so handsome; he held him closer to his heart than Hylas or Abderus <note>Hylas and Abderus were youthful favorites of Hercules; Hylas was lost to water nymphs, and Abderus was killed by the man-eating mares of Diomedes</note>, who were but young pages, so indiscreet and ignorant that they could hardly speak a word correctly. In contrast, when Hercules became acquainted with him, Nestor had already reached young adulthood, such that he exercised virtue of both mind and body. For this reason, Hercules loved him singularly, and was loved by him in return. And as men were not yet accustomed to swearing by Hercules <note>original: "iurer par Hercule" — referring to the common classical oath "Mehercule," which the author attributes to Nestor's invention</note>, Nestor was the very first who instituted it, and taught those going to Troy to do so.

As for the age he might have had when he went to the siege of Troy, since he is placed here as the oldest of all the Greeks, and the most wise and eloquent, *Homer* in the first book of the *Iliad* says that he had then passed two ages of man. In the administration of a republic <note>Referring generally to the management of public affairs or the state</note>, he conducted himself in such a way that he never flattered the common people. **Homer** depicts **Nestor** everywhere as very prudent and highly eloquent: And **Plato**, imitating him in the *Phaedrus*, shows that the principal study of both him and **Odysseus** was devoted to speaking well. And in the *Hippias*, he notes that **Homer** intended to represent **Achilles** as the most valiant of all the Greeks found at the siege of **Troy**; **Nestor** as the most wise and prudent; and **Odysseus** as the most cautious and cunning. Furthermore, in the fourth book of the *Laws*, he writes that in truth **Nestor** surpassed all those of his time in eloquence and the knowledge of infinite things. 

As for what follows thereafter—that he did not flatter the people to acquire their goodwill, but otherwise his remonstrances <note>Formal advice or corrections given to those in power</note> were neither harsh nor bothersome—one can see this very naturally represented in **Homer**. ...will do all things that please him, however unjust and illicit they may be: so much so that they are the cause of many evils in a state, and sometimes its ruin, and indeed most often their own. And in this regard Plutarch, in the 18th Greek Question <note>Referring to Plutarch's *Quaestiones Graecae*, a collection of short essays on Greek history and customs</note>, notes that the Megarians, after having driven out their tyrant Theagenes, did not remain long in good order in their affairs. For suddenly, the orators and flatterers of the people encroached upon them, inviting them to a licentious and insolent liberty against the principal citizens. For the poor and needy, led by these "plagues of Republics," went about ransacking the houses of the wealthy, and finally passed a decree to be quit and absolved of their debts, along with other such infinite malversations <note>Corrupt practices or misuse of public authority</note>.

Neleus and his children stole the oxen of Geryon from Hercules. Neleus, the father of Nestor, was the son of Neptune and the Nymph Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus (he who wished to counterfeit the thunder of Jupiter, for which he was struck by lightning). Having been ousted from Thessaly by his twin brother Pelias, he retired to the region of Laconia, where he built the city of Pylos, as Homer states in the eleventh book of the *Odyssey*. He had twelve male children by his wife Chloris, eleven of whom were put to death by Hercules for having tried to forcibly take from him the oxen he had won from Geryon. Nestor was absent at the time, according to what he tells Tlepolemus in Ovid toward the end of the 12th book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> That father of yours once leveled the walls of Messenia, and destroyed the undeserving cities of Elis and Pylos, bringing fire and sword against my household gods. And to say nothing of the others he slew, we were twelve sons of Neleus, a notable youth; twelve fell to the strength of Hercules, save for me alone.
<note>original: "Ille tuus genitor Messenia Mænia quondam / Strauit, & immeritas urbes Elimque Pylúmque / Diruit, inque meos ferrum flammásque penates / Impulsit. vtque alios taceam quos ille peremit, / Bis sex Neleidæ fuimus, conspecta iuuentus, / Bis sex Herculeis ceciderunt, me minus vno, / Viribus." — Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XII, 542-548.</note>

Plutarch remarks in this regard that from a bad father such as Neleus there came a good child, Nestor, which is a rare thing; this is in his treatise on the delayed vengeance of God <note>Plutarch’s *De sera numinis vindicta*</note>, following Homer in the second book of the *Odyssey*.

The city had already been founded by a man named Pylus, son of Pleson, but he was dispossessed by Neleus, after whom it was also called the Neleian city according to Homer.

But Pausanias does not say that Neleus or his children had wanted to steal the cattle of Hercules; rather, that in the said city of Pylos, there was a cave where those of Nestor used to be stabled, which he had by succession from his father. *Hercules* gave *Messene* to *Nestor*. This was a very ancient city in the *Peloponnese*, which through a long succession of years had great wars against the *Lacedaemonians* <note>the Spartans</note>, by whom they were finally entirely ruined and destroyed, and reduced to a miserable servitude, as one can see at length in the 4th book of *Pausanias*: who, in the *Corinthiaca* regarding that which is here in question, says this. *Hercules*, having put to death *Hippocoon* with his children, restored the Kingdom of *Argos* to *Tyndareus*, on the condition of returning it under certain requirements when it should be requested, for he left it to him only in keeping, and as if in trust <term>as if in deposit [comme en depost]: a legal arrangement where property is held for another to be returned later.</term>. And likewise, having taken *Pylos*, he placed the Kingdom of *Messene* into the hands of *Nestor* as if in trust. The *Heraclidae* afterward—that is to say, the descendants of the said *Hercules*—drove *Tisamenus* out of *Messene* and *Argos*, and similarly the posterity of *Nestor* from *Messene*: namely *Alcmaeon* son of *Silla*, son of *Thrasymedes*, son of *Nestor*, and the children of *Paeon*, son of one of the children of *Antilochus*, son of *Nestor*.

Now this manner of swearing by Hercules, "by Hercules" <note>original Greek: *νὴ τὸν ἡρακλέα*</note>, in Latin *Herculè*, and *Hercle*: *Terence in "The Eunuch"*, "*By Hercules, this was done*" <note>original Latin: *Hercle hoc factum est*</note>: and *Cicero in "Pro Plancio"*: "*Truly, by Hercules, I shall speak*" <note>original Latin: *Verè me hercule dicam*</note>: *whether it was first introduced by Nestor or otherwise, it was very ancient and used in Paganism, at least among people of quality, where the oath was held in great respect and religious awe, considering it inviolable, as one can see in the eleventh book of the Laws in Plato*: "*Altogether it is a truly beautiful practice*" <note>original Greek: *πάντως μετὰ δὴ καλὸν ἐπιτήδευμα*</note>, etc. In any case, it was a very fine ordinance and institution not to use the name of the gods lightly, for fear of contaminating it by using it for various things, as most of our people commonly do, whereas the majesty of the gods should only be employed in a holy and venerable purity. *For which reason, for fear of committing perjury—in which one would do a great injury to God, who is then called as a witness and guarantor of the promise made, which is ratified by his name: for which reason Homer in the 3rd book of the Iliad shows perjurers to be severely punished in the underworld,*

<margin>James 5.</margin> —ly <note>The text continues the word "purely" or "simply" from the previous page's discussion on avoiding perjury.</note> by these words "yes" and "no," just as Clement of Alexandria explains very well in the 7th book of the *Stromata* <note>original: *Stromates*; a series of miscellaneous writings on Christian life and philosophy</note>, where he defines an oath as being nothing other than a resolute affirmation of what is, or what is not, with the divinity called upon there as a witness. *On this subject, Suidas, under the letter N, in the entry for <term>ναὶ μὰ τὸ</term> <note>original Greek: "Yes, by..."—a formula used to begin an oath</note>, "by my wrinkled skin," notes that the ancients were not in the habit of swearing rashly by God, but rather by the first thing that presented itself: as in Callimachus's "Hecale," "By this tree here, even though it be dead." And Menander calls to witness "this Apollo, and this gate." Homer also, in the first book of the "Iliad", has Achilles swear by his scepter;*

> But I will tell you, and I will swear a great oath upon it, 
> Yes, by this scepter, which shall never again put forth leaves or shoots, etc. <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ἔκ τοι ἐρέω, καὶ ἐπὶ μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμοῦμαι, Ναὶ μὰ τόδε σκῆπτρον, τὸ μὲν οὔ ποτε φύλλα καὶ ὄζους φύσει, &c.</note>

Others swore by the head of a poppy, etc. The Romans swore by "Jupiter the Stone" <note>original Latin: *Iuppiter Lapis*; an oath where a stone was cast to symbolize the rejection of the swearer if they lied</note>, as seen in Festus and Polybius in the 3rd book of his histories: but Livy <note>original: *Titeliue*</note> in the 21st book says they swore "by the Stone" simply: which was a greater thing than they realized. Aristotle in the "Constitution of the Athenians" <note>original: *Rep. des Atheniens*</note>: and Philochorus: also Demosthenes in his speech against Conon, "leading them to a stone and making them swear" <note>original Greek: Καὶ πρὸς λίθον ἄγοντες, καὶ ἐξορκῦντες</note>, leading them to a stone to adjure them by it. Socrates also used to swear by the Goose, and the Dog, and Zeno by a Caper-bush: a practice still observed today in Rome where they use this word *Cappari* <note>Caper</note> as a form of exclamation, just as we say "by my little fig," "onion head," "virtue of a little fish," "body of an ox" <note>The author lists French euphemisms—*ma figuette*, *vertu d'un petit poisson*, etc.—used to avoid taking the Lord's name in vain</note>: and other similar expressions that could go on to infinity.

Such did this brave Hero show himself in combat: whereas Sthenelus is only like a spectator of Diomedes' prowess, having even advised him at times to take flight, and to show him the way, he is the first to head for the high ground <note>This refers to an incident in the Iliad where Sthenelus suggests a retreat, highlighting a contrast between his pragmatism and Diomedes' relentless fury.</note>: but Protesilaus <note>Protesilaus was the first Greek to die at Troy; here he likely refers to a dialogue in Philostratus's *Heroicus* where the ghost of Protesilaus defends Sthenelus's reputation.</note> is not of this opinion, but rather alleges that Sthenelus then performed no less a duty than Diomedes: and that the friendship between the two of them was in no way inferior to that of Achilles and Patroclus, having in the heat...

## ANNOTATION.

Diomedes, King of Aetolia, was the son of Tydeus and the beautiful Deiphile, daughter of Adrastus, King of Argos. Regarding this marriage, here is what Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Latin author of the 1st century AD, whose "Fabulae" is a primary source for Greek myths.</note> records in chapter 69: Adrastus, son of Talaus and Eurynome, received a revelation from the oracle of Apollo at Delphi to marry his daughters, Argia and Deiphile, to a boar and a lion. During this time, Polyneices, son of Oedipus, having been driven from Thebes by his brother Eteocles, arrived before him. Tydeus, also the son of Oeneus and Periboea, having likewise been driven away by his father for having put to death his brother Melanippus during a hunt, arrived there at nearly the same time. When the guards went to inform Adrastus that two young men in strange dress had arrived—one dressed in the skin of a boar and the other in the pelt of a lion—Adrastus, remembering the oracle, had them brought before him and asked them for what purpose they had come into his territories so equipped. Polyneices replied that it was in testimony that Hercules, who wore this lion skin, had taken his origin from Thebes; and Tydeus declared that he was the son of Oeneus and a native of Calydon, so that in remembrance of the Calydonian boar, he had clothed himself in its hide. Therefore, Adrastus, following his prediction, gave the elder of his daughters, Argia, to Polyneices, from whom came Thersander; and the younger, Deiphile, to Tydeus, who had by her Diomedes, the—

I do not wish to overlook the birds of Diomedes, which Juba <note>Juba II (c. 48 BC – AD 23), King of Mauretania and a renowned scholar who wrote on natural history.</note> named Cataractes <note>original: "Cataractes" — likely referring to a species of seabird like the Great Skua or a shearwater.</note>: alleging them to have teeth, and eyes that sparkle like fire, but otherwise their plumage is white. They usually have two leaders: one who goes in front and leads them, and the other remains behind at the tail like a sergeant of the band. If they wish to mute <note>original: "esmeuttir" — a falconry term for a bird voiding its droppings.</note>, it is always while flying in the air and against the wind. And not a day passes that they do not sprinkle his chapel with water they bring there in full throats, and they sweep and clean it with their wings wet with that same water. This is said to have given rise to the fable that his companions were transformed into these birds.

This was in exchange for his father, who in the other war had been the only one of all seven leaders to escape, due to the speed of his horse. The others, his companions, remained victorious and took Thebes, which they restored to Thersander, son of Polynices, who was later killed by Telephus in Mysia during the voyage to Troy. He was the son of **Poeas** <note>original: "Pæan"</note>, and went late to the Trojan War; he was, moreover, the most certain and skilled archer of all others, having been instructed and trained in this art, so it is said, by **Hercules**, son of **Alcmena**. # ANNOTATION.

Regarding **Philoctetes**, and his bow, and his arrows, together with everything that might concern this subject, enough has been spoken of previously in his portrait and elsewhere. A few details remain here to be deduced, and in the first place, regarding the **Hydra** <note>A venomous water-snake, not to be confused with the multi-headed Lernean Hydra.</note> by which it is said he was bitten in **Lemnos**, as **Homer** also does in the second book of the *Iliad*, from which this is taken:

> *But he lay on the island suffering grievous pains,* <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἐν νήσῳ κεῖτο κρατέρ’ ἄλγεα πάσχων"</note>
> *In sacred Lemnos, etc.* <note>original: "Λήμνῳ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ, &c."</note>
> *Philoctetes had remained behind*
> *Suffering from great pains, on the Island*
> *Of Lemnos, where the sons of the Greeks*
> *Had left him very ill*
> *From a bite of the serpent*
> *Which is called Hydrus, and is very venomous.*
> *He had therefore remained there*
> *Filled with a great sadness.*

This is a serpent that resides in the waters, from which it took its name in **Greek** <note>From "hydor," meaning water.</note>, and likewise the **Latins** call it *Natrix* <note>original: "Natrix"</note> from "swimming." **Pliny**, in book 29, chapter 4, says: "The most beautiful of all serpents is that which lives in the water, called for that reason the **Hydrus**, yielding in its venom to none of all the other vermin." This beauty consists in the varied speckles of different colors with which it is dappled all over; and from this comes the proverb <term>ποικιλώτερος ὕδρας</term> <note>original: "poikilōteros hydras," meaning "more varied than a water-snake."</note>, "more changeable than a Hydra," used for those who are so fickle that one cannot truly know them. **Aelian**, in book 9, records that in **Corfu** <note>The text uses "Corsou," an old name for the island of Corfu.</note> Hydras are born which turn back against those who pursue them, spraying them with such a foul and infected odor that they are forced to stop. And on this subject, Pliny, in book 27, chapter 12, speaks of a herb called *Natrix*, whose freshly pulled root smells of a very disagreeable stench and goat-like odor <note>original: "faguenas & boucquin," referring to the rank smell of an armpit or a male goat.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the legendary history of the Greek regions and notable figures. # PHILOCTETES.

As for the oracles of **Boeotia** <note>A region in central Greece, known for its powerful city-states like Thebes.</note> and **Phocis**, there was formerly that of **Tiresias** <note>The famous blind seer of Thebes who appears in many Greek tragedies.</note> in Boeotia, which was discussed regarding the painting of **Hercules** in the cradle. However, over the passage of time it ceased, and was rendered completely silent by an earthquake, as **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer (c. 46 – 120 AD) who wrote extensively on the decline of oracles.</note> records in his work *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. But he says in that same work that there was yet another Oracle in Boeotia, namely in the city of **Tegyra**, where it was held that **Apollo** (the god of predictions and Oracles) had been born; there are two streams that flow around it, one called the **Palm** and the other the **Olive** <note>In traditional myth, Apollo was born on the island of Delos under a palm tree; the inhabitants of Tegyra claimed this honor for their own city.</note>. It was at this place that Apollo, through the mouth of his minister **Echecrates**, announced to the **Greeks** that they would gain the upper hand over the **Persians** when they came to make war against them. And a little before this, he stated that in his time all the Oracles of Boeotia had failed, except for that of **Lebadeia** <note>The site of the famous underground oracle of Trophonius.</note>. Regarding those of Phocis, I find none anywhere except for the aforementioned **Pythian** oracle at **Delphi** on **Mount Parnassus**, in that same Phocis, according to **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC – 24 AD).</note> in his ninth book.

By this, he also intended to designate what would happen to **Cyrus**. He was the son of **Cambyses**, King of the **Persians**, and of **Mandane**, daughter of **Astyages**, King of the **Medes**, from whom he transferred the empire to his own nation, as **Justin** <note>A Latin historian who lived under the Roman Empire.</note> writes in his first book. And before him, **Xenophon** in his *Cyropaedia* <note>A semi-fictional biography of Cyrus the Great, written in the 4th century BC, portraying him as the ideal ruler.</note>, where he describes at great length all his deeds and exploits. Finally, being an ambitious Prince and insatiable for dominion, after having conquered **Asia** and reduced the entire **East** under his power, he wished to turn toward the **North** and initiated war against the **Scythians**. He initially obtained some fine and happy victories over them, but thereupon **Tomyris**, Queen of the **Massagetae** <note>An ancient Eastern Iranian nomadic tribal confederation.</note>—whose son he had killed—set a great ambush for him. She cut into pieces some two hundred thousand of his men, and he himself remained there as a forfeit. She had his head struck off and placed into a vessel full of human blood, saying: "Satiate yourself with blood, you wretch, for you were ever thirsty for it," as **Herodotus** and Justin record in the third book.

# AGAMEMNON, AND
## MENELAUS.

<image-desc>A large ornate woodcut initial letter 'A' decorated with complex floral patterns and classical motifs.</image-desc> Regarding **Agamemnon** and **Menelaus**, **Protesilaus** <note>A Greek hero who was the first to die at Troy; here he is cited as an authority on the appearances and characters of the Trojan War figures, likely following the tradition of Philostratus’s *Heroicus*.</note> alleged that they resembled each other neither in face nor in prowess. For the former [Agamemnon], in the matter of arms, was very valiant in his person, and in this regard inferior to none of the **Greeks**, however brave they might be. Furthermore, he was very well instructed and practiced in everything a **King** should possess, and highly experienced in what pertains to a **commander of an army**, having the grace to persuade others to his will above all others. Finally, he was ignorant of nothing that could be suitable and worthy of a general of the Greek forces. In this, he was greatly aided by his fine, grave, and haughty bearing, and the venerable majesty of his countenance. For he was of a magnificent and royal manner, and yet, despite all that, courteous and kind toward everyone, as if he had sacrificed to the **Graces** <note>The Graces, or Charites, were goddesses of charm and beauty; to "sacrifice to the Graces" means to possess a pleasing and diplomatic disposition.</note>. And as for **Menelaus**, one could well place him in terms of **valor** after several other Greeks, relying for the rest upon the prompt and good will of his bro- <note>The text breaks off mid-word; it is clearly intended to be "brother," referring to Agamemnon.</note>

By these means **Orestes** <note>The son of Agamemnon, famous for avenging his father's murder by killing his mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus.</note> acquired a great reputation in **Athens**, and throughout the rest of **Greece**, for having thus magnanimously avenged the death of his father. And while in **Argos** he was in great danger to his person—already wounded by stones and spears through the contempt of the **Argives**—**Orestes**, having rushed upon them with the aid of the **Phocians**, put some to flight and terrified the others, so that despite **Menelaus's** opposition, he recovered his paternal kingdom.

Regarding **Menelaus**, he wore long hair <note>The original French uses "perruque," which in this period referred to a full head of natural hair or a specific hairstyle rather than a modern synthetic wig.</note> in the fashion of young adolescents, because in **Sparta** it was customary to wear the hair very long; and for this, the **Greeks** would have excused him, since he maintained the customs of his homeland. Nor did they mock those who came from the **Island of Euboea**, even though they were ridiculously long-haired. **Protesilaus** says, moreover, that **Menelaus** spoke more fluently than all others, and in very brief terms, mixing a certain charm <note>original: "volupté"; here implying a pleasing or delightful quality to his speech.</note> with his reasoning.

## ANNOTATION.

**Agamemnon** and **Menelaus** were the children of **Atreus** (son of **Pelops** and the beautiful **Hippodamia**), and for this reason, they are commonly surnamed the **Atrides** <note>Meaning "sons of Atreus."</note>. The former was King of **Argos** and **Mycenae**; having married **Clytemnestra**, daughter of **Tyndareus** and **Leda**—and consequently the sister of **Helen**—he was, upon his return from the **Trojan War**, inhumanely murdered by her. During his absence, she had fallen in love with **Aegisthus**, the son of **Thyestes**, as was mentioned in the description of **Cassandra**, who had predicted this to him many times; however, he had refused to believe her. **Menelaus**, King of **Sparta** (or **Lacedaemon**), married **Helen**, the daughter of **Leda** and **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note>, who approached Leda disguised as a swan. When the time of her delivery arrived, she laid two eggs: from one hatched **Pollux** and **Helen**, and from the other, **Castor** and **Clytemnestra**. However, **Paris Alexander**, the son of King **Priam**, abducted Helen from him, which gave rise to the **Trojan War**.

**Agamemnon** was very valiant in his own person, etc. This point is expanded here from what **Helen** relates to **Priam** concerning **Agamemnon**: <term>both a good king and a mighty spearman</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀμφότερον, βασιλεύς τ' ἀγαθὸς, κρατερός τ' αἰχμητής" from the Iliad, Book 3.</note>; both a very fine King and brave in battle. And in the second book of the *Iliad*:
<term>Exulting because he stood out among all the heroes,</term> <note>original Greek: "Κυδιόων, ὅτι πᾶσι μετέπρεπεν ἡρώεσσιν"</note>
<term>Since he was the greatest, and led by far the most people.</term> <note>original Greek: "Οὕνεκ' ἄριστος ἔην, πολὺ δὲ πλείστους ἄγε λαούς."</note>

> ->Exulting in his excellence<-
> ->Above all other heroes,<-
> ->Because he was the best,<-
> ->And commanded the most people.<-

Nevertheless, as for such great valor, **Homer** does not always attribute it to him in the same manner, but rather speaks of it diversely. But in the eleventh book, he has him perform many fine and courageous feats of arms, after having very specifically described his equipment and armor, saying thus: In the first place

## ANNOTATION.

IDOMENEUS, son of *Deucalion*, grandson of *Minos*, and King of *Crete*—as *Homer* records in the 13th book of the *Iliad* and the 19th of the *Odyssey*—accompanied the Greeks to the siege of *Troy* with eighty ships. In the 2nd book of the *Iliad*, it is written: "And Idomeneus, famous for his spear, led the Cretans." <note>original Greek: "Κρητῶν δ' Ιδομενεὺς δουρικλυτὸς ἡγεμόνευεν"</note> Idomeneus led the Candiots <note>An old name for the inhabitants of Crete, derived from its former capital, Candia.</note>, specifically those from Knossos, Gortyn, Lyctus, Miletus, Lycastus, Phaistos, Rhytion, and other cities numbering up to the hundred by which this island is inhabited. He was accompanied by *Meriones* and followed by eighty ships. Elsewhere, the poet depicts him performing many feats of prowess, comparing him in the 4th book to a wild boar in terms of his strength, and describes his close friendship with the aforementioned *Meriones*. *Dictys* of *Crete* <note>The supposed author of a journal of the Trojan War, providing an alternative account to Homer.</note> also notes this in his first book, though *Homer* makes *Meriones* even more valiant than *Idomeneus*. However, *Hyginus* (chapters 81, 21, 270) says that Idomeneus was exceptionally handsome and was one of the suitors of *Helen*. He returned safe and sound to his country with all his men after the fall of *Troy*, without losing a single one, as stated in the 3rd book of the *Odyssey*:

> "And Idomeneus brought back to Crete all his companions,
> Who escaped from the war, and the sea took none of them away."
> <note>original Greek: "Πάντας δ' Ιδομενεὺς κρήτην εἰσήγαγ' ἑταίρους, Οἱ φύγον ἐκ πολέμου, πόντος δέ οἱ οὔτιν' ἀπηύρα."</note>

For upon his return, having been caught in a severe storm, he vowed that if he escaped, he would sacrifice to the gods the first thing he encountered upon landing in his kingdom. This happened by chance to be his own son. Having sacrificed him according to his promise (or as others say, being on the verge of doing so), he was driven out by his subjects, so that he went to *Calabria* <note>A region in Southern Italy.</note>, where he built a city upon the *Salentine* promontory. Nevertheless, the same *Dictys* writes in his 6th book that ten years after his return—at the same time, he says, that *Ulysses* exterminated the Suitors <note>original: "Proques." The men competing to marry Penelope in the Odyssey.</note> who were pursuing his wife in marriage—Idomeneus died in *Crete*, leaving the kingdom by succession to his beloved companion *Meriones*, son of *Molus*. *Suidas* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> mentions this under the entry "to act like a Cretan." <note>original Greek: "κρητίζειν" (krētízein). This term often implied lying or cheating, reflecting an ancient stereotype that "all Cretans are liars."</note>

<meta>catchword: To act like a Cretan</meta>

...or Mentir <note>This may be an OCR error for a classical author's name, or a reference to a specific myth where Idomeneus was accused of dishonesty in arbitration.</note> states that the duty of distributing the booty taken at the siege of Troy having been given to Idomeneus, he reserved the best portion for himself, from which this manner of speaking later proceeded.

The Prince who possesses the Kingdom of Minos in Crete offers you a hundred cities. Crete, now called Candia, is surnamed *hekatompolis* <note>from the Greek for "hundred-citied"</note> in the 2nd book of the *Iliad*: *and others who inhabited Crete of a hundred cities* <note>original Greek: "ἄλλοι δ' οἳ κρήτην ἑκατόμπολιν ἀφενέμοντο"</note>. This is certainly a large number for its size, being some eighty leagues long and eighteen or twenty wide, unless one wished to include even the towns and villages; likewise, in the 19th book of the *Odyssey*, he [Homer] gives it only ninety, which is not a great reduction. The three principal cities today are Candia—from which the entire island has taken its modern name, formerly called Matium—and the second is Canee, formerly Cydon, which the Greeks used to call the "mother of cities," according to *Florus* (Book 3, chapter 7). From this city, the quinces <term>Mala Cydonia</term> <note>literally "Cydonian apples," the origin of the English word "quince"</note>, which were there in great abundance, were named. # IDOMENEUS.

...accompanied the Sons of Atreus to Troy with many ships. And as for me, my name is Aethon <note>In Book 19 of the *Odyssey*, Odysseus assumes the name "Aethon" while in disguise, claiming to be the younger brother of Idomeneus</note>, the younger brother of him who went before, and much less of a worthy man than he. The third city is Rethymno, which is not far removed from the ancient name *Rhythymna*, and from Homer’s *Rhytion*, where there is only a small cove or unsafe harbor. All the other settlements are Castles of little importance scattered here and there throughout the Island: such as Voulismeni, formerly Panormus; Sitia, which still keeps its ancient name of Cytea, looking toward Rhodes. Kissamos is on the side of the Aegean Sea toward the North; and Selino directly opposite to the South. There is furthermore a fine, large town called Sfakia, at the foot of the mountains once called *Leuci-montes*, the **White Mountains**, for the snow with which they are covered at all times.

But Mount Ida surpasses all others in size and height—in the common tongue *Psiloritis*—which is in the middle of the Island. At its foot can be seen an ancient quarry called the Labyrinth; and indeed there are infinite windings where one could easily become lost without a good guide. Nevertheless, this is not the one Daedalus built for the Minotaur, based on the design of that so-renowned one in Egypt (which was discussed in the description of the painting of Ariadne), of which he did not even copy a hundredth part, as *Pliny* records in Book 36, chapter 13. Near there are also seen the ruins of Knossos and Gortynna, which King Minos had built, of which Homer speaks in the aforementioned places of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*.

But because the country is so mountainous throughout, it cannot be as fertile as the epithet he [Homer] attributes to it, **fertile** <note>original Greek: πίειρα (*pieira*), meaning "fat" or "rich"</note>, meaning rich and abundant—unless perhaps this referred to the pastures and sustenance for sheep and goats, which they call *Striphoceli* <note>likely a local name for the Cretan ibex or "Kri-kri"</note>, and above all for the excellent Malmsey <term>Mal-voisies</term> <note>Malvasia, a sweet wine famous across Europe during the Renaissance</note> which are produced there along the hillsides, which Homer calls Pramnian wine. Furthermore, he describes the Candiots <note>the inhabitants of Candia, the Venetian name for Crete</note> as having been very good archers in all ages, as *Caesar* also does in the 2nd book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*: **Numidians and Cretan archers, and Balearic slingers** <note>original Latin: "Numidas, & Cretas Sagittarios, & funditores baleares"</note>. And *Livy* in his 4th Decade. They are still so today, even better than the Turks themselves. This island is possessed by the Venetians.

And as for me, my name is Aethon, the younger brother of him who was there before, and a much more honorable man than I am <note>The author is quoting the *Odyssey*, where Odysseus, in disguise, speaks to Penelope and uses the name "Aethon" while claiming to be the brother of Idomeneus</note>. The third city is Rethymno, which is not far from the ancient name Rhythumna, and from the Rytion mentioned by Homer, where there is only a small cove or insecure harbor. All other settlements are castles of little importance scattered here and there throughout the island: such as Voulismeni, formerly Panormus; and Sitia, which still keeps its ancient name of Cytea, looking toward Rhodes. Kissamos is on the side of the Aegean Sea toward the North; and Selino is directly opposite to the South. There is, furthermore, a fine large village called Sfakia, at the foot of the mountains once called *Leuci-montes*—the White Mountains—so named for the snow with which they are covered at all times.

But Mount Ida surpasses all others in size and height, known in the common tongue as Psiloritis, which stands in the middle of the island. At its foot can be seen an ancient quarry called the Labyrinth; in fact, there are infinite twists and turns where one could easily become lost without a good guide. Nevertheless, this is not the one built by Daedalus for the Minotaur, based on the famous model in Egypt, which was discussed regarding the painting of Ariadne; of that one, however, this quarry does not even replicate a hundredth part, as Pliny writes in Book 36, Chapter 13. 

Nearby are also seen the ruins of Knossos and Gortynna, which were built by King Minos, and mentioned by Homer in the previously cited passages of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*. But because the country is so mountainous throughout, it cannot be as fertile as the epithet Homer attributes to it, "rich and abundant" <note>original: "πίειρ'" (pieir); meaning fat, fertile, or fruitful</note>, unless perhaps he refers to the pastures and the rearing of sheep and goats, which they call *Striphoceli* <term>Striphoceli: likely a local term for the Cretan wild goat, now known as the kri-kri</term>. Above all, the island is known for the excellent Malmsey wines produced along the hillsides, which Homer calls "Pramnian wine." 

Furthermore, he describes the Cretans <note>original: "Candiots," from Candia, the Venetian name for Crete</note> as having been very good archers since ancient times, as Caesar also does in the second book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*: "Numidians, and Cretan archers, and Balearic slingers" <note>original: "Numidas, & Cretas Sagittarios, & funditores baleares"</note>. Livy also mentions them in his Fourth Decade <note>A "Decade" is a unit of ten books in Livy's massive history of Rome, *Ab Urbe Condita*</note>. To this day, they remain even better [archers] than the Turks themselves. This island is currently possessed by the Venetians.

## ANNOTATION.

Ajax the Locrian, son of Oileus <note>The original text uses "Ocleus," but modern scholars identify him as Oileus, King of Locris</note>, was so named for the city and region of Locris on Mount Parnassus, of which Pliny speaks thus in book 4, chapter 3: "The near neighbors of the Aetolians <note>original: "Etholiẽs"</note> are the Locrians, called the free Ozolians, and the capital city is Oeanthea <note>original: "Æanthe"</note>, with the port of Apollo Phaestius on the Gulf of Crissa <note>original: "Chryſſee"</note>. Further inland are the cities of Argon, Eupoleia, Phaestus, and Calamise; and further still the plain of Phocis, which are called the Cirrhean fields from the city of Cirrha; the port is called Caleon. Two leagues from there, moving further inland, is the city of Delphi, free and exempt from all taxes, at the foot of Mount Parnassus, very famous for its renowned oracle of Apollo, the Castalian spring, and the river Cephissus which flows past Delphi, having its sources near Islea, formerly a city. There is also that of Chrysa; and with the Bulians: Anticyra <note>original: "Antiore"</note>, Naulochus, Pyrrha, Amphissa (also free and exempt), Trichonium, Tritaea, Ambrysum, and Trimetis; the region of Aulon; and inside the gulf, a corner of Boeotia is washed there by the sea waves. Additionally, the cities of Gymne and Thebes, surnamed the Chorsic [cities] joining Helicon. The third city of Boeotia on this sea is that of Pagae, from which the neck of the Peloponnese extends." I have included all of this to show the extent of the lands possessed by Oileus <note>original: "Ocleus"</note>, father of this Ajax, following what was said at the beginning of this chapter: that he was born of a father who possessed very great power. Of these Ozolian Locrians, Pausanias speaks more particularly toward the end of the 10th book, noting that while Orestheus <note>The original French says "Oreste," but the reference to Pausanias describes Orestheus, son of Deucalion</note>, son of Deucalion, reigned in those parts, it happened that a pregnant bitch <note>original: "liſſe pleine"</note> brought forth a piece of wood instead of her puppies. This wood, having been buried in the earth by Orestheus at the beginning of Spring, produced a vine stock; and from its branches, called in Greek *ozoi* <note>original: "ὄζοι," meaning branches or shoots; also a pun on "ozein," meaning to smell, which is another mythical origin for the name Ozolian</note>, the people took their name.

Others claim that the Centaur *Nessus*, who occupied himself with ferrying people across the river *Euenus* <note>original: "Euene"</note>, was wounded there by *Hercules*, as one could see previously in his own entry; nevertheless, he did not die from it immediately, and so retreated to this region. But later, being ashamed of that name, they preferred to call themselves *Aetolians*. *Pausanias* <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> records all of this, and notes that the capital city was *Amphissa*, located some four leagues from *Delphi*.

But *Strabo* <note>An ancient Greek geographer</note> in book 9 divides the *Locrians* into two groups, according to the two different aspects of Mount *Parnassus*. Those who inhabit the western side as far as the Gulf of *Crissa* <note>original: "Crissee"</note> between the *Aetolians* and the *Phocians*, are called the *Ozolians* (as if one were to say "the stinking ones") because of the strong odor of the country. For a little below *Calydon* is the mound of *Zaphossus* <note>Usually identified as Mount Taphiassus</note>; it is believed that this was the tomb of *Nessus* and the other Centaurs, and that from the corruption of their carcasses a very strong and foul odor spread to the foot of the mountain, even to the point of thick drops trickling down. The other side of the mountain, exposed to the rising sun as far as the *Euboean* sea, is of two types: some are called *Epicnemidians*, from the city of *Cnemis*, and the others *Opuntiens* from the city of *Opus* <note>original: "Opunte"</note>.

In the year 1550, when I was in Rome, there was one at my lodging seven or eight feet long, and as thick as the lower part of a leg; its scales were like those of a medium-sized carp, mottled with gray and black, and so tame otherwise that it came to eat bread and fruit thrown to it under the table—and meat as well, if one had wished to give it some. For once, when quails had been put in a room to make them fight <note>original: "iouster"; to joust or contest</note>, as is the custom in those parts toward the end of April, having entered there, in less than a quarter of an hour it swallowed four or five of them like pills. Leuca <note>Also known as Leuke or Snake Island in the Black Sea</note>, consecrated to Achilles, which may have a circuit of one small league or slightly less, is entirely surrounded by thick woods and full of beasts, both wild and domestic; there is also a small temple of the same Achilles with his image. Some time after having recovered his health, upon his return he recounted how he had seen Achilles there, and the two Ajaxes <note>Ajax the Great and Ajax the Lesser</note>, Patroclus likewise, and Antilochus; and that Helen was married there to Achilles, who had commanded him to inform Stesichorus, when he arrived at Himera, that the misfortune of having lost his sight had happened to him through the indignation of Helen. Having heard this from him, he <note>Stesichorus, the lyric poet</note> retracted what he had written about her, and sang a palinode <term>palinode: a poem in which the author retracts or recants a sentiment expressed in a former poem</term> in her praise, contrary to the blame he had given her in his verses. This is anciently somewhat besides the point, yet it fits very well with the subject of his *Heroics* <note>Referring to the "Heroicus" by Philostratus, a work written as a dialogue about the spirits of Trojan heroes</note>, which is entirely sprinkled with similar accounts.

# CHIRON.

<margin>Pindar, *Pythian Ode 3*.</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter 'I' featuring floral and leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>
He made his home on Mount Pelion, born in the likeness of a man, very wise in other respects and most prudent in words and deeds; devoted to various kinds of hunting, and one who instructed youth very well in all that pertained to the practice of arms and the conduct of war. He taught by the same means medicine and surgery, as well as music, both of the voice and of instruments, and made those who departed from his school into very good men, just and equitable. He lived a long life; for it was he who educated Asclepius <note>The god of medicine</note>, and Peleus <note>Father of Achilles</note>, and Theseus. Hercules also would have often come to visit him, when he was not detained by his voyages and undertakings. All this is said by Protesilaus regarding Chiron, noting that he had shared in his company and conversation along with Palamedes, Achilles, and Ajax.

as he desired death several times because of the pain <note>Chiron was accidentally wounded by Hercules with an arrow dipped in the poisonous blood of the Hydra; being immortal, he could not die but suffered eternal agony until he traded his immortality with Prometheus</note>, Jupiter supposedly translated him to the heavens and made him one of the twelve signs of the Zodiac called Sagittarius or the Archer. Pausanias in the *Messenian Books* <note>Referring to *Description of Greece*, Book 4</note> writes that he went to wash his wound in the Aniger river, which from then on took its stench; for it is foul-smelling. And Pliny, Book 25, Chapter 5, states that he was cured by means of the herb called the Centaury. <note>original Latin: "Chiron cum Herculis exceptus hospitio pertractanti arma Sagitta excidisset in pedem, Centaurea curatus dicitur, quare aliqui eam Chironium vocant." Translated: When Chiron, while being hosted by Hercules, was handling his weapons and an arrow fell upon his foot, he is said to have been cured by Centaury; for this reason, some call it the Chironian herb.</note> Which in the preceding chapter he [Pliny] takes to be the fourth species of the <term>Panacea</term> <note>A legendary plant capable of curing all diseases; the name literally means "all-healing"</note>, which took its name from his discovery. He also discovered this kind of vine which was named after him, *Chironie*, and previously *Bryenie*, and *Gynocanthe*, and *Apronie*, Book 23, Chapter 1. There is furthermore a kind of thorn called *Pyxocanthes Chironia* after his design, Book 12, Chapter 7, and Book 33, Chapter 14.

# PALAMEDES. 5

...immediately to Aulis <note>A port in Boeotia where the Greek fleet assembled before sailing for Troy</note>, knowing well enough that he had been enrolled among the first by the Greeks by reason of his eloquence, for which he and Palamedes entered into a rivalry against one another. 

Then <margin>E.</margin> afterward, when an eclipse of the sun occurred before Troy, the army became greatly discouraged and quite distraught, taking this as a bad omen. Palamedes went among them to explain that this failure of light <note>original: *desaillement*; referring to the "fainting" or obscuring of the sun</note> resulted from the fact that the moon, in its waning and conjunction, coming to oppose the sun from below, darkened it from our view; and by this same means, it drew forth many clouds that obscured the air. But, he said, if some future evil were signified by this, it should fall upon the Trojans, for it was they who had been the authors of the wrong; and we, he said, feeling the weight of their outrage, have come here to avenge ourselves. Therefore, we must offer our prayers to the sun at its rising, sacrificing a beautiful white colt, not yet broken. 

The Greeks approved of this, <margin>F.</margin> having been persuaded by Palamedes' reasoning. But Ulysses, taking the floor, said: "And what business have we with sacrifices or prayers, or any other such superstitions that Palamedes might allege? For all of this is but a sign and omen of what must infallibly come to pass. On the other hand, everything in the heavens, everything that depends..."

As for me, I have not studied medicine, but all things are understood through wisdom <note>original: *sapience*; here meaning a deep, philosophical understanding of the natural world</note>. 

Having said this, he had the butcheries in the Greek camp closed, and forbade that any more meat be sold in any way whatsoever, but rather that they content themselves with the common food of soldiers, reducing the army to small dishes of spreads, and fritters, salads, and other herbs both wild and domestic, and similar nourishment of light digestion. This was easy for him to obtain, for everyone obeyed him and held a marvelous faith in him; and everything that came from his mouth was taken as divine, and proceeding from some oracle. In fact, the plague he had predicted suddenly invaded the cities of the Hellespont <note>the narrow strait in northwestern Turkey, now known as the Dardanelles</note>, having taken its beginning, so it is said, from the Pontus <note>the region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note>.

And certainly not only to Achilles, but to all the others who revered both valor and wisdom, this Hero seemed worthy of being admired and celebrated by them in their songs.

Protesilaus <note>According to myth, Protesilaus was the first Greek to die at Troy; his spirit is often depicted as maintaining an interest in the war's events</note> himself, when we happened upon this topic, shed tears in abundance, praising him for his great courage, and among other things, because at the moment of death he never deigned to ask anything of Agamemnon, nor did he let anything unworthy or cowardly escape his mouth to move him to compassion and pity. He did not even weep, but rather uttered only these words: "Alas, how I pity you, O innocent truth, for you have perished before me!" And thereupon he freely offered his head to the strikes of the stones <note>Palamedes was executed by stoning after being framed for treason by Ulysses</note>, as if he foresaw the punishment that would befall them for it.

He led no forces or ships to Troy, but rather crossed there in a small passenger boat with his brother Oates <note>Usually identified as Oeax in Greek mythology</note>, not thinking that he should compare himself to anyone [simply] for having many arms and hands <note>Meaning he valued individual merit over the size of a military command</note>. As Achilles said to him one day: "You seem to many very coarse, O Palamedes, in that you have no one to take care of you." Another time, when the Greeks had given him his share of the booty in ready money from coins raised from tributes, admonishing him to enrich himself: "I shall do no such thing," he told them, "but rather I exhort you to poverty, rather than making yourselves thus subjects and slaves to obedience." 

Another time, when Ulysses had asked him, as he had just come from contemplating the sky and the stars: "And what do you see up there more than we do?" 

"Villains," he said.

...stone. There would be too many things to address in this place, which will come more appropriately one by one, each in its proper place, rather than piling them all here together in confusion. But it is a very strange thing that Homer was so partial and affectionate toward Ulysses <note>The Greek hero Odysseus, known for his cunning</note> that in no part of his poetry did he ever wish to mention Palamedes, nor anything concerning him. For even if he had been ill-disposed toward him for the love of Ulysses, at the very least he should not have kept silent about the great desolation and ruin that Nauplius <note>The father of Palamedes</note> maliciously brought upon the Greeks on their return, against the Capharean rocks <note>Dangerous cliffs on the coast of the island of Euboea</note>. This led Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note> in his eighth book to regard this as a fable; however, several good authors give it as truth.

<margin>Distinction of the day and of the night, nor of the year by the seasons.</margin>
Before Palamedes, it was not known what the distinction was between day and night, nor of the year by the seasons. Philostratus <note>A Roman-era author who wrote about the heroes of the Trojan War</note> attributes several beautiful inventions to Palamedes here; however, it should not be understood that he was the first author of them, but rather that he was the first who brought their use to the Greeks before Troy. As people entirely focused on war, they had neither eyes nor heart for anything else, caring only day-to-day for what concerns the course of human life. In the same way, the invention of fire in Egypt was attributed to Vulcan <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, god of fire</note>, who supposedly observed and received it from a lightning bolt that happened to fall into dry leaves and other such flammable materials where it ignited; wheat was attributed to Ceres <note>Goddess of agriculture</note> and her son Triptolemus; and wine to Bacchus <note>The god of wine</note>, and so on. The same could also be said of the Indies <note>A reference to the Americas, common in Renaissance writing</note>, regarding all that these poor Barbarians—differing little from brute beasts—have received in civility and refinement from the Western peoples who first discovered them and showed and taught them that which they were ignorant of, such that they [the Westerners] would be considered the first inventors in their eyes. <note>This comparison reflects the 16th-century European view of the "New World" as a place of primitive people being "civilized" by explorers.</note> But to come to the distinction of the year by its seasons, and from there to the months, days, and hours, which are the parts of time: the year, in the first place, is called by the Greeks *etos* <note>original: ετὸς</note> and *eniautos* <note>original: ενιαυλὸς - both terms refer to a year or a cycle of time</note>, as if returning into itself; for where one ends and finishes, the other immediately begins again, which is the course that the Sun passes through...

->ANNOTATION.<-

...the twelve signs of the Zodiac constituting as many lunations <note>Lunar months</note> or months, and a little more: divided, moreover, into four seasons which the Greeks call <term>seasons</term> <note>original: "ὥραι" (horai), referring to the personified seasons or divisions of time</note>, Winter, Spring, Summer, and Autumn. Of these, the Egyptians recognized only three: Spring, Summer, and Autumn, which they confounded with Winter, which produces nothing; they represented these by roses and other flowers, ears of wheat, and fruits and grapes. But to expand further on this point would lead to infinity. Additionally, we have treated this elsewhere following several other authors; and likewise concerning the hours, which are either equal (otherwise called equinoctial) or unequal (or planetary, as they are called, because their dominion is attributed to the seven planets, which rule them in rotation). The equal hours are the twenty-four of the natural day, which consists of the daylight (which is called the artificial day) and the night; for in this space, the first movable heaven <note>The *primum mobile*, the outermost sphere in geocentric astronomy that moves all others</note> completes its revolution each day and carries all the other underlying spheres with it, from the East through the South to the West, and from there through the North to the East. The unequal or planetary hours are always twelve for the artificial day and as many for the night. And since the day and the night continually increase or decrease in the oblique sphere <note>The celestial sphere as seen from any latitude other than the equator or poles</note>—for in the right sphere <note>The celestial sphere as seen from the equator</note> under the equinoctial they are always equal, as are the hours—it follows that these unequal hours must also vary according to the proximity or distance of each climate from the said equinoctial circle. Thus, in Paris, which is at about 48 degrees of elevation of the arctic pole <note>48° North latitude</note>, the days being almost half as long again in Summer as in Winter, the hours of the day must also be twice as long as those of the night, and in winter quite the reverse. But to come to the clocks <note>Devices for telling time, specifically sundials and early mechanical timers</note> in question here, which distinguish and mark the hours, these consist of two types: one by quadrants <note>A type of sundial</note> using the rays of the Sun, where the hours are marked by the shadow; for it is the Sun, as has been said, which by its daily course traces and designates the natural day of 24 hours. ...the Egyptians would have called him *Horus*, from whom the hours took their name, which also extend to the four seasons of the year, as in *Horace* speaking of *Jupiter*: *And he tempers the world with varying seasons.* <note>original Latin: "Variisque mundum Temperat horis"</note> The hours, therefore, are known by the quadrants of the day by the rays of the Sun, and at night by certain stars. *Pliny, Book 18, Chapter 14,* speaking of lupines, and *Apuleius* in his rustic writings, state that they serve as a clock for the peasants because they turn daily with the Sun, so much so that even when the sky is cloudy and covered, they know approximately what hour it is; the same is done by the <term>heliotrope</term> <note>A plant that turns toward the sun; likely the common marigold or "soulcie" mentioned in the text</note> or marigold. ...which was reformed ten or twelve years later by the Censor Quintus Marcius Philippus. Until then, they had been guided in Rome by *solar clocks* <note>sundials</note>; *and eight years later, Scipio Nasica introduced one made of water, which marked the hours of the day and night by means of a stick planted upright like a mast in a small floating vessel in a basin filled with water; as the water drained out from below, the vessel lowered, and the mast along with it, upon which the hours were marked. As for the Greeks, the certainty is not so great; but I remember having read somewhere, I know not exactly where, that the first use of* <term>clepsydrae</term> <note>From the Greek meaning 'water thief', these were ancient devices that measured time by the regulated flow of liquid</note> *or water clocks was practiced in the city of Acanthus in Egypt, where there were 360 priests—as many as there are days in the year, excluding the five days and six hours that they called the* <term>epacts</term> <note>Intercalary or "added" days used to harmonize the calendar with the solar year</note> *or the "added days," for such an occasion as Plutarch alleges in the treatise on Osiris in this manner:* That the Goddess Rhea, having secretly consorted with Saturn, the Sun became aware of it and cursed her so that she could never give birth in any year, nor any month; but Mercury, having fallen in love with her, found this expedient: playing at dice with the Moon, he won from her the seventieth part of her illuminations, from which he made five days, which he added to the 360 of the Egyptian year; and by this means Rhea had the opportunity to deliver her children during these days: namely, on the first day, *Osiris*, King of the world; on the second, *Haroeris* <note>Original: "Arneris"</note> who is Apollo; on the third, *Typhon*, but he did not come at the full term, rather he burst violently out from his mother’s side; on the fourth, *Isis*; and on the fifth, *Nephthys*, whom they otherwise name Venus or Victory. The priests, then, each had the charge on his day to bring water from the Nile into a large vessel, which, flowing out through a bung-hole, marked the hours. Clocks that move by counterweights, and portable <term>watches</term> <note>Original: "monstres portatives"</note> moved by springs, came a long time afterward, arriving little by little at the perfection where everything has finally ended up. But regarding the hours insofar as they signify the seasons of the year, they have been sufficiently treated in their own table; wherefore nothing remains here but to insert their *Hymn of Orpheus*, which would have been forgotten there.

### ANNOTATION.

To go back so far before the Great Flood, that which is read of Abraham in *Genesis* 13 is even more significant: that he was wealthy in gold and silver, which should be understood as <term>minted currency</term> <note>original: "monnoié"</note>. This is sufficiently confirmed by what follows in chapter 20, where *Abimelech, King of Gerar*, made him a gift of a thousand pieces of silver. Likewise, in chapters 42, 43, and 44, express mention is made of <term>money</term> <note>From the French "pecune," derived from the Latin "pecunia."</note> that the children of *Jacob* carried into *Egypt* to buy grain. It is well known that this occurred more than 500 years before the fall of Troy. *Herodotus*, for his part, states that the *Lydians* <note>An ancient Iron Age kingdom of western Asia Minor.</note> were the very first to coin pieces of gold and silver, though he does not specify the date. And *Strabo*, in the 8th book of his *Geography*, attributes this to one *Pheidon of Elis*, the tenth in descent from *Temenus*, along with the measures—and also the weights—which were named *Pheidonian* after him. *Pausanias* in his *Eliaca* <note>A description of the region of Elis in Greece.</note> places him around the *8th Olympiad*, which falls some 400 or so years after the ruin of Troy. In *Rome*, currency arrived much later, but that would henceforth be outside our current purpose. Regarding weights, measures, and numbers—which are the three primary bonds of human society, proper and particular to the rational creature—*Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> in the previously cited passage also attributes their first invention to *Cain*. However, *Eutropius* at the beginning of his history refers this to a certain *Sidonius*, in the time when *Procas* <note>A legendary king of Alba Longa in Roman mythology.</note> reigned in *Alba*, some 370 years after the destruction of Troy. Holy Scripture, which is far more certain, shows us quite clearly that weights, measures, and numbers must have been much older; as in the 43rd chapter of *Genesis* regarding the children of *Jacob*:
> We opened our sacks, and found our money in the mouth of them, which we have now brought back at the same weight.

And in the 19th chapter of *Leviticus*:
> You shall do no injustice in judgment, in rule, in weight, or in measure; you shall have just balances, just weights, a just bushel, etc.

*Pliny*, in book 7, chapter 56, agreeing with *Strabo*, attributes it to the aforementioned *Pheidon*:
> Pheidon of Argos invented weights and measures; or Palamedes, as Gellius preferred <note>original: "mensuras & pondera inuenit Phidon Argiuus: aut Palamedes, vt maluit Gellius:"</note>

But this is not that *Aulus Gellius* whose *Attic Nights* we possess, for he lived long after *Pliny*. Others attribute it to the second *Mercury* in *Crete*, son of *Jupiter*. The same

Regarding numbers, *Livy* <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian.</note> attributes their invention to *Minerva* at the beginning of his 7th book. However, the method of counting has varied among different peoples: for the *Hebrews*, *Greeks*, and *Romans* proceeded by using the characters of their own writing systems. Nevertheless, the most exact and easiest of all is that of <term>algorism</term> <note>The system of Arabic numerals and decimal calculation.</note>, as it is called, using the marks and rules of the <term>cipher</term> <note>The digit '0' and the decimal positions.</note>; an invention certainly more divine than human. Some believe it originally came from *China*, and others from the *Arabs*, who in truth contributed much to it.

<margin>C.</margin> Letters were not yet discovered. All of this was previously touched upon in the chapter on *Protesilaus*, under the letter *Y*, regarding the subject of *Tlepolemus*, brother of *Telephus*. He communicated by word of mouth through one of his messengers because letters had not yet been found. *Palamedes* <note>A Greek hero of the Trojan War famed for his cleverness.</note> devised them from the various positions and transpositions that cranes mark while flying; from which he also learned the arrangement of battles, the guards and sentinels, and the passwords, along with other such military observations that natural instinct has placed in these birds, which were thereafter called the "birds of Palamedes."

<margin>D.</margin> While the Greeks were staying at *Aulis*, *Palamedes* invented the checkerboard and the games of chess and tables <note>An early form of backgammon.</note>, as well as dice. I have thus expanded the meaning of the word <term>pessos</term> <note>original: "πεττὸς", an ancient Greek term for games played with counters or pebbles.</note> which is in the text, following the common opinion that it was Palamedes who discovered the games of chess and tables.
