# ANNOTATION.

The Lydian peoples of Asia <note>original: "diens peuples de l'Asie." The text refers to the Lydians, whom the historian Herodotus credits with inventing games to endure a famine.</note> were the first who found these games of dice and tables—if at least they were the same or nearly the same as those of today, which I would hardly believe. This was done not so much for recreation or for greed, but to ward off boredom and beguile the time during a cruel famine in which they found themselves. During this period, they took their nourishment only every other day; and the other day they spent as best they could playing the aforementioned games, to which they became so attentive and devoted that it made them somewhat forget eating and drinking. *Polydore Vergil*, <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar known for his history of "firsts" or inventions.</note> *a modern author, in the 2nd book of "On the Inventors of Things," chapter 13,* states—without, however, citing the original author—that in the year of the world 3685, which falls around the time of *Alexander the Great*, a wise man named *Xerxes* <note>In medieval and Renaissance lore, this "Xerxes" or "Philometor" was a philosopher credited with inventing chess to counsel a tyrant.</note> invented the game of chess to restrain the violence of a certain Tyrant, whom he does not name. He did this to make him understand, through the progress of that game, that a King has very little power and security in his person if he is not aided and maintained by the goodwill of his subjects, who watch over him and strive, each in their own place, to cover and protect him from the machinations and enterprises that his adversaries brew against him.

But the inventions of all these games are very doubtful and uncertain, having come about little by little, differently according to the times and the nations that practice them—some in one way, others in another. This can be seen regarding <term>trictrac</term> <note>A traditional French board game in the backgammon family.</note>, where for fifteen or twenty years so many things have been increased and added, such as <term>bredouilles</term> <note>A "skunk" or double-win in backgammon.</note> and various types of <term>jans</term> <note>Specific winning positions or "games" within a match of trictrac.</note>, as they are called, which were not previously in use, at least among us. We owe these to the *Italiens*, along with <term>tarot</term> and several other such inventions. As for the rest, the principal and most common board games are *trictrac*, *renette*, *lourche*, *all-tables*, and *sbaraglin*. This last is more common among the *Italiens* than among us; in it, for every point on the two dice thrown, one always adds an extra six. For example, if they throw <term>double sixes</term> <note>original: "seines."</note>, they count eighteen. They are so accustomed to using it this way that even when playing *trictrac* or *lourche*, they ordinarily count <term>eighteen</term> <note>original: "dicidotto."</note> for double sixes, even though they should only play twelve. On the back of the gameboard are checkers and chess.

<margin>E.</margin> As a solar eclipse occurred before Troy <note>A reference to a historical or mythological celestial event cited in classical literature to mark significant battles.</note>. It is a thing well enough known to those even moderately instructed in Mathematics <note>In the Renaissance, "Mathematics" encompassed astronomy and the study of the heavens.</note> that the cause of the eclipse or darkening of the Sun in our view—for the Sun itself is not actually obscured as the Moon is <note>The author distinguishes between the Moon's phases and a solar eclipse, where the Sun's light is merely blocked from our perspective.</note>—as Virgil well understood in this verse: *The various failings of the moon, and the sun’s labors* <note>original: "Defectus lunæ varios, solísque labores." The Moon is a dark and opaque body in itself, and when it comes to be directly opposed between the Sun and our sight, it creates an eclipse, just as one can see in a mirror placed at the bottom of a basin full of water when this eclipse happens. Therefore, this cannot occur except during the waning of the Moon at its conjunction with the Sun. For the eclipse that occurred during the Passion of the Savior, when the Moon was full, was against the order of nature <note>A common medieval and Renaissance theological point: because the Crucifixion occurred at Passover (a full moon), a solar eclipse was astronomically impossible, thus marking it as a divine miracle.</note>. But a lunar eclipse is quite the opposite, occurring when the Moon is full, and this by means of the shadow of the Earth which comes to be diametrically opposed between the Moon and the Sun. On this, see more fully beyond Aristotle in his *Meteorology*, Plutarch’s second book of the *Opinions of the Philosophers*, chapters 24 and 29, in the treatise *On Osiris*, and in that of *The Face which Appears in the Moon's Orb*. Indeed, it is in infinite books of Mathematics, for nothing is more common.

Naturalists and physicians attribute this <note>The observation that the plague strikes animals before humans</note> to the fact that horses, mules, and dogs, having their noses continually toward the ground, inhale the imprinted contagion sooner than people, who have their faces turned upward. And this matches what follows later in Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus, a Greek author of the Roman imperial period</note>, stating that while the land around Troy was infected with the plague, the sea air was healthier for the Greeks.

Let us pray to Apollo Lycian <term>Lycean: an epithet of Apollo, from the Greek "lykos" for wolf, or "lyke" for light</term> and the Phyxian <term>Phyxios: an epithet meaning "God of Flight," protector of those in exile</term> to exterminate these pernicious animals <note>Likely referring to the wolves mentioned on the previous page</note> with his arrows. Regarding this epithet of "Lycian," it was discussed previously in the section on Hyacinthus: to which one can add that these animals see clearly even in the darkest nights, more than any others. And it is known that the entire benefit of light, which is the cause of sight, depends on Apollo, who is none other than the Sun. Furthermore, the wolf is accustomed to hunting its prey a little before daybreak, as if it sensed <margin>•</margin> its arrival, which it knows very well according to Plutarch in the treatise on the word *EI* <note>A reference to Plutarch’s essay "On the E at Delphi"</note>: this matches the 49th chapter of Genesis: *Benjamin is a ravenous wolf who in the morning shall devour the prey, and at night shall divide the spoil.* <note>original: "Benjamin loup rauissant qui au matin prendra sa proye ; & au soir rendra sa despouille."</note> Thus, for the love of Apollo, the Athenians respected the wolf so much that whoever killed one was summoned to judgment and condemned to pay for the expenses of its funeral rites. Some attribute this to the fact that Leto <note>Latone</note>, being pregnant with Apollo and Diana, transformed herself into a wolf for twelve days, and thus arrived at Delos where she was able to give birth. From this comes the belief that all she-wolves, when bearing their young, one sooner, another more—

Later, a temple was built there to Apollo, surnamed "Phyxian" for this occasion, as the author of flight; though this quality is also attributed to Pan.

*Alon*, *Alope*, *Trachis*, *Phthia*, and *Greece of the beautiful women* <note>original French: "la Grece aux belles femmes," a translation of the Homeric epithet *Kalligynaika*</note>, were names for those called *Myrmidons*, *Greeks*, and *Achaeans*, who embarked in fifty ships under the leadership of *Achilles*. *Strabo* in book 8, citing this passage, interprets *Pelasgian Argos* as *Thessaly*. And a little further in the same book, he notes that the *Myrmidons* were not so named for having formerly been ants in the Isle of *Aegina*—which, having been entirely depopulated by a pestilence, saw these small creatures transformed into men at the request of *Aeacus*—but because, in the manner of ants digging the earth, they removed stones to make it fit for plowing; and they lived in caves they excavated to avoid the labor and expense of making bricks. In book 9, he says that all the subjects of *Achilles* and *Patroclus*, who followed *Peleus* when he fled from the Isle of *Aegina*, were called *Myrmidons*.

*Heralds had already been dispatched by sea to Lesbos.* *Plutarch*, in his treatise on the cessation of oracles, states that *Agamemnon* had nine *Heralds*, and even then he could hardly restrain the assembly of the *Greeks* or maintain silence among them because of their great number. This Dares <note>Dares Phrygius, the purported author of an eyewitness account of the Trojan War, favored by medieval readers over Homer</note>, not remembering having previously accused him of ambition and a desire to command the army—for which reason he had often caused trouble and turmoil, and had Agamemnon deposed from his position, which he did not re-enter upon his [Palamedes'] death. Dictys of Crete <note>Dictys Cretensis, another legendary chronicler whose account often contradicts Homer</note> describes in Book 2 how Diomedes and Ulysses, unable to bear that he excelled them in authority and reputation, and being full of envy and rivalry, pretended to want to share a great treasure with him. They claimed it had been revealed to them in a well at the edge of the camp, where they lowered him with a rope and crushed him inside with stones from the well-curb <note>original French: "pierres de l'anneau"</note>. It was said that Agamemnon was not ignorant of this plot because of the hatred he bore him, as all the Greeks desired that Palamedes command them rather than himself. And thus (says he) such a virtuous man ended his days unworthily—one whose good counsel and effort had never come to naught—through the malice of his enviers. He was burned with great solemnity, and his ashes placed in a gold vessel. 

But Hyginus in the 10th chapter speaks of it more clearly thus: Ulysses, having been discovered in his pretense <note>referring to Ulysses feigning madness to avoid the war, a ruse Palamedes exposed by placing the infant Telemachus in front of Ulysses' plow</note> by Palamedes, son of Nauplius, never ceased since then to plot how he might bring about his death. Finally, he decided to make Agamemnon believe that he had been warned in a dream to move his camp on a certain day which he designated to him. Agamemnon, giving credit to this, did as he said. And thereupon Ulysses went by night to hide a large sum of gold and silver in the place where the tent of Palamedes used to be. Then, having forged a letter in the name of Priam, he gave it to a Trojan he held captive as if to carry it to Palamedes; but he sent ahead one of his henchmen to wait for him on the road and put him to death. And the next day a soldier passing by, having found this letter in his breast, brought it to Agamemnon; it contained news of how Priam assured him he would send on the first day the same sum of money that Ulysses had buried, if on such a day he would betray the Greek army. Nauplius, King of Euboea or Negroponte <note>Negrepont was the medieval Venetian name for the Greek island of Evia</note>, one of the Argonauts and son of Neptune and Amymone, daughter of Danaus, King of the Argives, having heard of the injustice the Greeks had committed against his son Palamedes, went out of spite from one side of Greece to the other to suborn the wives of the absent men to the love of handsome young men, hoping thereby to stir up grievous quarrels in the future. And not content with this, after the fall of Troy as the army was returning by sea tossed by a storm, he maliciously went to light great fires by night at the top of Mount Caphareus <note>A treacherous promontory on Euboea</note>, where the surrounding coast is unapproachable because it is entirely strewn with rocks and sandbanks. The Greeks, interpreting these as signals that they should steer their course there to make landfall, went and crashed into them, and the greater part of them perished; for those who escaped the waves and reached the shore, he had them cut to pieces. Later, having heard how Diomedes and Ulysses—who had been the principal authors of the massacre of his late son—had escaped safe and sound, out of the spite he felt for it, he threw himself into the sea: Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Roman mythographer</note>, chapter 116.

**P**ROTESILAUS <note>A Greek hero who was the first to die at Troy; here, the author likely refers to the "Heroicus" by Philostratus, where Protesilaus' ghost describes the various heroes</note> describes him as a man very well-spoken and eloquent, yet otherwise serious and stern <note>original: "rhabarbatif," meaning forbidding or surly</note>, greatly praising the severity of manners; he was gloomy and pensive, always meditating on something within himself. He appeared more courageous <note>original: "genereux," here meaning noble or brave in spirit</note> in the heat of battle than he truly was in reality. He was little trained in the rules of battle, nor in the weaponry of soldiers, nor in the equipping and leadership of land and sea forces; he lacked the skill to besiege cities, nor could he strike well with a lance or shoot with a bow. He did, in truth, many things, but few worthy of admiration, except for one alone: namely, that wooden horse which Epeus built with the help of Minerva <note>the Roman name for Athena, goddess of wisdom and war</note>. Nevertheless, the invention came from Ulysses, who also proved to be the boldest and most resolute of all those who shut themselves inside it, as he was in all other kinds of plots and ambushes. ### ANNOTATION.

Philostratus reveals here more and more his secret animosity toward Homer, for all these *Heroics* <note>Referring to the book *Heroicus*, written as a dialogue about the true nature of the heroes of Troy</note> tend toward nothing but challenging him in whatever way possible, and establishing a true spirit of contradiction toward him. Since Homer chose Ulysses as his favorite subject for praise, this author debases, blames, and restricts him in every fashion—along with his Poet, all in one stroke—mostly for having dwelled on forging fictions that are merely delightful, whereas he ought to have mixed in some verisimilitude <note>likeliness to truth</note> without so impudently overstepping the bounds of all belief.
Ulysses, moreover, was the son of Laertes, Prince of Ithaca and Dulichium—two small islands in the Ionian Sea near Cephalonia and Zacynthus on the coast of Epirus—and of Anticlea, daughter of Autolycus. After she had been betrothed in marriage to the said Laertes, while she was being led to him, she was abducted on the road by a bandit named Sisyphus, the son of Aeolus, who impregnated her with Ulysses. By this means, he inherited the manners and temperament of his father. This is what Ajax reproaches him for in the 13th book of the *Metamorphoses*: *And sprung from Sisyphian blood.* <note>original: "Et sanguine cretus ---- Sisyphio." From Ovid’s account of the contest for Achilles' armor.</note>
Hyginus, in his 221st fable, notes that Autolycus would steal the cattle of Sisyphus from day to day, disguising them as he pleased according to the power granted to him by his father Mercury, the patron of thieves—who had sired him by Chione. Finally, Sisyphus took it into his head to mark his beasts under the sole of the foot, so that having once gone to the house of Autolycus to recover some of them, which he recognized by...

Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>, in the entry for <term>Sisyphus <note>original: σίσυφος</note></term>, says the same: but adds that it was Autolycus himself <note>Ulysses' maternal grandfather, known for his own thievery</note> who, to redeem himself for the theft of Sisyphus's cattle, prostituted her to him before marrying her to Laertes. Homer, moreover, in the sixth book of the *Iliad*, describes Sisyphus in a single phrase, calling him the most malicious of all mortals: <term>“There lived Sisyphus, who was the craftiest of men” <note>original: Ἕνθα δὲ Σίσυφος ἔσκεν, ὃ κέρδιστος γένετ' ἀνδρῶν</note></term>. Regarding this subtlety and malice, Plato, in the dialogue *Hippias*, cites these verses from the ninth book of the *Iliad*, which Achilles addresses to Ulysses:

> Son of Laertes, sprung from Zeus, resourceful Ulysses,
> For as hateful to me as the gates of Hades is that man
> Who hides one thing in his heart and speaks another.
<note>original: Διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν' ὀδυσσεῦ, / Εχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς ἀΐδαο πύλησιν, / Ὅς χ' ἕτερον μὲν κεύθει ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, ἄλλο δὲ βάζει.</note>

Through this, Homer intended to designate two sorts of men: one type who are straightforward, candid, and truthful, represented by Achilles; and the other type who are dissimulating, secretive, and liars, having one thing in their heart and another in their mouth, represented by Ulysses. For this reason, he calls him <term>polymēchanos <note>original: πολυμήχανος; meaning "of many devices" or "resourceful," but here interpreted as sly and crafty</note></term>, meaning sharp, wily, subtle, and malicious: as also that other quality of <term>polytropos <note>original: πολύτροπος; "of many turns"</note></term> which he gives him at the very beginning of the *Odyssey*. But Plato interprets this further in a negative sense, as a trickster, as is clearly denoted by what Circe says to him in the tenth book of the *Odyssey*: <term>“Surely you are Ulysses, the man of many turns” <note>original: ἦ σὺ γ' ὀδυσσεύς ἐσσι πολύτροπος</note></term>. Cicero likewise, in the second book of *The Nature of the Gods*, calls him <term>“shrewd and crafty” <note>original: Versutus & callidus</note></term>, one who knows how to feign and disguise himself as he wishes to deceive others. Awakening then quite joyfully, for he immediately recognized the word of the Goddess, especially as he continually had his mind set upon the artifices and inventions over which she presides <note>Minerva, or Athena, was the patron of craftsmen and strategic wit.</note>, as soon as bright Aurora <note>The Roman goddess of the dawn.</note> had driven the shadows back beneath the earth, he went to reveal his dream to the Greeks. The valleys and ravines <note>Original: "baricaues," referring to hollows or rocky clefts in the mountainside.</note> resounded loudly from the felling taking place, and the hillsides were stripped of their ancient coverings, so that one could easily scan with the eye right through the forest. The trunks, cut and laid low, waited only for the sweet breaths of the winds to dry out. 

These were carried to the shore of the Hellespont <note>The narrow strait, now known as the Dardanelles, where the Greek camp was located.</note>, with all the young men of the army sweating in this laborious duty, alongside mules and other pack animals; for everyone willingly lent a hand to the work to assist Epeus—some in one way, some in another. Some were occupied with sawing the planks as well as the beams and the rafters, and others with axes were cleaning them of branches, squaring and smoothing them; still others were employed in different kinds of labor. 

Therefore, Epeus, having his materials prepared, first set about building the feet of the horse along with the legs; then the belly, the spine, and the flanks; then the neck, adorned with long mane-hair; and finally the head at one end and the tail at the other, which moved just like that of a living animal—for he attached ears to it, and sparkling eyes. Thus, everything was finished on the third day, because the Goddess assisted the craftsman whom she had endowed with singular industry <note>In this context, "industrie" refers to technical skill and ingenuity.</note>. Because of this, the Greeks leaped for joy and marveled how in dead, unfeeling wood there could be such an appearance of movement; for it seemed that this horse was breaking into a gallop and neighing.

# ULYSSES

[...to extract] some truth from him, even going so far as to cut off his nose and ears; he endured this without confessing anything to them, except that the Greeks, following the advice of Calchas <note>The primary prophet or soothsayer of the Greek army during the Trojan War.</note>, had built this wooden horse to present it to Minerva and appease the wrath she felt toward them because of the Trojans. He claimed that at the instigation of Ulysses, they were on the point of sacrificing him to the deities of the sea to ensure a prosperous return home. As they were preparing what was necessary for this sacrifice, he said he had fled for safety under this horse, so that out of respect for the Goddess, they would not dare touch him. 

But Laocoon <note>A Trojan priest of Apollo or Poseidon who famously warned: "I fear the Greeks, even bringing gifts."</note> came to tell them that this was a spy planted by the Greeks, and that they must specifically uncover if anything was hidden within this machine before introducing it into the city. Minerva, being indignant at this, blinded him on the spot and sent two great serpents from a nearby hollow in the rocks. These serpents, entwining themselves around his two sons, strangled them. Consequently, the Trojans, believing this was vengeance for what they had attempted against Sinon, set their own hands to dragging the horse into the city, despite everything Laocoon could argue—that they should instead set it on fire.

# AJAX THE TELAMONIAN.

He was not called "the Great Ajax" by the Greeks because of the size of his body, nor because the other Ajax <note>Referring to Ajax the Lesser, son of Oileus.</note> was smaller than he, but for the greatness of his deeds; for which he was established by the Greeks as a model and pattern for fighting well and waging war. This was due to what his father Telamon had formerly done regarding Laomedon <note>A king of Troy who failed to reward Hercules for his services, leading to the first sack of the city.</note>, who had deceived Hercules, with whom Telamon went to Troy, which they sacked together. All of Greece rejoiced to see him even unarmed: for he was of a very handsome and tall stature, by which he surpassed all others in the Greek army, possessing a steady and pleasant gravity, neither boastful nor arrogant. But when he was armed, they all remained ravished in admiration to see him thus bravely march to combat against the Trojans, wielding his heavy <term>round shield</term> <note>original: *rondache*; a type of circular shield. met. <note>This completes the word "helmet" from the previous page.</note> In the melees and skirmishes, he proceeded very wisely and with "leaden feet" <note>A phrase meaning with great caution and deliberation.</note>, just as lions are accustomed to do, waiting for the right moment to charge, and he never directed himself except against the most valiant. He believed that whoever could strike them down deserved to have renown for it, so that it was not a dishonorable thing to be sometimes wounded while putting them to death. Nevertheless, he abstained from their spoils, claiming it to be the act of a brave man to kill his enemy, and that of a <term>brigand</term> <note>original: *brigand*; here meaning a lawless bandit or common thief.</note> to despoil and loot him. 

Now, whoever heard him speak would never thereafter have uttered anything insolent or insulting, even toward those with whom he had some pique or quarrel; and everyone rose before him to do him honor, not only the common soldiers, but even the most prominent men of the army. He shared a close friendship with Achilles, without bearing envy toward one another; for they would not have deigned to do so, nor would their nature have known how to permit it. Thus, all the troubles and indignations felt by Achilles, though they were not light, were nevertheless softened by him, partly by commiserating with him, and partly by rebuking him for afflicting himself in such a manner.

man here (Telamon) a son destined from his wife *Eriboea*, who may be
bold: and whom I shall hold as my guest and my
friend: and may his body be of an invulnerable disposition,
like this lion’s skin that wraps around me, which I put
to death in *Nemea* as the first of my masterpieces:
and may magnanimity of courage always keep him com-
pany. Having said this, the God sent him his great eagle,
chief of all birds; and it thrilled him within with a
sweet joy; saying, you have spoken like a Prophet, and
it shall be done for Telamon as he asks. From then on
the child was called Ajax, from <term>ἀετὸς (aetos)</term>, meaning eagle. <note>In Greek mythology, the appearance of an eagle was an omen from Zeus confirming Hercules' prayer; the name Aias (Ajax) was derived from aietos (eagle).</note>

The Athenians loved Ajax dearly, holding him as
their Captain. *Homer in the Catalogue in the 2nd book of the Iliad*,
states that the Athenians armed fifty ships to send
to Troy under the leadership of *Menestheus*, son of *Peteos* <note>The original text says "Peleus," likely a printer's error for Peteos, who was the father of Menestheus.</note>, son of *Or-*
*neus*, son of *Erechtheus*; who was its leader as Lord of *At-*
*tica*, according to *Pausanias in the Corinthiaca*. And in the *Attica*; that
*Theseus*, who had dispossessed *Menestheus*, having been held pris-
oner in *Thesprotia* with *Pirithous*, for having attempted
to kidnap the King's wife; the children of *Tyndareus* <note>The Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux.</note> came to
take the city of *Aphidnae*, and restored *Menestheus* to the Kingdom;
where he behaved so kindly toward the people that, when *Theseus*
returned, they no longer wished to receive him. But as
for *Ajax*, *Homer* assigns him only the superintendence and con-
duct of those from the island of *Salamis*, from which he brought twelve
ships, and camped with the *Athenians*.

Menestheus <note>A legendary King of Athens who led the Athenian forces during the Trojan War</note> delivered the funeral oration in the Athenian fashion. Plato, in the dialogue titled *Menexenus*, written specifically on this subject, shows how it was customary in Athens to publicly praise, during their funerals, those who had died honorably in war for the service of their Homeland. For this purpose, they would choose an eloquent and well-spoken man who could duly fulfill the task according to the merits and qualities of the deceased, which these orators <term>harangueurs: formal public speakers or speech-makers</term> intended to recount and thereby honor his memory.

In such a way, these funeral orations and praises were not only performed for each individual at their obsequies <term>obseques: funeral rites or burial ceremonies</term>, if they had at least deserved it; but every year a general anniversary was held for all those who had thus laudably ended their days in war. This is something we also practice, though more religiously, among ourselves in our funeral rites and in prayers for the departed. With these remonstrances driving their lamentations back into the depths of their souls, they came to take the body; and lifting it upon their shoulders, as large and heavy as it was, they carried it to the ships. There, washing away the blood and filth that had gathered upon it, they sent young men to nearby Mount Ida to cut a great deal of wood, from which they built a funeral pyre. <meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient funeral customs, specifically contrasting cremation and burial. # AJAX THE TELAMONIAN.

...gained the upper hand, and the *Palladium* <term>Palladium</term> <note>A sacred wooden statue of the goddess Pallas Athena, believed to protect the city of Troy; its theft by the Greeks was a turning point in the war.</note> remained in the keeping of *Diomedes*.

Moreover, the custom of burning dead bodies at their funerals was very ancient among the Greeks, as witnessed by the obsequies that *Achilles* performed for *Patroclus* in the 23rd book of the *Iliad*; and in the 7th book, the Trojans send to ask the Greeks for a truce to burn the dead bodies, which is granted to them. Nevertheless, they sometimes buried them whole, as can be seen with *Brasidas* <note>A famous Spartan general during the Peloponnesian War.</note> in *Thucydides*. And this way of burying them as we do today first came to them from *Cercops* <note>A legendary figure often associated with early Egyptian influence on Greece.</note> according to *Cicero* in the second book of *The Laws*, who was Egyptian; and from there it passed to *Draco* and *Solon* <note>The famous lawgivers of Athens.</note> as *Arnobius* writes, following *Antiochus*. For the Egyptians, who had some inkling of the future resurrection, were the most diligent of all others in exquisitely embalming their bodies to make them last several thousands of years—which can be seen by their mummies—expecting that the souls would one day come to reclaim these bodies and reanimate them once more.

The Jews also, under the same expectation, embalmed their own; but our religion does not take it from there: for he who was devoured by wild beasts, and those beasts then burned, and then their ashes thrown to the wind or into the sea, will be resurrected just the same as one who had only just died a moment ago, or who had been as preciously embalmed as was ever *Amasis*, King of Egypt, to whom *Cambyses* <note>The Persian Emperor who conquered Egypt.</note> could do no greater outrage after his death than to burn his body.

Regarding the Romans, there is some variety in this: for *Pliny* writes in the 54th chapter of the 7th book that it was not the ancient institution to burn dead bodies, but rather they were buried whole. But after it was seen in the civil wars that those who had been buried were being dug up, they began the practice of burning them; and *Sulla* was the first of the *Cornelian* family who commanded it at his death, for fear that the same would be done to him as he had done to *Marius* <note>Sulla had previously dug up the remains of his rival Marius and thrown them into the river Anio.</note>. Nevertheless, more than 260 years before his death, the son of the Consul *Manlius*—whom his father had decapitated for having fought beyond his command, even though he had been victorious over his enemy—was burned at his funeral, as *Livy* records in the 8th book: "The youth's body, covered with spoils..." <note>original: "Vt spoliis contectum iuuenis cor-" (from Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 8.7: "Ut spoliis contectum iuuenis corpus...").</note>

...[the body], with as much military honor as any funeral can be celebrated, should be cremated on a pyre built outside the rampart. <note>original: "...pus, quantum militaribus studiis funus vllum concelebrari potest, structo extra vallum rogo cremaretur." This Latin fragment likely refers to the burial of a hero or commander during a siege.</note> And *Plutarch*, in the life of *Numa*, writes that he expressly forbade at his death that his body be burned, which implies enough that the custom [of cremation] existed even then. Regarding the peoples of *Asia*, they were not accustomed to burning bodies either, as can be seen by this inscription from the tomb of King *Cyrus*;

> Passerby, do not pity me, I pray you----This little bit of earth which my body--
> Covers here, and do not disturb me----In my perpetual sleep.

Furthermore, this relates to what follows concerning fire: the *Persians*, who commanded all of *Asia*, revered fire as a great deity; therefore, they did not believe it was permissible for such a sacred and divine thing to feed upon such an infection as dead and stinking flesh, which is naturally subject to rot. The *Egyptians*, on the contrary, considered fire to be a ravishing and insatiable animal that devours everything that is born and grows, and after having well-fed and gorged itself, it extinguishes and dies along with its "pasture" <note>The author uses "pasture" metaphorically to mean the fuel or material consumed by the fire.</note>. But the *Greeks* were moved to burn bodies by certain considerations: first, believing that what is divine within us is of the nature of fire, according to the Poet in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*:

> Fiery is their vigor, and of celestial origin; <note>original: "Igneus est ollis vigor, & cælestis origo"; from Virgil's Aeneid.</note>

which is in continual movement, and always tending upwards. For this reason, they added a new fiery spirit to the body that had been abandoned by its own spirit, to serve as a guide and transporter to return to the heights more freely, since by the separation made by the fire, the more subtle and superior parts strip away the coarse and terrestrial. Thus, through this burning, they sought some form of restorative purgation <term>purgation</term> <note>A cleansing or purifying process, here referring to the ritualistic or physical separation of the soul from the decaying body.</note> here below, regarding the spirits submerged in the blood and other humors of the body—and consequently the soul, for which the spirits are like a tether and bond <term>retinacle</term> <note>From the Latin 'retinaculum', meaning a rope, cable, or stay used to hold something in place.</note> that joins and unites it with the body, which is the bond of the spirit. This continues until the Ethereal body <term>Ethereal body</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the soul was thought to possess a "vehicle" or "chariot" made of celestial ether, which it acquires as it descends through the planetary spheres to be born in a physical body.</note>—which, according to the Platonists, is the first vehicle and chariot of the soul during its infusion into the coarse and decaying body—is totally stripped away and reduced to its pure simplicity. To which end this...

# AJAX THE TELAMONIAN.

<page-num>71</page-num>

...which we previously cited from the 23rd book of the *Iliad*; where **Patroclus**, appearing in a dream to **Achilles**, tells him that he will no longer be troubled by the other souls down there in the underworld, who banish him from their company as a thing still holding onto bodily infection: and he will no longer return to the world above after he has been burned. For fire is *hagnistikos* <note>original: "άγνιστικός"; a Greek term meaning "purifying" or "purgative."</note>, which is to say, having a purifying virtue: and as **Raymond Lulle** <note>A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and mystic.</note> says of it: *Fire desires nothing but pure things.* <note>original: "Ignis non vult nisi res puras."</note> Therefore, **Plutarch** says in *Roman Questions*, number 96, that it did not seem reasonable (to come to the other point of this clause: That it was not permissible to burn the bodies of those who had killed themselves) to defile such a clean and holy thing as fire with a **Vestal Virgin** who had forfeited her life through misconduct. But the ancient Roman laws, which we still follow in many things, and especially in this matter, deprived those who had hastened their final days by their own hand of any burial at all, not just of cremation:

->HE WHO LAYS HANDS UPON HIMSELF,<-
->LET HIM BE UNBURIED:<-
<note>original: "QVI SIBI MANVM ADMOVERIT, INSEPVLTVS ESTO:"</note>

it not being permitted, as **Cicero** says after **Plato** in his *Phaedo*, to abandon this post where that great Captain <note>Referring to God or the Divine Creator.</note> has placed us as if on guard and sentinel duty, without his express command and permission. He reiterates this again in the *Axiochus* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato concerning death and the soul.</note>. For this reason, it is quite reasonable, according to what **Hegesippus** says, that those who would not wait for the ordinance and command of God their father, should also be deprived of the earth, as if from the lap of their dear mother. And **Aeschines**, in his oration *Against Ctesiphon*, alleges that the ancient custom of the **Greeks** was to cut off the hand of one who had killed himself, so that it might be buried separately from the rest of the body, as if it were some foreign thing that had deprived him of life. For otherwise, it would be the same as a prison break, which is a capital crime: seeing as the soul is as if imprisoned here below within the dungeon of this body until a certain time determined by the foreknowledge of the **Creator**, which it is not permitted to shorten or anticipate.

### A N N O T A T I O N.

Regarding the knightly deeds and prowess of Hector, everyone has been so steeped in them for all time that it would only uselessly bore the readers to wish to use repetition here. Homer sometimes exalts him to the heavens, and sometimes debases him by making him perform very cowardly and unworthy acts: for in the eleventh book of the *Iliade* <note>The Iliad</note> he says he was knocked to the ground, completely fainted from a javelin strike thrown at him by Diomedes, even though he had not wounded him. And in the 14th book, likewise by a stone strike from Ajax. And finally in the 22nd, he makes him flee shamefully before Achilles, who pursues him around Troy until circling it three times. He was so named, as Plato writes in the *Cratylus*, from the Greek phrase meaning "from holding the city" <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔχειν τὴν πόλιν"; *apo tou echein tēn polin*</note>. Because as long as he lived, he preserved the city of Troy in its entirety (but this <term>etymology</term> <note>The study of the origin of words; here, the author suggests the linguistic link between "Hector" and "holding" is a bit forced</note> is quite strained), which Homer also testifies to in the 12th book of the *Iliad*.

> As long as Hector remained alive, <note>original Greek: "Ὄφρα μὲν Ἕκτωρ ζωὸς ἔην, καὶ μήνι᾿ Ἀχιλλεύς, Καὶ πριάμοιο ἄνακτος ἀπόρθητος πόλις ἔπλε."</note>

Hector was killed not while fleeing, etc. Dares the Phrygian <note>A writer once believed to be an eyewitness to the Trojan War, though his account is now considered a later forgery from the 5th century AD</note> states that having wounded Achilles in the thigh, Hector was finally put to death by him, for Achilles aspired to nothing other than to massacre him. He writes that thereupon all the Trojans who had gone out with him were put to flight and driven back to the gates of the city, where Memnon <note>The King of Ethiopia and ally of Troy</note> encouraged them again and sustained the combat until night separated them. But Dictys of Crete <note>Another legendary historian whose account often provides a more "grounded" or cynical alternative to Homer's epic</note> writes in his third book that as Hector wished to rally the Trojans, whom the Greeks were driving back too shamefully before them, and had already killed several of the enemy, Achilles arrived. Hector did not dare wait for him, but began to flee, and Achilles pursued him. With a javelin he threw, Achilles killed the driver of Hector's chariot; but Helenus <note>A son of Priam and a gifted seer</note> pierced Achilles's hand through and through with an arrow, so that he was forced to withdraw. Some days later, Hector having put Patroclus to death, Achilles was so angered by it that from then on he sought only the occasion and the means to kill him. Having been informed that Hector, with a small handful of men, had gone to meet Queen Penthesilea <note>The Queen of the Amazons</note>—who with her Amazons was coming to the aid of the Trojans—Achilles went to set an ambush for him at a river crossing. There he put Hector to death while he was not on his guard; then he dragged him, and did to him what Homer has written of it.

# AENEAS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'I' featuring intricate floral and foliate vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc> He was somewhat inferior in combat compared to Hector, but in wisdom and ingenuity he surpassed all the Trojans, for which he was held in the same dignity and esteem as Hector. For he knew the counsels of the Gods, as well as what was promised to him by the fates after Troy would be taken; during the siege of which he was never struck by fear, having a very clear mind and a lucid and transparent <term>ratiocination</term> <note>The process of logical reasoning or thinking things through step-by-step.</note> to know what was to be feared or not. Thus, the Greeks called Hector the "hand" of the Trojans and Aeneas their "understanding" and "counsel." Aeneas, through his wisdom and wise conduct, would have given more trouble to the Greek army than all the efforts and fury of Hector. They were, moreover, of the same age and of a similar physical stature; but Aeneas’s appearance seemed less showy and vigorous, leaning more toward a steady and composed demeanor. And above all, he was not at all fussy about his hair, which he did not arrange with care, nor did he devote any study to it; rather, he sought only to adorn himself with virtue, which was his sole ornament. # AENEAS.

...neither fierce nor severe, except insofar as was necessary to intimidate those who broke their formation and abandoned the ranks where they had been placed.

### ANNOTATION.

Aeneas was held by the Trojans in the same dignity and respect as Hector. *Homer in the eleventh book of the Iliad;*
<note>original: "Αἰνείαν δ' ὃς τσί θεὸς ὣς τίετο δήμῳ."</note>
> "And Aeneas, who was honored like a god by the people."

->Aeneas was revered<-
->As the equal of a God by those of Troy.<-

He knew the counsels of the Gods, together with what was promised to him by the fates after Troy would be taken. *In the 20th book of the Iliad, Neptune prophesies thus of Aeneas:* that he was destined one day to have dominion over the Trojans, and his children's children who would descend from him, so that the lineage of Dardanus <note>The mythical founder of Troy and ancestor of the Trojan royal house.</note>—whom Jupiter loved above all those he had fathered by mortal women—would not be entirely extinguished; for Jupiter henceforth hated the house of Priam.
<note>original: "Νῦν δὲ δὴ Αἰνείαο βίη Τρώεσσιν ἀνάξει, / Καὶ παῖδες παίδων, τοί κεν μετόπισθε γένωνται."</note>
> "But now the might of Aeneas shall rule over the Trojans, and his children's children, who shall be born in the time to come."

These verses *Virgil*, in the 3rd book of the *Aeneid*, translated thus, adapting them to the monarchy of the Romans who descended from Aeneas.
<note>original: "Hic domus Æneæ cunctis dominabitur oris; / Et nati natorum, & qui nafcentur ab illis."</note>
> "Here the house of Aeneas shall rule over all shores; both his children's children, and those who shall be born from them."

The Greeks called Hector the "hand" of the Trojans, and Aeneas their "understanding" and "counsel." *This conforms somewhat to what is read in Plutarch and some others: that the Romans were accustomed to call Claudius Marcellus <note>The text reads "Marullus," but refers to Marcus Claudius Marcellus.</note>—the one who took the city of Syracuse <note>The text reads "Sarragosse" (Saragossa), but historically refers to the Siege of Syracuse in Sicily.</note> in Sicily and performed many noble feats of arms—their "sword" because of his valor and boldness; and they called Fabius Maximus their "shield" because of his wise <term>temporizings</term> <note>The strategy of delaying or avoiding direct battle to wear down an opponent, famously used by Fabius against Hannibal.</note>.*

# SARPEDON.

...[to the aid of] King Priam, where after having performed many feats of bravery and fine exploits of arms, as one can see in the 5th book of the *Iliad*—where he puts to death Tlepolemus, who was the brother of Telephus and son of Hercules—and in the 12th book several others, he is finally slain by Patroclus in the 16th book. There, their entire combat is described in great detail: how, having met in the fray and both having courageously stepped down from their chariots to fight on foot, Jupiter, who foresaw that his beloved son must end his days there, remained for a long time in suspense, wondering if he should let him die there or snatch him away and transport him alive to Lycia. But Juno came to remonstrate with him, saying that if he wished to act in such a way, there was no god so minor who would not wish to do the same for his own children, which would entirely subvert the oracles of destiny. Jupiter, moved by her words, gave free rein to fate, though only after shedding a few drops of bloody rain as a final lament for his son, who was going at that very moment to receive death at the hands of Patroclus. And there was a great contest and dispute over the body; the Greeks striving to possess it to desecrate it <note>The original French "villenner" implies treating the body with villainy or shameful dishonor.</note>, and the Lycians along with the Trojans striving to protect and rescue it; until, after having been stripped and mired in the filth <note>original: "tantouillé dedans la fange"</note>, Jupiter commanded Apollo to withdraw him from the press of the crowd and go wash him in a stream, then anoint him with ambrosia and send him to his own country to be honorably buried.

Glaucus was the son of Hippolochus, son of Bellerophon, and consequently the first cousin of Sarpedon, as is written in the 6th book of the *Iliad*, where their genealogy is recounted at great length by this same Glaucus to Diomedes—a passage we have cited elsewhere. But he is so simple-minded, at least according to Homer's account, that he exchanges his gold armor, valued at a hundred oxen, for that of Diomedes, which was only made of copper and was worth barely nine: an event that has passed into a proverb: "gold for bronze" <note>original Greek: "χρύσεα χαλκείων" (chrysea chalkeion)</note>. This is used when one wishes to denote any very unequal exchange where one receives worse things in place of better ones. Socrates uses it in regard to Alcibiades in Plato's *Phaedrus* <note>While the author cites the *Phaedrus*, this famous exchange regarding the "gold for bronze" value of Socrates's wisdom versus Alcibiades's beauty is actually found in Plato's *Symposium* (218e).</note>, remonstrating with him that he must not exchange his gold for copper; and in truth gold for cop- <note>original Greek: "καὶ τῷ ὄντι χρύσεα, χαλ-" (kai tō onti chrysea, chal-). The text breaks off mid-word, likely continuing "chalkeion" on the next page.</note>

### S A R P E D O N.

<meta>catchword: He prayed</meta>

"Do you intend to exchange for gold?" <note>original: χρυσῶν ἀμείβεσθαι νοεῖς;</note>, meaning to exchange the gifts of grace of the soul for those of the body. Plutarch, in his critique of the Stoics, explains this by saying that if one only looks at this exchange superficially and literally, Diomedes was the one more significantly benefited than Glaucus. This is because, being at war, armor of iron or steel—for so must we understand what Homer usually calls "bronze" or "brass" <note>The author is clarifying that although Homer uses the word "chalkos" (copper/bronze), in a military context, it represents the functional utility of harder metals like iron.</note>—was more useful and necessary than armor of gold, which is soft and heavy. 

But mystically, whoever prefers the strength, health, and disposition of the body over the virtues of the soul—and over what is proper and honest—that person truly changes his armor of gold for armor of bronze. And yet, Glaucus would not have been so simple and ill-advised in this instance as Homer says: 

"Then Zeus, son of Cronus, took away the wits of Glaucus," <note>original: Ἔνθ’ αὖτε Γλαύκῳ Κρονίδης Φρένας ἐξέλετο Ζεύς</note>

meaning that Jupiter had then deprived him of his understanding. Martial touches upon this in the 5th book of his *Epigrams*:

->I think not even you, Glaucus, were ever so stupid,<-
->To give golden things to him who had given bronze.<- 
<note>original: Tam stupidus num-quam nec tu puto Glauce fuisti, / Χρύσεα donanti, χάλκεα qui dederat.</note>

It is said that Glaucus was put to death by Ajax during the dispute that arose between the Greeks and the Trojans over the body of Achilles. Having been carried by the winds to Lycia, he was transformed there into a river that falls upon a shore without forming a harbor; both the river and the shore bear the same name, according to Strabo in his 14th book. This name, moreover, is shared by several people and things.

Pandarus is said to have been aided by **Lycian Apollo**, who taught him how to shoot the bow. This "Lycian Apollo" was discussed previously in the entry on the painting of Hyacinth, and in the chapter on Palamedes. As for Pandarus, Homer in the 4th book of the *Iliad* says he was the son of Lycaon and had brought a sizable troop of shield-bearers <term>rondelliers: soldiers armed with round shields</term> from that part of Lycia through which the river Aesepus flows, not far from the foot of Mount Ida. 

Minerva, in order to rekindle the combat between the Greeks and the Trojans, came to incite him under the likeness of Laodocus, son of Antenor, to let fly an arrow against Menelaus during the suspension of arms <note>A formal truce or ceasefire.</note> agreed upon for the duel between Menelaus and Paris. But regarding this Lycian Apollo, Pandarus makes to him a certain vow and prayer, which is the point Philostratus intends to address here.

The Aeacidae <term>Aeacidae: The descendants of Aeacus.</term> were celebrated for being descended from Jupiter. He refers here to Achilles and Ajax the Telamonian, for Aeacus was the son of Jupiter and Aegina, daughter of the river-god Asopus. As Hyginus writes in chapter 52, Jupiter, fearing that Juno might discover this adultery, transported Aegina to the island of Delos <note>The text says "Ennie," likely referring to Oenone, the old name for Aegina.</note> where he impregnated her, and she had Aeacus. When Juno learned of this, she sent a serpent into the fountain from which the people drank, infecting it such that all who tasted of it thereafter instantly ended their days. In light of this, Aeacus, seeing himself deprived of inhabitants, requested of Jupiter that it please him to convert a large mound of ants that appeared there before his eyes into as many living creatures. This he granted, for which they were called Myrmidons, because *myrmex* <note>original: μύρμηξ</note> signifies ants; and the island was given the name Aegina, as Pausanias recounts in his *Description of Corinth*. From Aeacus, furthermore, came Peleus, the father of Achilles, and Telamon, the father of Ajax.

...from Jupiter and Electra, the daughter of Atlas. *And what follows, where he finishes telling him how the whole affair passed. This is also touched upon by Dictys <note>Dictys Cretensis, the purported author of a diary of the Trojan War</note> in the 5th book. *Polydamas. There were two of this name; one was the son of Antenor and Theano (the sister of Hecuba), who, despite having married Lycaste, a bastard daughter of King Priam, nonetheless conspired to betray Troy along with his father and Aeneas. The other was the son of Panthus, and consequently the brother of Euphorbus; this is the one intended by Philostratus, and by Homer as well in several places of the Iliad. Homer depicts him as very wise, cautious, and prudent, offering sound counsel and always opposing the overly hasty and boiling impetuosity of Hector. For example, in the 13th book, he rebukes Hector for wanting to hazard a disorganized attempt to force the Greek ramparts:* "Hector, you are too hard to persuade by words of advice," <note>original: Ἕκτωρ ἀμήχανος ἐσσὶ παρηρήτοισι πιθέσθαι</note> *etc.*

> Hector, you are too unteachable,
> And do not wish to believe good advice.
> Since God has made you in arms
> So excellent, do you also wish
> To precede all others in counsel?
> But you cannot possess everything alone;
> For to some, he gives prowess,
> To others, the art of dancing well,
> Of singing, and playing the lyre;
> To others, he gives a good understanding,
> From which many men draw benefit.

*...having advised him in the preceding book to desist from this enterprise because of the omen that appeared: an Eagle carrying a Snake to its young was bitten by it, and by this means was forced to let it go. Polydamas argued that if Hector was totally resolved to proceed, he should at the very least have his men dismount to attack the ramparts more effectively. And in the 18th book, he gives them the sound advice to retreat back into the city during the night.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring ornate floral scrolls and architectural motifs.</image-desc>As for Euphorbus, son of Panthus, you may have heard tell of how there was one so named at Troy whom Menelaus <note>The King of Sparta and husband of Helen</note> put to death, particularly in the tales told of Pythagoras of Samos. Had he reached full manhood, he would have been in no way inferior to Hector in valor and boldness. But his beauty above all would have captivated the Greeks, for he resembled a statue of Apollo—than which nothing more pleasing could be seen—with a great mane of flowing hair, upon which no force or shears <note>original: "cizeaux"</note>...

### ANNOTATION.

Euphorbus, son of Panthus the Trojan, was put to death by Menelaus as he obstinately sought to strip the body of Patroclus, whom he had been the first to wound, according to what is recorded in the 16th and 17th books of the *Iliad*: and in the 15th of Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, where there is deduced at great length what Philostratus <note>Philostratus the Elder (c. 170–250 AD), the supposed author of the *Heroicus*, from which this dialogue is drawn</note> touches upon here concerning Metempsychosis <term>Metempsychosis: The philosophical concept of the transmigration of the soul, especially its reincarnation after death</term>, and Palingenesis <term>Palingenesis: A Greek term for rebirth or "being born again"</term>, transanimation, and regeneration of Pythagoras, upon which we must dwell a little:
> I myself—for I remember it—at the time of the Trojan war, was Euphorbus, son of Panthus, in whose breast once remained the heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus. <note>original: "Ipse ego, nam memini, Troiani tempore belli / Panthoides Euphorbus eram, cui pectore quondam / Hæsit in aduerso grauis hasta minoris Atridæ." This quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book 15) illustrates Pythagoras's claim that he was once a Trojan hero.</note>

Pythagoras, moreover, a Philosopher so renowned, was the son of Mnesarchus, an engraver of stones from the island of Samos, son of Euphron, son of Hippasus, according to Pausanias in his *Description of Greece* (Corinth); but Theodore after...

<header>->E V P H O R B E<-</header>

Aristoxenus, Aristarchus, and Theopompus show that he was Tyrrhenian <note>Tyrrhenian: An ancient name for the Etruscans of Italy</note>; a fact also confirmed by Plutarch in the eighth book of his *Table Talk*, questions 7 and 8, because the Tuscans observed—as he says—in practice that which the **Pythagorean Symbols** <term>Pythagorean Symbols: Brief, cryptic maxims (e.g., "do not poke a fire with a sword") used by Pythagoras to teach moral lessons through allegory</term> carry. In his youth, he was a student of Pherecydes of Syros, and after his death, a student of Hermodamas, who was then quite old. As he saw the tyranny of Polycrates beginning to rise in his homeland, being a contemporary of Anacreon according to Strabo in his 14th book, he sailed to Egypt to learn their theology and traditions. There, he studied under Oenuphis of Heliopolis, as Plutarch says in his treatise *On Isis and Osiris*. He was more esteemed by the Egyptians than any other of the sages of Greece; but he also so highly valued their doctrine and manner of philosophizing that he adapted his **Symbols** to their hieroglyphics. These symbols sound like one thing literally, but beneath that "bark" or outer shell, another meaning is understood, using small things to signify greater ones, just as he writes in the 72nd *Roman Question*. Furthermore, he took many things from their traditions, such as the practice of not eating fish, nor beans <note>Pythagoras was famously known for his prohibition against eating beans, though the exact reason remains a historical mystery</note>, which the Egyptians held in such abomination that they could not even bear to look at them.

From there, he traveled to Babylon, where he learned **Astrology**, both regarding the course of the stars and their movements, and their effects here below on the changes of the air, the cycles of the years, and **Genethliacs** <term>Genethliacs: The art of casting horoscopes or predicting a person's fate based on their birth</term> or the nativities of persons. Pliny, in book 24, chapter 2, states that he traveled even further, expressly for the study of **Magic**, as did Democritus. "Both," <note>original: "Ambo"</note> speaking of these two, "traveled through the Mages of Persia, Arabia, Ethiopia, and Egypt." And in book 30, chapter 1: "Certainly Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato sailed to learn this Magic, undertaking what were more like exiles than voyages. Upon their return, they preached it, yet they held it among their secret mysteries." <note>original: "Certè Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Plato, ad hanc Magiam diſcendam nauigauere : exiliis verius quàm nauigationibus ſuſceptis. Hanc reuerſi prædicauere : hanc in arcanis habuere."</note> Finally, when Pythagoras returned to his own country and saw the tyranny still persisting there, he went to settle in Magna Graecia <note>Magna Graecia: "Greater Greece," the name for the Greek-settled coastal areas of Southern Italy</note> in Italy, according to Plutarch in the first book of *The Opinions of the Philosophers*, chapter 3. He settled at Croton and Metapontum, where he established his school; he had no fewer than six hundred listeners, most of whom were learned and very famous men, such as Archytas of Tarentum, Alcmaeon and Philolaus of Croton, Hippasus of Metapontum, Lysis, and others—even—

### -> E V P H O R B E . <-

*Zaleucus* and *Charondas* <note>Two famous lawgivers of Magna Graecia (Southern Italy) who were traditionally said to be students of Pythagoras</note>; who commonly met together by night, because he taught several things that were entirely new and unheard of, such as, among others, his **Metempsychosis** <term>Metempsychosis: The philosophical concept of the transmigration of the soul, where a soul is reborn into a new body after death</term> and **Palingenesis** <term>Palingenesis: A term for rebirth or recreation; in this context, the cycle of the soul's return to Earth</term>. To persuade others of this, he claimed that he had first been *Ethalides*, the son of *Mercury*, from whom he had obtained the right to ask for whatever he most desired. He chose that, both during his life and after his death, he might remember everything that happened to him. Thus, he had a memory of how, after his death, he was reborn as **Euphorbus**, and from him as *Hermotimus*; then as a Delian fisherman named *Pyrrhus*; and finally as *Pythagoras*. This is the point *Ovid* intends to make in the passage cited previously:

> Souls are free from death, and having always left their prior 
> seat, they live and dwell, received into new homes.

...apart from his moral teachings—for that is not the question here—and likewise the claim that he was among the first of the Pagans to affirm the immortality of souls; for his teacher Pherecydes <note>A Greek thinker from Syros (c. 6th century BC) often credited with being the first to teach the immortality of the soul in prose</note> held this opinion before him. And long before Pherecydes, Homer taught this, as one can clearly see in several places in his poetry: *His soul flies out of the limbs, straight to the mansions of Pluto* <note>original Greek: Ψυχη δ' ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη, ᾄϊδος δὲ βεβήκει. There it is said that this is because unclean spirits greatly delight in the heat and the human form imprinted where one has slept during the night, striving with all their power to reach it and substitute themselves in place of the people—neither more nor less than how servants, in the absence of the master, take pleasure in sitting in his chair and imitating him. 

Thus, when one rises from bed, or during the rest of the night, one may have had several impure thoughts and apprehensions. The unclean and polluting spirit from which this proceeds—which the Kabbalists call Liliths <note>In Jewish folklore, Lilith is a female demon; here the author uses it as a general term for a class of "polluting" spirits</note>—finding the place still warm and still smelling of the spirits of the person to whom the bed belongs, introduces itself into that form and can cause many bad accidents to both the spirit and the body through a symbolic connection from one to the other. We see this through the experience of a certain charm and sorcery: that one can lame a horse by driving a nail into the print of the foot it has left in the earth while passing. In the same way, one can mitigate the pain of teeth by driving a pin that has touched them into a plank; and furthermore, heal a wound by tending to the iron <note>original: "ferre"; referring to the "weapon salve" or sympathetic magic, where a wound was treated by applying ointments to the weapon that caused it rather than the body</note>...

**Diogenes Laertius, in his *Life of Pythagoras***, citing **Aristotle** in his treatise *On Beans*, states that the motive for prohibiting them was either because they somewhat resemble the private parts, or the gates of hell; or because in the election of magistrates and in trials, votes were cast using beans. This is why **Plato** commands us that upon going to bed, our bodies should be disposed in such a way that nothing can bring us any fear or disturbance. Indeed, it is the general opinion that the use of beans was entirely forbidden to the Pythagoreans because they cause significant bloating; and it is well enough known that this food is quite contrary to those who seek rest and tranquility of spirit. 

However, **Aristoxenus** contradicts this (as **Aulus Gellius** continues in **Book 4, Chapter 11**, from which the above was taken). **Aristoxenus** was a disciple of **Aristotle**, and in the book he wrote concerning **Pythagoras**, he claims that Pythagoras never used any other legume more frequently than this one, because beans gradually soften the bowels and purge them gently. Now, the cause of this error would have been this verse by **Empedocles**, who embraced the Pythagorean doctrine:

-> Wretches, oh utter wretches, keep your hands away from beans! <-

-> Abstain from the bean: <-

# -> E V P H O R B E <-
<note>Euphorbus: A Trojan hero. Pythagoras claimed to be his reincarnation to prove the soul's immortality.</note>

...which word some have interpreted as beans; but it also signifies the genitals: <note>The author refers to the Greek word *kyamos* (bean), which was sometimes used as a euphemism for the testicles.</note> so that **Empedocles** would not have wished by this to warn humans to abstain from beans, but rather from lust. Furthermore, that **Pythagoras** and his followers abstained entirely from fish is quite commonly noted by several authors, and especially by **Plutarch** in the *Symposiacs* <note>original: "Symposiaques"; refers to Plutarch's *Table Talk*, a collection of dinner-table philosophical discussions.</note> Book 8, chapter 8, which is entirely about this: where he provides several reasons for it; and among others, one from a Spartan named **Tyndares**, who believed it was for the honor they gave to taciturnity and silence: for there is nothing more mute than fish. And they held this in singular regard, commanding it quite strictly for five consecutive years for all those who were initiated into their sect: without being permitted to say anything, nor even to inquire: rather, they had to remain quiet and attentive to listening. They called this silence *Echemythia* <note>original: "Echemytie"; from the Greek *echemytheia*, meaning "hushing of the voice" or "secrecy."</note> according to **Plutarch** in the treatise on curiosity, which usually carries with it much babbling; and **Aulus Gellius** <note>original: "Aulugelle"; a 2nd-century Roman author known for his miscellany *Attic Nights*.</note> book one, chapter 9, from which there will be no harm in bringing the entire passage here since it is so relevant. From the very beginning (as the philosopher **Taurus** recounts there), the curious young people who presented themselves to be taught were very exquisitely scrutinized from head to toe by **Pythagoras** in everything that could be perceived from the outside in their physiognomy—that is to say, the traits and features of the face, and the air of it; along with their gestures and bearing; and in short, their entire bodily disposition. Being judged fit and suitable to receive his doctrine, they were both admitted and received immediately: and then a silence was imposed on them in everything and everywhere—not to all equally, but to some more, to others less, according to their capacity and reach. This novice listened without saying a word to what the others discussed, it not being permissible for him, even if there were something he did not understand well enough to his liking, to inquire further: and moreover, there were none who kept this silence for less than two years: during which time of remaining silent, and doing nothing but listening...

...recite <note>The text continues from the previous page, finishing the word "recite."</note>, they were called **auditors** <note>original: "auditeurs"; students in the first stage of Pythagorean instruction who were only permitted to listen without speaking.</note>. Then, after they had learned to keep silent regarding the most arduous and difficult matters, and through this silence they already began to be instructed—which they called among themselves **taciturnity** <note>original: "ἐχεμυθία" (echemythia); a Greek term for a vow of secrecy or silence.</note>—then they could open their mouths, speak, discourse, and more openly instruct themselves in the things they had heard, recording them in writing, and even giving their own opinion. Being then called **Mathematicians**, that is to say, those devoted and attentive to the disciplines: namely those in which they had already begun to meditate and learn, such as Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and similar high sciences. Among the common people, it is customary to call "Mathematicians" those whom, in their own country, they should call **Chaldeans** <note>original: "Chaldees"; a term often used in the Renaissance to refer to astrologers or soothsayers.</note>. And thus, these disciples, advanced in the study and knowledge of such doctrines, consequently moved on to the notice of the works of the universe and the Principles of nature: and were then called **natural philosophers**.

*But to return to the fish, the same **Plutarch** continues that **Theon the Grammarian** <note>A 1st-century scholar and teacher of rhetoric.</note> believed **Pythagoras** had learned this from the sages of Egypt, who never ate them: because they have nothing in common with other animals: for the air that nourishes us, and even the plants themselves, are contrary, pernicious, and mortal to them. But there were those who challenged this opinion as irrelevant, because **Pythagoras**, having one day purchased from certain fishermen all the fish that were in their net, let them go into the water and returned them to liberty as if he had paid their ransom: which demonstrated well enough that it was rather due to a certain humanity within him—as it is said again in the treatise on **the utility one can receive from one’s enemies** <note>One of Plutarch's moral essays, "De capienda ex hostibus utilitate."</note>—not wanting to deprive any creature of the life that God and nature had given them to maintain his own; rather than for any abomination of fish; especially since they do us no offense or harm, as lions, wolves, bears, deer, wild boars, and other such creatures might. For even if they had the will to do so, they could not carry it out, living thus*...

...separated from us as they are, and almost in another world: so that, to always better exercise pity and mercy toward people, the Pythagoreans wanted one to become accustomed to using gentleness toward irrational animals. > We too are part of the world, since we are not only bodies but also winged souls, and we can enter into the dwellings of wild beasts, and be hidden in the bodies of cattle; bodies which might have held the souls of parents, or brothers, or those joined to us by some bond, or of men; surely let us allow them to be safe and honored. <note>original: "Nos quoque pars mundi, quoniam non corpora solum / Verumetiam volucres animę sumus, ínque ferinas / Possumus ire domos, pecudúmque in corpora condi; / Corpora quæ possunt animas habuisse parentum, / Aut fratrum, aut aliquo iunctorum foedere nobis, / Aut hominum ; certè tuta esse & honesta sinamus."</note>

# -> EUPHORBUS <-

...that man was my progenitor, or rather the one who engendered this body that you see me in now; which is what Pythagoras meant when he said he had formerly been **Euphorbus** <note>A Trojan hero in the *Iliad* who wounded Patroclus. Pythagoras famously claimed he could remember his past life as this warrior to prove his theory of reincarnation.</note>. From this, one can clearly see that these words do not denote a transmigration of souls from one body to another, but rather a **transmutation of matter**, which is capable of receiving all forms: as if a lion had long been nourished and raised on human flesh, one could say that these human bodies had become a lion; or a man fed on beef, that the beef had been transformed into a man. The same for a dog that had eaten a horse—that for this reason, the horse had become a dog: and so for the rest, which is more or less what **Ovid** wished to touch upon in the passage cited above:

> All things change, nothing perishes; the spirit wanders, and comes from there to here, and from here to there: and it occupies whatever limbs it pleases, and passes from wild beasts into human bodies, and ours into beasts, nor does it perish at any time. <note>original: "Omnia mutantur, nihil interit, errat, & illinc / Huc venit, hinc illuc : & quoslibet occupat artus / Spiritus, éque feris humana in corpora transit, / Inque feras noster, nec tempore deperit vllo." — Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book XV.</note>

**Caesar** touches upon nearly the same thing in the 6th book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* when speaking of the **Druids**, whose doctrine conformed in many things to that of Pythagoras. In the first place, they wish to persuade people of this: that souls do not perish, but that after the death of the body they pass from one to another. But **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero."</note>, in the place cited above from the 3rd book of *False Wisdom*, chapter 18, tries to show that what moved Pythagoras to put forward this **Metempsychosis** <term>Metempsychosis: The philosophical term for the soul's transition into a new body after death.</term> and **Palingenesis** <term>Palingenesis: Rebirth or "re-engendering"; the concept of being born again.</term> or re-engendering, was a vain glory; that being born of ignoble and unknown parents, he wished to trace his origin to an illustrious Trojan Prince: *Unless by chance we believe that foolish Old Man who lied about being Euphorbus in a prior life. He, I believe, because he was born of an ignoble line, adopted a family for himself from the poems of Homer.* <note>original: "Nisi fortè credimus inepto illi Seni qui se in priore vita Euphorbum fuisse mẽtitus est. Hic, credo, quod erat ignobili genere natus, familiam sibi ex Homeri carminibus adoptauit."</note> And in the 7th book of *Divine Reward*, chapter 23, he shows that the opinion of **Chrysippus** <note>A Stoic philosopher who believed in the periodic destruction and renewal of the universe.</note> in the treatise on providence, where he speaks of the renewal of the world, was much healthier than that of Pythagoras; *this being so, it is clear that nothing is impossible, and that we also, after dying, once certain periods of time have passed, shall be restored again to the state in which we are now.* <note>original: "τούτου δ’ οὕτως ἔχοντος, δῆλον ὡς οὐδὲν ἀδύνατον, καὶ ἡμᾶς μετὰ τὸ τελευτῆσαι, πάλιν περιόδων τινῶν εἰλημμένων χρόνου, εἰς ὃ νῦν ἐσμεν καταστήσεσθαι"</note>

As for the rest, he was not placed in safekeeping and entrusted to the island of Scyros, nor raised there among the young maidens as they say; for it would not have been plausible that **Peleus**, <note>Achilles' father and king of the Myrmidons.</note> who was the most valiant man of his time, would have wished to send this son of his into some hiding place to make him avoid wars and dangers. ## A N N O T A T I O N.

Of Achilles and his childhood, much has already been said in the section concerning his upbringing; so much so that nothing remains to be deduced in this chapter except for certain small details mentioned here, which we shall run through each in its own right.

<margin>B.</margin> Peleus sent Achilles to Scyros, etc. The common opinion is that he was raised among the daughters of King Lycomedes <note>A famous myth where Achilles was disguised as a girl to avoid the Trojan War</note>; Philostratus here contradicts this. In this regard, Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> says in his *Attics*: "This seems to me to have been well written, that Scyros was taken by Achilles, quite the opposite of those who say he was raised on that island among women." This is a version that Polygnotus <note>A famous ancient Greek painter</note> also followed in his paintings.

<margin>C.</margin> He would have brought armor such as no other human had ever donned the like. He does not mean the armor described by Homer in the 18th book of the *Iliad*—which Vulcan <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the smith-god</note> forged for him after the death of Patroclus—but rather the first set that he brought to Troy, in which Patroclus was killed while wearing it. Nevertheless, Philostratus disputes this a little later. Regardless, Homer in the 16th book describes it roughly thus:

### ACHILLES. A 372

The festival of Apollo **Thymbraeus** <note>original: "Thymbreen." Apollo was called 'Thymbraean' after his temple in Thymbra near Troy</note> approached, which was celebrated every year in his temple near the city. King Priam sent his herald, **Idaeus**, to tell Achilles that he was ready to hear the request Achilles had made, if he would come to this temple to discuss it more particularly. Having traveled there at the appointed time, **Ajax**, **Diomedes**, and **Ulysses**—who had already conceived some suspicion after seeing King Priam's messengers coming and going several times to Achilles—followed him from a distance to observe what he would do.

Having entered the temple, Achilles found **Paris** waiting for him there with his brother **Deiphobus**. The latter, under the pretext of greeting him warmly <note>original: "de le bien venger." This likely uses an older form of "bienveigner," meaning to welcome or receive someone</note>, embraced him tightly around the waist, so that Paris had the opportunity to murder him with dagger thrusts; this was possible because Achilles had come there unarmed, except for his sword. This done, they slipped out through the back door.

**Boccaccio** in his *Genealogy of the Gods* <note>original: "genealogie des Dieux." Referring to Giovanni Boccaccio's 14th-century work *Genealogia Deorum Gentilium*</note>—though he is not a reliable <note>original: "authentique"</note> author—writes that as Achilles knelt before the altar to say his prayer, Paris, who was hidden in wait, shot an arrow directly into the sole of his foot, from which he expired on the spot. For **Thetis**, his mother, immediately after he was born, had gone to plunge his entire body into the river **Styx** in the underworld; she thus rendered him invulnerable, except for the sole of the foot where she held him. 

Boccaccio borrowed this, among others, from **Fulgentius**, Bishop of Carthage, in the third book of his *Mythologies* <note>original: "Mythologique"</note>, in the chapter on **Peleus** and **Thetis**. There, he attributes this vulnerability to what **Anatomists** find: that from the heel proceed certain veins that reach the thighs, the groin, and the loins; and from there, other branches are born which extend even to the big toe <note>original: "poulce." In this context, the 'thumb' of the foot</note>. These are the parts where **Orpheus** established the principal seat of the **Venereal sting** <note>The "sting of Venus," or sexual desire. The author is linking Achilles' physical vulnerability in his heel to his "vulnerability" to love/lust</note>. 

But this matter was already touched upon in the discussion of the painting of Achilles on the island of **Scyros**. **Dares Phrygius** <note>A supposed eyewitness to the Trojan War, though the text attributed to him is a later Latin forgery</note>, having expanded on this more diffusely, says that after the death of **Hector**, Priam and **Hecuba**, accompanied by their daughter **Polyxena**, went to visit the tomb of Hector outside the city during a truce. Achilles wished to be there; at the first sight of Polyxena, he fell so deeply in love that the very next day he sent word to Hecuba, offering that if they would give her to him in marriage, he would return to Greece with his **Myrmidons** <note>The elite warriors commanded by Achilles</note>, and that very soon after there would be no more war.

Some, wishing to see an allegory in this, take Achilles' chariot to represent Man: Pedasus, who is mortal, represents the failing, perishable, and corruptible body; Balius represents the soul; and Xanthus represents that portion of divinity joined to it which the Greeks call *nous* <term>the mind or higher intellect</term>, the Latins *mens*, and the Hebrews *Nessamah* <term>Neshama; the "breath of life" or divine soul in Jewish mysticism</term>; we can only represent it by the word Intellect.
