**I.** Having known what had happened in Tymbria. This was a plain adjacent to Troy, through which a river of the same name flowed, emptying into the Scamander near the temple of Apollo, surnamed Thymbraeus, which had a sacred grove where Achilles was put to death in an ambush by Paris. From this comes the opinion <gloss>n</gloss> <note>The gloss completes the word "opinion" in the original French "opinio<gloss>n</gloss>".</note> that it was Apollo himself who did the deed, as Servius writes on the third book of the *Aeneid*: *Give us, O Thymbraean, a home of our own* <note>original: "Da propriam Tymbræe domum"</note>; and Lactantius the Grammarian on the first book of the *Thebaid* by Statius: *Whether as the Thymbraean thou holdest Troy.* <note>original: "Seu Troiam Tymbræus habes."</note> This name, moreover, comes from the herb "thymbra" <note>likely summer savory or a type of thyme</note>, which is very common in that place. Homer, in the fifth book of the *Iliad*, writes that Aeneas, having been wounded by Diomedes, was protected by Apollo, who transported him out of his hands to his temple in Pergamus—that is to say, in the plain of Troy—which must have been this very place, where he was tended to by Leto and Diana.

**K.** The Muses, after the death of Achilles, are said to have come to mourn him with their songs. All of this is taken from Homer in the 24th book of the *Odyssey*, where Agamemnon recounts to the soul of Achilles in the underworld everything related to this subject: *O happy son of Peleus, Achilles like unto the gods* <note>original: "ὄλβιε Πηλέος υἱέ, θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ"</note>, etc. "O blessed son of Peleus, and like—"

->### ACHILLES.<-

...godlike Achilles, you who died at Troy far from Argos, along with many of the most valiant Trojans and Greeks who fought around you while you lay dead in the dust, no longer caring for your arms <note>This refers to the "greatness" of the hero even in death, echoing the Homeric image of a fallen warrior "forgetting his horsemanship."</note>. We persisted in the fray throughout the entire day, and we would not have departed from it had Jupiter <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note> not constrained us to retreat with a great storm. 

After we had carried you to the ships, we washed your entire body with warm water, anointing you with various oils and perfumes; and we placed you on a beautiful bed of state where all the Greeks shed warm tears and cut their hair <note>Cutting one's hair was a traditional Greek sign of deep mourning.</note>. At that moment, your mother <note>Thetis, the sea-nymph.</note> arrived from the sea, accompanied by a great number of immortal sea nymphs, as soon as she received news of your piteous misfortune, for the report had suddenly spread across the sea. 

At her coming, all the Greeks were seized with a great fear, so much so that they would have fled for refuge to their ships if Nestor had not restrained them. He was a man old and wise, possessed of long experience, whose advice had always been found most excellent and wholesome; he spoke to them in this manner: "Stay, men of Greece, and do not seek to flee; it is the mother of the deceased who has come with the sea goddesses to visit him." 

Having said this, they cast off their fear. Around the body gathered the daughters of the Old Man of the Sea <note>The Nereids, daughters of Nereus.</note>, lamenting piteously and dressed in mourning garments—immortal ones—from head to foot. All the Muses also mourned him with their beautiful voices, one after the other, each in her turn, which moved the army to such compassion that there was not a single man who did not weep most bitterly. For seventeen whole days and nights without ceasing, we lamented you, both gods and men; and on the eighteenth day, we burned you solemnly upon the funeral pyre, having first sacrificed many sheep and oxen, all black, fat, and well-fed...

# A C H I L L E S.

...capable of summoning the spirits of Heroes and great personages. "O Achilles," I was about to say, "the common rumor everywhere is that you are dead, which I do not wish to believe, any more than would **Pythagoras**, whose sect I follow; therefore, so that we may believe only what is true and be able to speak of it with certainty, show yourself to me in your true likeness." Having made this request of him, his tomb began to crumble slightly, from which suddenly emerged a young man seven or eight feet tall, dressed in a long cavalry cloak <term>reittre</term> <note>A heavy, full-length cloak, here described in the style of Thessaly, Achilles's homeland.</note> in the Thessalian fashion. For the rest, his beauty and his appearance did not show him to be arrogant and boastful <term>oultrecuiddé</term>, as many claim he was; rather, they reflected a certain gracious kindness accompanied by a venerable majesty. And I can say that I do not think anyone until now has praised and recommended his beauty with enough dignity, even though **Homer** exerted himself as much as possible; for I hold it to surpass everything one could imagine in the mind, let alone write down. Having then seen him appear as such, it seemed to me that at that very instant he grew to double size, so that he might well have reached sixteen or eighteen feet in height, his beauty always increasing threefold. Then he said to me that he had never had his hair shorn, but had always kept it whole to make an offering of it to the river **Sperchius** <note>A river in central Greece; in the Iliad, Achilles’s father Peleus vowed his son’s hair to the river-god if he returned safely from Troy.</note>; for **Homer** writes that it was around this river that he spent his youth, when the first soft down <note>Original: "poil fol," referring to the first fuzz of a teenager's beard.</note> of his beard was only just beginning to fuzz his chin and cheeks. Calling me then by my name, he said to me: "I converse with you willingly, **Apollonius**, for I have long desired to meet such a personage. Many years have already passed since the **Thessalians** stopped the sacrifices and duties they were accustomed to rendering to me; and nevertheless, I have not yet wished to grow angry with them..."

<meta>This page continues the historical account of the cult of Achilles in Thessaly. While the previous page described specific ritual sacrifices performed at his tomb in Troy, this page explains how the public devotion to Achilles and the lineage of Aeacus fluctuated over time due to political shifts, natural disasters, and the eventual intervention of Alexander the Great.</meta>

# NEOPTOLEMUS.

The descendants of Aeacus <note>The Aeacids, the royal lineage of Aegina and Thessaly which included the heroes Peleus, Achilles, and Ajax.</note> ruled over Thessaly. However, the Thessalians themselves began to neglect them; for there were cities that were quite willing to send [tributes], others who did not consider it lawful to do so, and others who dragged the matter out; but in every way, this practice was overturned. 

Now, when the land was afflicted by an excessive drought and sterile, parching heat, the oracle admonished them to honor Achilles *as was fitting*. Consequently, they curtailed the duties they used to perform for him as if to a God, interpreting those words—*as was fitting*—to mean they only needed to perform the same duty rendered to other deceased mortals. Thus, they sacrificed to him only items of little importance, whatever came first to hand, until Xerxes <note>The Persian King whose invasion of Greece in 480 BCE forced the Greek city-states into a defensive alliance.</note> descended into Greece. For the Thessalians, finding themselves completely stripped of resources, abandoned what they used to do for Achilles after the ship from Aegina <margin>Plutarch in the *Life of Themistocles*.</margin> arrived at Salamis, bringing—along with the other allied Greeks—the gift of the Aeacids <note>According to Herodotus and Plutarch, the Greeks sent for the statues of the Aeacids to provide spiritual protection before the Battle of Salamis.</note>. 

Later, when Alexander, son of Philip <note>Alexander the Great, who claimed maternal descent from Achilles and famously sought to emulate the hero's life.</note>, had brought the rest of Thessaly under his rule, he reserved Phthia <margin>In the first treatise on the *Fortune of Alexander*.</margin> for Achilles. Upon going to wage war against King Darius, and once he had arrived at Troy, he took Achilles as his companion; thus, the Thessalians once again took up the care of Achilles’ honors, for whom Alexander staged combats between his men-at-arms...

## ANNOTATION.

**C**oncerning Neoptolemus, otherwise known as Pyrrhus <note>Neoptolemus was given the name Pyrrhus, meaning "red-haired," during his youth</note>, son of Achilles and Deidamia (daughter of King Lycomedes), enough has been said in the description of the Island of Scyros and in that of Pyrrhus and the Mysians. Thus, Philostratus <note>The third-century Greek author of the *Heroicus*, the source text being annotated here</note> only has him wait here in passing, in order to continue the previously started discourse on Achilles, of whom he recounts strange things that we shall touch upon point by point where they require clarification.

<margin>A.</margin>
Inasmuch as naturally beautiful men are surpassed by statues. This refers to what one reads of the painter Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE known for his realism</note> in the 35th book of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of *Natural History*</note>, chapter 9: that wishing to paint a panel for the Agrigentines to dedicate in the temple of Juno Lacinia, he chose five of the most beautiful girls of the region, from whom he took the most beautiful and perfect features of each to complete his image. This was because it is very difficult for a single person to be so exactly endowed with all perfections of the body that nothing could be found wanting. And in fact, there was never a man or woman—be it Alcibiades <note>An Athenian statesman renowned for his physical beauty</note> or Hippodamia—whom nature so perfectly accomplished in all beauties as is the statue of Adonis belonging to Master Francesco da Norcia <note>A noted 16th-century collector in Rome</note> in Rome, or the Venus that was made by Praxiteles in Cnidus <note>The Aphrodite of Knidos, one of the most famous sculptures of antiquity</note>.

<margin>B.</margin>
From Thessaly, they went every year to visit the tomb of Achilles. This was explained in the first book of the *Images* regarding the painting of the marshes, in this text here: *The Amaranths beat the water* <note>original: "Les Passevelours battent l'eau." Amaranths were flowers symbolic of immortality used in hero-cults</note>. Therefore, there is no need for repetition.

<margin>C.</margin>
As were Bura, Helice, and Atalanta. Bura was a city of Achaea on the Corinthian Gulf (Pliny, book 4, chapter 5): <note>original: "Primæ ibi quas diximus Lecheæ Corinthiorum portus: oppida Helice, Bura."</note> "First there are, as we have said, Lecheae, the ports of the Corinthians; and the towns of Helice and Bura." These three cities were formerly swallowed up by floods of the sea and earthquakes. The same author in book 2, chapter 94 says: <note>original: "Elicen & Buram sinus Corinthius abstulit, quarum in alto vestigia apparent."</note> "The Corinthian Gulf carried away Helice and Bura, whose remains are visible in the deep." ...[He]lice submerged by the sea waves. This he reiterates again in the 8th book, where he describes more specifically this submersion of Helice. Two years before the Battle of Leuctra <note>A decisive battle in 371 BCE where Thebes defeated Sparta, marking a shift in Greek power</note>, Helice was ruined; concerning this, Eratosthenes <note>A Greek polymath and head of the Library of Alexandria, known as the father of geography</note> writes of having seen the place where it once stood. Those living near the strait claimed that at the site, there was a tall bronze statue of Neptune holding a large charioteer’s whip to warn fishermen of the danger in that place. 

But Heraclides <note>Heraclides Ponticus, a philosopher and astronomer of the 4th century BCE</note> recounts that in his time, this ruin occurred at night; the city, located a short half-league from the sea, was overwhelmed by waves along with its surrounding area. Upon this, the Achaeans <note>A confederation of city-states in the northern Peloponnese</note> sent as many as two thousand men to recover the dead bodies, but they returned without having accomplished anything, so they divided the territory among the nearby neighbors. Furthermore, this calamity is said to have occurred because of the indignation of Neptune; for the Ionians, having fled from Helice, had sent their deputies to the inhabitants to recover his image. If they were unwilling to return it, the Ionians requested at the very least the utensils and jewels belonging to his sacrifices. They could not obtain these either. Therefore, they sent to request them from the Achaeans, who also deputized some men, but they achieved no more than the others. Consequently, the following winter, this desolation befell them. On this subject, Ovid writes in the 15th book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> If you seek Helice and Bura, Achaean cities,
> You will find them under the waters; and even now, sailors
> Are accustomed to point out the tilted towns with their walls submerged.
<note>original: "Si quæras Helicen & Buram, Achaidas vrbes, / Inuenies ſub aquis; & adhuc oſtendere nautæ / Inclinata ſolent cum mænibus oppida merſis."</note>

Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century CE</note> writes in his *Achaics* that this name Helice came from the daughter of Selinus, King of the Aegialians, whom Ion married; it was Ion who founded this city and gave it his wife's name. He adds that its ruin proceeded partly from the flooding of the sea and partly from an earthquake in winter. As for Atalante, Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, the 6th-century author of a major geographical dictionary</note> in his *Book of Cities* states that it was the city the Athenians founded near Locris, as well as an island still near Piraeus. Strabo <note>A Greek geographer of the Augustan era</note> also mentions this in his 9th book.

...river called the Thermodon. <note>original: "Thermodo"; a river in modern-day Turkey associated in mythology with the Amazons</note> *Today known as the Pormos.*

The Borysthenes <note>The ancient Greek name for the Dnieper River</note> is a river of Sarmatia separating Poland from Kyiv <note>original: "Chionie," likely referring to the Kyiv region</note>; commonly called the Dnieper; which, from the European side, flows into the Euxine Sea, just as the Thermodon does from the Asian side. It rises a little above the Duchy of Smolensk near a castle named Versura <note>A Latinized reference to the source of the Dnieper in the Valdai Hills</note>, which the Grand Dukes of Muscovy <note>Russia</note> have seized from the Kings of Poland: and from there, taking its course to the south, it reaches the city of Kyiv, the capital city of Russia: then toward the rising sun <note>eastward</note>, more than four hundred leagues from its sources, it empties into the Euxine Sea not far from Perekop <note>original: "Precop"</note>, where the Tauric Chersonese <note>The Crimean Peninsula</note> is located.

The Danube is the largest river in Europe, which takes its birth in the land of the Grisons <note>The Swiss canton of Graubünden</note>, a little above Chur <note>original: "Couere"</note>, not far from the sources of the Rhine and the Rhône. From there it goes to Vienna in Austria, and passes right through Hungary and several other underlying regions, until finally it reaches the Euxine Sea through six large mouths and entrances near the city of Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi <note>original: "Moncastre," a historic port in Ukraine</note>; as specified by Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> in Book 4, chapter 12. Strabo <note>Greek geographer and philosopher</note> in Book 7 lists seven: having received sixty large rivers into its channel. From its falls or cataracts below Buda <note>part of modern Budapest</note> where it is more navigable than upstream, it is called the Ister <note>The ancient name for the lower Danube</note>: and from there upwards, the Danube; commonly called the Donau <note>original: "Dunovve"</note>.

<margin>F.</margin> And as an infinite quantity of water comes to discharge into the Euxine Sea. Strabo in his first book, as we have already cited in the "Tableau of the Fishermen," <note>A reference to Philostratus's *Imagines*, a work describing a gallery of paintings</note> states that in his time, which was under Augustus Caesar, this sea was held as another Ocean, so much so that it was called "The Pontus" <note>original: "le Pont," from the Greek *Pontos*, meaning 'The Sea'</note> by a certain antonomasia <note>A rhetorical term where a common noun is used as a proper name</note>; to which relates the name it has today of the "Great Sea" <note>original: "mer-maiour"</note>: but it is the shallowest of all others, so that one can almost find bottom everywhere; and this because of so many large rivers that come to flow into it from all sides: forty of the most notable among others; such as the Danube, Tanais <note>The Don River</note>, Borysthenes <note>The Dnieper</note>, Hypanis <note>The Southern Bug</note>, the Phasis <note>The Rioni River in Georgia</note>, Thermodon, Halys <note>The Kızılırmak River</note>, etc., which fill it with silt: which results in the fish there being very fat, and its water being the least salty of all the other seas.

<margin>G.</margin>
The marshes of Maeotis <note>The ancient name for the Sea of Azov</note>. The river Tanais <note>The Don</note>, descending from Muscovy <note>Russia</note>, comes toward the Cimmerian Strait <note>The Strait of Kerch</note> to empty into the Maeotis, which from there expands into a kind of sea commonly called the *Mar delle Zabacche* <note>Sea of Zabache</note>, otherwise known as the White Sea—in contrast to the Euxine, called the Black Sea—where these marshes deliver their waters toward the Strait of Perekop <note>original: "Precop"</note>. Pliny describes it in Book 6, Chapter 7, where he says it was named *Temerinde* by the Scythians, which signifies "mother of the sea," because it seems the Euxine Sea takes its birth from it. And in Book 4, Chapter 12, he writes that it took this name "Maeotis" from the peoples called the Maeotians who dwell along its shores; Strabo, in Book 11, records its length as being some hundred leagues from the mouth of the Bosphorus to the Euxine.

<margin>H.</margin>
This was around the Olympiad in which Leonidas of Rhodes first won the stadium race. Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> mentions him in Book 6, without specifying the exact Olympiad. The most beautiful victory of all others in the race was obtained by Leonidas of Rhodes, through a marvelous speed of legs: for during four consecutive Olympiads, he was victorious twelve times in running.
<margin>X</margin>
Regarding what is said here—that he carried away the victory in the stadium race—this does not mean, however, that they only ran one hundred and twenty-five geometric paces (the length of a stadium, each pace being five Royal feet <note>A traditional French unit of length</note>); for the race was repeated several times, and thus the distance must have been greater. But as Pausanias notes in the place previously cited, the stadium was a course in the form of a high earthen causeway: where at one of the ends was erected the scaffold of the Hellanodikai <note>The "Judges of the Greeks" who presided over the Olympic Games</note>, the judges who presided over these prize games. Aulus Gellius, in the first book and first chapter of his *Attic Nights*, speaking of the means by which Pythagoras proceeded to find how much the stature of Hercules exceeded that of common men, writes that this Hero, having measured the Olympic stadium at two hundred of his own feet (I would suspect that one should read two hundred paces instead of feet), and as other stadiums or courses were much smaller, he came thereby to conjecture that Hercules must have surpassed other men in proportion to the size of his stadium.

This *Cocytus* was, according to *Suidas* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>, the coldest river of the underworld, just as the *Phlegethon* was the most ardent and fiery, so that there would be two extreme torments of cold and heat. Regarding these infernal rivers, *Virgil* touches upon this, among other things, in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*:

> From here is the path that leads to the waters of Tartarean Acheron; here a whirlpool, thick with mud and a vast abyss, seethes and belches all its sand into Cocytus. <note>original: "Hinc via tartarei quæ fert Acherontis ad vndas, Turbidus hic cœno vastáque voragine gurges Æstuat, atque omnem Cocyto eructat arenam."</note>

*Pausanias* in his *Description of Greece* (within the section on *Attica*) places all these infernal rivers and marshes in *Thesprotia*, a region of *Epirus* where the oracle of *Dodona* was located. Near *Cichyrus* (he says; it was a city otherwise called *Ephyre*) is the marsh called *Acherusia*, and the river *Acheron* which flows from it. The *Cocytus* also passes through there, carrying a most unpleasant water. The *Phlegethon* is another river of Hell, burning as was mentioned above, from the Greek <term>phlego <gloss>to burn or blaze</gloss></term> <note>original: Φλέγω</note>. And as for *Acheron*, which signifies *without joy*, there is one of this same name in *Calabria*, where *Alexander*, King of the *Molossians*, was put to death by the *Lucanians* (these are the people of *Basilicata*). He was deceived by the *Dodonian* oracle, which had warned him to be on guard against the water of *Acherusia* and the city of *Pandosia*; he believed these were the ones in *Thesprotia*, as *Livy* writes in Book 8 and *Strabo* in Book 6. In Book 7, *Strabo* notes that near Cape *Cheimerium* there is a freshwater port where the *Acheron* enters, having flowed from the *Acherusian* marsh and received several other freshwater rivers which make that port so mild. But in Book 8, he mentions another *Acheron* in *Arcadia* which flows into the river *Alpheus*; it is thought that this was considered an infernal river because the highly revered temples of *Ceres*, *Proserpine*, and *Pluto* <note>The Roman names for the deities of agriculture and the underworld: Demeter, Persephone, and Hades</note> were located there. *Suidas*, after stating that *Acheron* is one of the mythical rivers of Hell, adds this: there is a place so named in the middle of the world where water pours out and rushes back in as far as the marsh of the universe—a dark place, deprived of all light, similar to...

One could well apply this to the visible beatitude—though spiritual—of the blessed; but that is not our current subject.

Regarding Styx and Lethe, even though Philostratus <note>Likely referring to Philostratus the Athenian, author of *Imagines*, which describes ancient paintings.</note> does not include them here, there will be no harm, however, in adding something about them. The Styx, then, if we wish to take it as historical and natural truth, is a fountain near Nonacris in Arcadia, as Pausanias <note>An ancient Greek traveler and geographer; the reference is to his *Description of Greece*.</note> says in the 8th book, where he speaks of it in this manner. The water that flows from this rock out of sight near the ruins of Nonacris first falls into another very high rock, which it penetrates, and from there falls into the river Crathis. It is deadly both to men and to all kinds of animals: and it is said that the first test made of it was on goats, which having once tasted it expired immediately: which by succession of time was afterwards perceived by enough other experiences. There is also in this water some kind of admirable occult <note>In this context, "occult" refers to hidden natural properties or "mysteries" of science rather than magic.</note> property: for neither crystal nor glass, nor porcelain, nor any pottery works, whatever they may be, could resist its violence even a little without breaking instantly:

# NEOPTOLEMUS.

...thought that from then on it would be the most respected oath of the Gods: <note>original Greek: "αὐτὴν μὲν γὰρ ἔθηκε θεῶν μέγα ἔμμεναι ὅρκον," from Hesiod’s Theogony.</note> *for he made her to be the great oath of the gods.* And Servius, commenting on the 6th book of the *Aeneid*: <note>original Latin: "Stygiámque paludem, Dii cuius iurare timent, & fallere numen."</note> *the Stygian marsh, by whose divinity the Gods fear to swear and deceive:* he writes that it was in favor of Victory, daughter of this same Styx, who was present at the war against the Giants, that Jupiter ordained that whichever of the Gods should break what he had sworn and promised by her, he would be deprived for an entire year and nine days of his distribution of Ambrosia and Nectar <note>The food and drink of the gods that granted immortality.</note>: the reason, he says, is because sadness—which this word Styx denotes <note>The name Styx is derived from the Greek word *stygein*, meaning "to hate" or "abhor," often associated with gloom or sorrow.</note>—is contrary to eternity, and joy to misery.

Lethe, another infernal river; once passed, souls would entirely forget all that had happened in their lives; likewise, this word signifies nothing other than forgetfulness. But whether souls, after the passing of persons, forget or remember their past life, is a doubtful point in our belief; for in the 3rd book of Kings <note>Known as 1 Kings in modern Bibles.</note> chapter 21, King Ahab <note>The text says "Achaz," but the biblical reference in 1 Kings 21 describes King Ahab.</note> having humbled himself before God and performed penance, He grants him this grace: that he will not see in his days the evils He had decided to send upon his house, but instead postpones them for Ahaziah <note>Ochosias</note> his son, after his death, so that he [Ahab] might not feel them. And on the contrary, in Saint Luke chapter 16, the bad rich man <note>Often referred to as Dives in the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus.</note> being tormented in hell, asks Abraham to please warn his brothers of his misery, so as not to incur his damnation; but let us leave that to the Theologians. Plato in the 10th book of his *Republic*, and Plutarch in the treatise *On the Tardy Divine Vengeance*, in the accounts they introduce of two who returned from death to life, make mention of this Lethe. As for historical truth, there have been several rivers of that name in various places, of which Strabo speaks in books 10, 11, and 19; but the one most relevant here is the Lethe of Africa, near the final point of the Syrtes <note>The Gulf of Sidra, off the coast of Libya, known for its dangerous shallows.</note>: which, after having flowed for some distance, is swallowed into the earth, and again, I know not how many leagues from there, comes to be reborn as a great quantity of water; which would have made the people believe that it had to pass through the underworld, and from there returned to the surface.
